options: Prepare for intubation because the son is the next of kin.
Ask the son to sign a form overriding the living will.
Call the rapid response team to intubate while the ethics committee reviews the case.
Follow the advance directive, provide comfort measures, and ask the provider to meet with the son.
rationales: A family member's wishes do not override a competent client's valid advance directive.
No such form exists; family members cannot cancel a client's legally valid advance directive.
Intubating would violate the client's documented wishes and the existing prescription.

The nurse advocates for the client's documented wishes, keeps the client comfortable, and supports the family by arranging a discussion with the provider (and an ethics consult if conflict continues).
takeaway: A valid advance directive reflects the client's autonomy and is followed even when family members disagree.

stem: A caller says he is a client's brother and asks how the client is doing after surgery. What should the nurse do first?
options: Check whether the client has authorized release of information to this person.
Give a brief update because family members are entitled to health information.
Tell the caller the client's diagnosis but not the test results.
Ask the caller for the client's date of birth to prove the relationship, then give an update.
rationales: Under HIPAA, health information is shared only with people the client has authorized (for example, through a listed contact or privacy code).
Being a relative does not by itself give a person the right to a client's health information.
A diagnosis is protected health information and cannot be shared without authorization.
Knowing a date of birth does not prove the client has authorized disclosure to the caller.
takeaway: HIPAA: share health information only with people the client has authorized, and verify before you speak.

stem: A nurse tells a client, "I will be back in 15 minutes to help you walk," and returns on time even though the unit has become very busy. Which ethical principle is the nurse demonstrating?
options: Autonomy
Fidelity
Justice
Veracity
rationales: Autonomy is respecting the client's right to make their own decisions.
Fidelity means keeping promises and being faithful to commitments made to the client.
Justice is fair and equal distribution of care and resources.
Veracity is telling the truth.
takeaway: Fidelity = keeping promises; veracity = truthfulness; autonomy = self-determination; justice = fairness; beneficence = doing good; nonmaleficence = doing no harm.

stem: Which situation best illustrates nursing malpractice?
options: A visitor slips on a wet hallway floor and sprains an ankle.
A nurse gives a scheduled medication 45 minutes late, and the client has no adverse effects.
A nurse documents an assessment 2 hours after completing it, with no effect on the client's care.
An RN skips prescribed hourly dressing checks for 8 hours, and the client hemorrhages and needs a transfusion.
rationales: This may be ordinary negligence by the facility, but it does not involve a professional duty owed by a nurse to a client.
Even if this is a breach of the standard of care, there is no harm, so the elements of malpractice are not met.
Late documentation without harm does not meet the elements of malpractice.
This meets all four elements of malpractice: a professional duty, breach of the standard of care, causation, and actual harm to the client.
takeaway: Malpractice is professional negligence and requires duty, breach, causation, and damages; negligence can be committed by anyone.

stem: At the start of a shift, a nurse notices that a coworker has slurred speech, an unsteady gait, and smells of alcohol. What is the nurse's best action?
options: Talk with the coworker privately after the shift.
Report the observations immediately to the charge nurse or nursing supervisor.
Report the coworker directly to the state board of nursing before telling anyone at the facility.
Offer to take the coworker's highest-risk clients and watch for errors.
rationales: Waiting until after the shift leaves clients in the care of an impaired nurse.
Client safety comes first; reporting through the chain of command immediately gets the coworker removed from client care, and the facility follows its policy for further reporting and referral.
Board reporting may be required later, but it does not remove the coworker from client care right now.
This enables the impaired coworker and still exposes clients to unsafe care.
takeaway: Suspected impairment on duty is reported immediately to the supervisor so the nurse is removed from client care.

stem: The nurse receives report on four clients on a surgical unit. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with type 2 diabetes whose blood glucose is 196 mg/dL before lunch.
A client 1 day after appendectomy who rates pain 6/10; the last opioid dose was 4 hours ago.
A client 2 days after total hip arthroplasty with sudden shortness of breath and sharp chest pain; HR 118/min, SpO2 89% on room air.
A client with COPD whose SpO2 is 90% on 2 L/min oxygen by nasal cannula, which is the client's baseline.
rationales: The glucose is high but not dangerous. The nurse can give prescribed correction insulin after seeing the unstable client.
Pain needs treatment soon, but it is expected after surgery and is not life-threatening.
Correct. Sudden dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia, and hypoxia after hip surgery suggest pulmonary embolism, an acute breathing and circulation emergency.
An SpO2 of 88–92% is often the target in COPD. This finding is stable and expected for this client.
takeaway: See first the client with a new, acute change in airway, breathing, or circulation, not the client with an expected or stable finding.

stem: A nurse on a pediatric unit receives report on four children. Which child should the nurse see first?
options: An 8-year-old in sickle cell crisis who rates pain 7/10; a morphine PCA was started 1 hour ago.
A 4-year-old with sudden high fever who is drooling, sitting upright leaning forward, and has a muffled voice.
A 6-year-old with asthma whose peak flow is 85% of personal best.
A 2-year-old with gastroenteritis whose last wet diaper was 4 hours ago and whose mucous membranes are moist.
rationales: Pain control is important, and treatment has started. This child's airway is not at risk.
Correct. These are signs of epiglottitis, which can cause complete airway obstruction at any moment. Airway comes first.
A peak flow above 80% of personal best is in the green zone, so the asthma is controlled.
These findings show adequate hydration. The child needs monitoring, not urgent care.
takeaway: In children, signs of a threatened airway (drooling, tripod position, muffled voice, stridor) take priority over all other problems.

stem: The RN is working with an experienced unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) on a medical unit. Which tasks can the RN delegate to the UAP? Select all that apply.
options: Measure and record vital signs for a client with pneumonia who is stable.
Help a stable client who is 2 days after surgery walk in the hallway.
Teach a client how to use an incentive spirometer for the first time.
Record intake and output for a client with heart failure.
Assess the skin of a newly admitted client who is at risk for pressure injury.
Feed a client who had a stroke yesterday and has difficulty swallowing.
rationales: Correct. Routine vital signs on a stable client are a standard, predictable task within UAP training.
Correct. Ambulating a stable client is a routine task with a predictable outcome.
Incorrect. Teaching is an RN responsibility. The UAP may remind the client to use it after the RN has taught.
Correct. Measuring and recording I&O is within UAP scope; the RN interprets the results.
Incorrect. Assessment, especially on admission, cannot be delegated to a UAP.
Incorrect. This client is at high risk for aspiration, so the outcome is not predictable. A licensed nurse should feed or supervise closely.
takeaway: Delegate to UAP only routine tasks with predictable outcomes on stable clients; never delegate assessment, teaching, evaluation, or care of unstable clients.

stem: The RN is working with a licensed practical nurse (LPN) on a medical unit. Which task is most appropriate to assign to the LPN?
options: Give a scheduled subcutaneous dose of enoxaparin to a client with a stable deep vein thrombosis.
Complete the admission assessment for a client with new-onset atrial fibrillation.
Develop a discharge teaching plan for a client newly diagnosed with heart failure.
Monitor a client during the first 15 minutes of a packed red blood cell transfusion.
rationales: Correct. Giving scheduled subcutaneous medications to a stable client is within LPN scope of practice.
The initial admission assessment is an RN responsibility. The LPN can collect data but not do the full initial assessment.
Planning care and creating a teaching plan are RN responsibilities. The LPN can reinforce teaching.
The first 15 minutes carry the highest risk of a transfusion reaction. This client is potentially unstable and needs RN assessment.
takeaway: LPNs can care for stable clients with predictable outcomes, including most medications; RNs keep initial assessment, care planning, initial teaching, and unstable clients.

stem: The RN watches a UAP measure the blood pressure of a client with a large upper arm. The UAP uses a standard adult cuff that does not fully wrap around the arm and records 152/94 mm Hg. What should the RN do?
options: Accept the reading because the UAP has been trained to take blood pressures.
Ask the UAP to repeat the measurement now with a large adult cuff and explain why cuff size matters.
Report the UAP to the nurse manager for unsafe practice.
Take all remaining blood pressures on the unit for the rest of the shift.
rationales: A cuff that is too small gives a falsely high reading. The RN is responsible for the accuracy of delegated tasks.
Correct. Supervision includes correcting errors right away and teaching, so the UAP performs the task correctly in the future.
This is a learning issue, not misconduct. The RN should correct and teach first; reporting is for repeated or serious problems.
This is not realistic and does not fix the UAP's knowledge gap.
takeaway: The RN stays accountable for delegated tasks: supervise, correct mistakes promptly, and teach.

stem: The charge nurse is making client assignments. Which pair of clients is safest to assign to the same RN?
options: A client with neutropenia from chemotherapy and a client with Clostridioides difficile diarrhea.
A client with herpes zoster (shingles) and a client taking immunosuppressants after a kidney transplant.
A client with diabetic ketoacidosis on an insulin infusion and a client with a new tracheostomy who needs frequent suctioning.
A client 2 days after laparoscopic cholecystectomy and a client with chronic heart failure who is waiting for discharge teaching.
rationales: The neutropenic client is at high risk of infection and should not share a nurse with a client who has an easily spread infection.
Shingles can spread varicella virus to an immunosuppressed client, causing serious illness.
Both clients are unstable and need frequent, intensive care. One nurse could not safely meet both needs.
Correct. Both clients are stable, and neither creates an infection risk for the other.
takeaway: When making assignments, balance acuity and never pair a client with a contagious infection with an immunocompromised client.

stem: A nurse calls the provider about a client who had surgery this morning. Place the nurse's statements in the correct SBAR order.
options: "I would like you to come see her now. Do you want a hemoglobin level drawn?"
"I am calling about Ms. Lee in room 12. Her blood pressure is 86/50 mm Hg and her heart rate is 124/min."
"Her dressing is soaked with blood, and I think she may be bleeding."
"She had a bowel resection this morning and takes metoprolol at home."
rationales: Recommendation comes last: what the nurse wants the provider to do.
Situation comes first: who the client is and what the problem is right now.
Assessment is third: the nurse's findings and interpretation of the problem.
Background is second: history that helps explain the situation. A beta blocker such as metoprolol can blunt the heart rate response, so blood loss may be worse than the heart rate suggests.
takeaway: SBAR = Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation; it gives clear, complete communication during calls and handoffs.

stem: A client is admitted to the hospital for elective knee surgery. Under the federal Patient Self-Determination Act, what is the nurse's responsibility regarding advance directives?
options: Require the client to complete an advance directive before surgery.
Tell the client that a do-not-resuscitate order is written automatically if there is no advance directive.
Have the client's lawyer review any advance directive before it is placed in the chart.
Ask whether the client has an advance directive and give written information about the right to make one.
rationales: Advance directives are voluntary. Care cannot depend on whether a client has one.
This is false. Without a directive or DNR order, full resuscitation is the default.
A lawyer is not required for an advance directive to be valid or placed in the record.
Correct. The law requires facilities to ask on admission and provide information about the client's right to make health care decisions.
takeaway: On admission, ask every client about advance directives and provide information; completing one is always the client's choice.

stem: A client with heart failure named her son as her agent in a durable power of attorney for health care. The client is alert, oriented, and able to make decisions. She refuses a cardiac catheterization, but her son insists it be done. What should the nurse do?
options: Support the client's decision and inform the provider that she refuses the procedure.
Follow the son's wishes because he is the legal health care agent.
Ask the ethics committee to decide between the client and her son.
Begin preparing the client for the procedure while the family talks.
rationales: Correct. A competent adult has the right to refuse treatment, even if the agent disagrees.
The agent's authority begins only when the client cannot make her own decisions. This client still has decision-making capacity.
There is no legal conflict to resolve. A competent client's decision stands.
Preparing a client for a procedure she has refused violates her autonomy.
takeaway: A health care agent decides only when the client lacks capacity; a competent client always speaks for herself.

stem: A client is scheduled for an elective cholecystectomy this afternoon. The surgeon explained the procedure, but the consent form is not signed. Twenty minutes ago the client received morphine 4 mg IV for abdominal pain. What should the nurse do?
options: Notify the surgeon that the client received an opioid so consent can be obtained after the drug's effects wear off.
Ask the client's spouse to sign the consent form instead.
Have the client sign the form now while the pain is controlled.
Witness the client's signature and document that morphine was given.
rationales: Correct. Consent must be given by a client who is alert and able to understand. The surgeon is responsible for obtaining it.
The client is a competent adult and the surgery is not an emergency, so the client must give consent.
Consent given while under the effects of an opioid may not be valid, because judgment can be impaired.
Documenting the drug does not make the consent valid. The nurse should not witness consent from a sedated client.
takeaway: Do not obtain or witness consent from a client affected by opioids or sedatives unless it is an emergency.

stem: Which conditions are required for a client's informed consent to be valid? Select all that apply.
options: The client is an adult or emancipated minor and is mentally competent.
The provider explained the procedure, its risks, benefits, and alternatives.
The client agreed freely, without pressure or threats.
The nurse explained the risks of the procedure in detail.
The client was told that he or she may refuse or withdraw consent at any time.
A family member co-signed the consent form.
rationales: Correct. The person giving consent must have legal and mental capacity.
Correct. Full disclosure by the person doing the procedure is required.
Correct. Consent must be voluntary.
Incorrect. Explaining risks is the provider's duty. The nurse confirms understanding and witnesses the signature.
Correct. The client must know that consent is voluntary and can be withdrawn, even after signing.
Incorrect. A competent adult does not need a family member's signature.
takeaway: Valid consent needs a competent client, full disclosure by the provider, voluntary agreement, and the right to withdraw.

stem: An unconscious adult is brought to the emergency department after a car crash with signs of internal bleeding: BP 74/40 mm Hg, HR 136/min. No family can be reached. The surgeon plans emergency surgery. Which statement about consent is correct?
options: Surgery must wait until a family member is found to sign the consent.
Two nurses may sign the consent form for the client.
A court order must be obtained before surgery.
Surgery may proceed under implied (emergency) consent; the team documents the emergency and attempts to reach family.
rationales: Delay could cause death. The law does not require waiting in a life-threatening emergency.
Nurses cannot give consent for a client. The emergency exception is applied and documented by the provider.
A court order is too slow and is not needed in an emergency.
Correct. When delay would threaten life and the client cannot consent, consent is implied.
takeaway: In a life-threatening emergency, when the client cannot consent and no surrogate is available, consent is implied.

stem: A client admitted with pneumonia says, "I am leaving now. I don't want to stay here." The client is alert and oriented. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Notify the provider.
Explain the possible risks of leaving before treatment is complete.
Ask the client to sign a form for leaving against medical advice (AMA).
Tell the client that insurance will not pay for the stay if they leave.
Stand in front of the door so the client cannot leave.
Remove the peripheral IV catheter before the client leaves.
rationales: Correct. The provider should know and may want to talk with the client about the risks.
Correct. The client needs this information to make an informed choice.
Correct. The form records that the client was told the risks. If the client refuses to sign, the nurse documents that.
Incorrect. This is usually untrue and is a form of pressure, not information.
Incorrect. Keeping a competent adult from leaving is false imprisonment.
Correct. Leaving with an IV catheter in place is a risk for infection, bleeding, and misuse.
takeaway: A competent adult may leave AMA: inform the provider, explain risks, request the AMA form, remove lines, and document; never restrain or threaten.

stem: A client with schizophrenia who was admitted voluntarily refuses the scheduled oral dose of risperidone, saying, "It makes me feel slow." The client is calm. What is the nurse's best action?
options: Respect the refusal, explore the client's concerns, notify the provider, and document.
Tell the client that refusing will lead to involuntary commitment.
Mix the medication into applesauce without telling the client.
Ask security to help give the dose as an intramuscular injection.
rationales: Correct. Clients keep the right to refuse treatment. The side effect concern can be reported so the provider can adjust therapy.
This is a threat (coercion) and is not true for a calm client who is not a danger to self or others.
Hiding medication deceives the client and violates the right to refuse. It may be considered battery.
Forced medication is only allowed in an emergency (danger to self or others) or with a court order.
takeaway: Psychiatric clients keep the right to refuse medication unless there is an emergency or a court order; never hide medication.

stem: The nurse is caring for a client in soft wrist restraints. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Make sure there is a time-limited prescription from the provider.
Accept a PRN (as-needed) restraint prescription.
Tie the restraint to the bed frame, not to the side rail.
Release one restraint at a time and check circulation, skin, and range of motion at the intervals set by facility policy (commonly at least every 2 hours).
Document less-restrictive measures that were tried before restraints were used.
Use a tight square knot so the client cannot untie it.
rationales: Correct. Restraints need a prescription that is renewed at set times based on the client's condition.
Incorrect. PRN prescriptions for restraints are never allowed.
Correct. Tying to a side rail can injure the client when the rail is lowered.
Correct. Regular release and checks, at the frequency required by policy, prevent injury to skin, nerves, and joints.
Correct. Restraints are a last resort, and the record must show alternatives were tried.
Incorrect. A quick-release knot must be used so the client can be freed quickly in an emergency.
takeaway: Restraints are a last resort: time-limited prescription (never PRN), quick-release knot to the frame, frequent checks, and documentation.

stem: The charge nurse observes four nurses. Which nurse's action breaks client confidentiality and needs the charge nurse to step in?
options: A nurse discusses a client's discharge needs with the case manager in a private office.
A nurse sends discharge records to the home health agency the client chose.
A nurse leaves a client's electronic health record open on a hallway computer while answering a call light.
A nurse gives bedside handoff report in a private room with the client's permission.
rationales: Sharing information with team members involved in care, in a private place, is allowed.
Sharing information for continuing treatment is allowed under HIPAA.
Correct. Anyone walking by can see protected health information. The nurse must log off or lock the screen.
Bedside report with the client's permission supports safety and client involvement.
takeaway: Always lock or log off the computer when you step away; open records in public areas breach confidentiality.

stem: A client who was just diagnosed with HIV tells the nurse, "Please do not tell my wife." What is the nurse's best response?
options: "I must tell your wife today because she is at risk."
"Your diagnosis will be kept secret from everyone, including the health department."
"Your wife will find out from her doctor anyway."
"Your diagnosis is confidential. Telling your wife protects her health, and the health department can help notify partners without using your name."
rationales: The nurse does not disclose a client's diagnosis to family. Partner notification is done by the client, the provider, or public health.
This is false. HIV is a reportable disease, and the health department must be notified.
This is not true and does not help the client make a decision.
Correct. This respects confidentiality, gives honest information, and offers partner services that protect the wife.
takeaway: Keep HIV status confidential from family, report it to public health as required, and encourage disclosure through partner notification services.

stem: A client is in the hospital. With whom may the nurse share the client's health information without the client's written permission? Select all that apply.
options: The respiratory therapist who is treating the client.
The client's employer, who calls to ask when the client can return to work.
The state health department, for a reportable disease.
The home health nurse who will care for the client after discharge.
A nurse from another unit who is the client's neighbor and asks how the client is doing.
The client's adult son, after the client asked that no information be given to family.
rationales: Correct. HIPAA allows sharing with health care team members for treatment.
Incorrect. Employers are not entitled to health information without the client's authorization.
Correct. Public health reporting required by law does not need the client's permission.
Correct. Sharing information for continuing treatment is allowed.
Incorrect. This nurse is not involved in care, so access is not allowed.
Incorrect. The client's request must be respected.
takeaway: Without authorization, share health information only for treatment, payment, operations, or legally required reporting; use the minimum necessary.

stem: At 1400, the nurse realizes that an oral oxycodone dose given to a client at 1000 was never documented. What should the nurse do?
options: Write the entry with a time of 1000 so the record looks complete.
Complete an incident report instead of documenting the dose.
Tell the next nurse verbally and leave the record as it is.
Add a late entry with the current date and time, labeled "late entry," stating the dose was given at 1000.
rationales: Back-dating an entry makes the record false. Entries must show when they were actually written.
The dose must be in the medical record. An incident report does not replace charting.
Verbal reports do not replace documentation. Another nurse could give a second dose by mistake.
Correct. A clearly labeled late entry keeps the record accurate and prevents a repeat dose.
takeaway: Document a missed entry as a labeled late entry with the current time; never back-date or alter records.

stem: A client falls in the bathroom. The nurse is guiding a new nurse through the follow-up. Which statement by the new nurse shows a need for more teaching?
options: "I will assess the client for injury and notify the provider."
"I will write in the progress note that I completed an incident report."
"I will describe only the facts in the incident report, without blame."
"Incident reports are used to improve safety, not to punish staff."
rationales: This is correct. Client safety and assessment come first after a fall.
Correct answer (needs teaching). The incident report is a confidential quality document; mentioning it in the chart can make it available in a lawsuit.
This is correct. Incident reports should be objective and factual.
This is correct. They help find and fix system problems.
takeaway: Document the event and the client's condition in the chart, but never mention the incident report itself.

stem: An 82-year-old client with mild dementia comes to the clinic with her son. The nurse sees bruises in different stages of healing on both upper arms. The son answers every question for her. What should the nurse do first?
options: Interview the client alone, away from her son.
Ask the son to explain how the bruises happened.
Call the police to report assault.
Document that the bruises are a normal part of aging.
rationales: Correct. A private interview lets the client speak freely, and it gives the nurse information needed to report to Adult Protective Services.
The son may be the abuser. Asking him first can put the client at more risk and will not give honest information.
The nurse must report suspected abuse, usually to Adult Protective Services, but first gathers information with a private interview.
Bruises in different stages on the upper arms suggest grabbing and are a warning sign of abuse.
takeaway: When you suspect abuse, separate the client from the possible abuser, assess privately, then report as the law requires.

stem: Which situations must the nurse report to an outside agency as required by law? Select all that apply.
options: A 5-year-old with small round burns the size of a cigarette tip.
A client diagnosed with active pulmonary tuberculosis.
A client with type 2 diabetes who does not take the prescribed metformin.
A dependent adult who is left in soiled clothing and is underweight under a caregiver's care.
An adult who smokes one pack of cigarettes a day.
rationales: Correct. Suspected child abuse must be reported to child protective services.
Correct. Tuberculosis is a reportable disease to the public health department.
Incorrect. Not following a treatment plan is the client's right and is not reportable.
Correct. Suspected neglect of a dependent adult must be reported to Adult Protective Services.
Incorrect. Tobacco use is a health teaching issue, not a reportable event.
takeaway: Nurses are mandatory reporters of suspected child, elder, or dependent-adult abuse or neglect and of reportable communicable diseases.

stem: A nurse gave a client the wrong dose of a medication. The client was not harmed. The client asks, "Was something wrong with my medicine?" The nurse honestly tells the client what happened, following facility policy. Which ethical principle is the nurse showing?
options: Beneficence
Justice
Veracity
Autonomy
rationales: Beneficence means doing good for the client. It is not the main principle shown by telling the truth.
Justice means treating people fairly and distributing resources fairly.
Correct. Veracity means telling the truth, including about errors.
Autonomy means respecting the client's right to make their own choices.
takeaway: Veracity is truthfulness; nurses are honest with clients, including about errors.

stem: A nurse has a moral objection to taking part in an elective termination of pregnancy. The nurse sees that she is assigned to care for that client tomorrow. What should the nurse do?
options: Tell the charge nurse ahead of time so the client can be reassigned, and give safe care until another nurse takes over.
Refuse to enter the client's room at the start of the shift.
Explain her personal beliefs to the client.
Call in sick for the shift.
rationales: Correct. Nurses may decline to take part based on conscience, but they must speak up early and must not abandon the client.
Refusing care without a handoff is client abandonment.
Sharing personal moral views with the client is unprofessional and may cause harm.
This is dishonest and leaves the unit short-staffed.
takeaway: A nurse may conscientiously object, but must tell the employer in advance and never abandon a client.

stem: A client with metastatic pancreatic cancer is alert and able to make decisions. He asks the nurse about hospice care. His wife says, "Please don't talk about dying in front of him." What is the nurse's best action?
options: Change the subject to respect the wife's request.
Leave hospice brochures at the bedside without discussing them.
Tell the client he can discuss hospice after he is discharged.
Answer the client's questions and tell the provider he wants to discuss hospice, including his wife if he wishes.
rationales: The client is competent and asked for information. Ignoring him does not respect his autonomy.
This avoids the client's questions and does not arrange the needed discussion with the provider.
This delays care the client is asking for now and does not advocate for him.
Correct. The nurse advocates for the client's wishes while supporting the family.
takeaway: Advocacy means speaking up for the competent client's own wishes, even when family members disagree.

stem: A nurse realizes she gave a client metoprolol 50 mg orally instead of the prescribed 25 mg. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.
options: Document the facts in the medical record: the dose given, the client's condition, and who was notified.
Notify the provider of the error and the client's condition.
Complete an incident (occurrence) report.
Assess the client's heart rate, blood pressure, and level of consciousness.
Carry out the provider's new prescriptions and keep monitoring the client.
rationales: Fourth. The chart records the objective facts after the client is safe and the provider has responded.
Second. The provider needs to know so new orders can be given.
Last. The report is for quality improvement and is done after client care is complete.
First. Client safety comes first; too much metoprolol can cause bradycardia and hypotension.
Third. Follow the provider's instructions, such as more frequent vital signs.
takeaway: After a medication error: assess the client, notify the provider, follow new orders, document facts, then complete the incident report.

stem: During handoff report, the night nurse gives information about a client receiving a continuous heparin infusion for a pulmonary embolism. Which information is most important for the oncoming nurse?
options: The client watched television until midnight.
The client's daughter visited last evening.
The next aPTT is due at 0800, and the infusion rate must be adjusted per protocol based on the result.
The client prefers coffee with breakfast.
rationales: This is not important for safety or treatment.
Useful for psychosocial care but not a priority for the shift.
Correct. Missing the aPTT or rate change can cause bleeding or new clots. Time-sensitive, high-risk information is the priority.
This is a preference, not a safety issue.
takeaway: Handoff must include time-sensitive, high-risk items such as pending labs and medication adjustments.

stem: The intensive care unit (ICU) needs a bed for a new admission. Which ICU client is most appropriate to transfer to the medical-surgical unit?
options: A client receiving a norepinephrine infusion for septic shock; mean arterial pressure 63 mm Hg.
A client with diabetic ketoacidosis on an IV insulin infusion; potassium 3.3 mEq/L.
A client 2 days after a bowel resection with stable vital signs, tolerating clear liquids, and pain controlled with oral medication.
A client with an upper GI bleed whose hemoglobin dropped from 9.8 g/dL to 8.1 g/dL in 6 hours.
rationales: This client needs a vasopressor and close titration, which requires ICU care.
Insulin infusion with low potassium needs frequent lab checks and possible cardiac monitoring in the ICU.
Correct. This client is stable with predictable needs that can be met on a medical-surgical unit.
This client is actively bleeding and may become unstable quickly.
takeaway: Transfer to a lower level of care the client who is stable, with predictable needs and no high-risk infusions.

stem: A client who had a stroke 2 days ago coughs and has a wet, gurgling voice after drinking water. The nurse stops oral intake. Which referral is most appropriate?
options: Occupational therapist
Physical therapist
Speech-language pathologist
Registered dietitian
rationales: Occupational therapy helps with daily activities such as dressing, not swallowing evaluation.
Physical therapy helps with mobility, strength, and gait.
Correct. The speech-language pathologist evaluates swallowing and recommends safe diet textures.
The dietitian plans nutrition but does not perform swallowing evaluations.
takeaway: Signs of dysphagia (coughing, wet voice) mean hold oral intake and refer to a speech-language pathologist.

stem: A 78-year-old client with heart failure is admitted for the third time in 2 months. He lives alone, says he often cannot afford his medications, and has no scale at home. Which referral is the priority?
options: Case manager
Chaplain
Physical therapist
Pharmacist, to teach about furosemide side effects
rationales: Correct. The case manager coordinates resources such as medication assistance, equipment, and home health follow-up to prevent readmission.
Spiritual support may help, but it does not address the cause of his readmissions.
Physical therapy may help strength, but cost of medications and lack of a scale are the main problems.
Teaching is useful, but it will not help if he cannot afford the medications.
takeaway: Frequent readmissions linked to cost, equipment, or living alone call for a case manager to coordinate care across settings.

stem: The nurse is planning discharges. Which clients need a referral to a social worker before discharge? Select all that apply.
options: A client experiencing homelessness who will be discharged with a wound vacuum device.
A client newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes who has no health insurance.
A client who tells the nurse that her partner hits her.
A client after an uncomplicated appendectomy who lives with a supportive spouse.
A client with stable hypertension who has all medications at home and a follow-up appointment scheduled.
rationales: Correct. The client needs safe housing and support to manage the device at home.
Correct. The client needs help getting insulin and supplies he can afford.
Correct. The social worker can help with a safety plan, shelters, and community resources.
Incorrect. This client has no social or financial needs that require a referral.
Incorrect. This client's discharge needs are already met.
takeaway: Refer to social work when housing, finances, insurance, or safety barriers could prevent safe discharge.

stem: The pharmacist calls the nurse and says a client's prescribed enoxaparin dose should be adjusted because the client's creatinine clearance is 25 mL/min. The next dose is due now. What is the nurse's best action?
options: Give the dose as prescribed because the provider wrote the prescription.
Give half of the dose until the provider calls back.
Give the dose the pharmacist recommends.
Hold the dose and contact the provider to clarify the prescription.
rationales: The nurse is responsible for giving safe doses. Reduced kidney function raises the risk of bleeding with enoxaparin.
Changing a dose without a prescription is outside the nurse's scope of practice.
The nurse cannot change a prescription based on the pharmacist's advice alone; the provider must approve it.
Correct. The nurse collaborates with the pharmacist and provider; only the provider can change the prescription.
takeaway: When a team member questions a prescription, hold the dose if unsafe and clarify with the prescriber before giving it.

stem: A client had a colostomy created 1 day ago. Using Maslow's hierarchy of needs, rank the client's problems from highest to lowest priority.
options: Says, "I feel ugly with this bag."
Is unsteady when getting out of bed and is at high risk for falls.
Has an SpO2 of 88% on room air with shallow breathing.
Feels lonely and asks when her family can visit.
rationales: Fourth. Body image is a self-esteem need, which comes after physical, safety, and belonging needs.
Second. Safety needs come right after physiological needs.
First. Oxygenation is a physiological need and the highest priority.
Third. Love and belonging come after physiological and safety needs.
takeaway: Maslow order: physiological (airway, breathing) first, then safety, love and belonging, self-esteem, and self-actualization.

stem: A nurse in a long-term care facility receives reports about four clients. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client with COPD whose SpO2 is 90% on 2 L/min oxygen, unchanged from yesterday.
A client with rheumatoid arthritis who reports 1 hour of joint stiffness this morning.
A client with chronic kidney disease whose potassium is 5.1 mEq/L, the same as last week.
A client with new slurred speech and right arm weakness that began 30 minutes ago.
rationales: This is a stable, chronic finding that is expected for this client.
Morning stiffness is a typical chronic symptom of rheumatoid arthritis.
This is slightly high but stable and expected in chronic kidney disease.
Correct. These are acute signs of stroke. Fast treatment is time-sensitive, so this client is the priority.
takeaway: An acute, new problem takes priority over a chronic, stable one, even if the chronic condition seems serious.

stem: The nurse reviews data on several clients on a surgical unit. Which findings need the nurse's immediate action? Select all that apply.
options: A client 6 hours after thyroidectomy has new high-pitched, noisy breathing (stridor).
A client 1 day after surgery has a temperature of 37.8°C (100.0°F).
A client taking digoxin has a potassium level of 3.0 mEq/L.
A client's urine output has been 20 mL/hr for the past 2 hours.
A client rates incision pain 4/10 and asks for the prescribed PRN analgesic.
A client's dressing shows a small amount of serous drainage.
rationales: Correct. Stridor signals airway obstruction from swelling, bleeding, or low calcium and is an emergency.
Incorrect. A low-grade fever on day 1 is common; the nurse encourages deep breathing and monitors.
Correct. Low potassium increases the risk of digoxin toxicity and dangerous dysrhythmias.
Correct. Output below 30 mL/hr (about 0.5 mL/kg/hr) may mean low blood volume or kidney injury and must be reported.
Incorrect. This needs attention soon but is not an urgent threat compared with the others.
Incorrect. A small amount of serous drainage is expected after surgery.
takeaway: Act first on threats to airway, heart rhythm, and perfusion; expected post-operative findings can wait.

stem: Four clients arrive at the emergency department at the same time. Which client should the triage nurse assign Emergency Severity Index (ESI) level 1?
options: A 58-year-old with chest pressure; BP 148/90 mm Hg, HR 96/min, SpO2 97%
A 24-year-old with hives, wheezing, and swollen lips after a bee sting; BP 78/44 mm Hg
A 40-year-old with right lower abdominal pain and temperature 38.1°C (100.6°F); other vital signs normal
A 30-year-old with a swollen ankle after a twisting injury who can bear weight
rationales: Possible acute coronary syndrome is high risk (ESI 2), but the client is stable and does not need an immediate life-saving intervention.
Correct. Anaphylaxis with hypotension and airway swelling needs immediate life-saving treatment (epinephrine, airway support), which defines ESI 1.
This client is stable but will need two or more resources (labs, imaging, IV fluids), so ESI 3 fits.
This client is stable and needs only one resource (an x-ray), so ESI 4 fits.
takeaway: ESI 1 = the client needs an immediate life-saving intervention right now (airway, emergency medications, or hemodynamic support).

stem: A 35-year-old client comes to the emergency department with a 3-cm forearm cut from a kitchen knife. Bleeding is controlled. BP 124/78 mm Hg, HR 82/min, RR 16/min, SpO2 99%, pain 3/10. The cut needs simple sutures. Which Emergency Severity Index (ESI) level should the nurse assign?
options: ESI 2
ESI 3
ESI 4
ESI 5
rationales: ESI 2 is for high-risk situations, new confusion, or severe pain or distress. This client is stable with mild pain.
ESI 3 is for stable clients who need two or more resources. Simple suturing counts as only one resource.
Correct. A stable client who needs exactly one resource (simple laceration repair) is ESI 4.
ESI 5 is for clients who need no resources, such as a prescription refill. Suturing is a resource.
takeaway: For stable clients, ESI is decided by the number of expected resources: none = ESI 5, one = ESI 4, two or more = ESI 3.

stem: The emergency department triage nurse uses the Emergency Severity Index (ESI) algorithm. Which clients meet the criteria for ESI level 2? Select all that apply.
options: A 70-year-old with new confusion that started this morning
A 45-year-old with flank pain rated 9/10 who is pale and sweating
A 52-year-old with substernal chest pain and stable vital signs
A 28-year-old with a sore throat who needs only a throat swab
A 19-year-old who is not breathing and needs bag-valve-mask ventilation
A 33-year-old who needs a refill of blood pressure medication
rationales: Correct. New-onset confusion or lethargy is a high-risk finding that makes the client ESI 2.
Correct. Severe pain or distress is an ESI 2 criterion.
Correct. Chest pain that could be acute coronary syndrome is a high-risk situation, so the client should not wait (ESI 2).
A stable client who needs one resource (a lab test) is ESI 4.
A client who needs an immediate life-saving intervention is ESI 1, not ESI 2.
A client who needs no resources is ESI 5.
takeaway: ESI 2 = high-risk situation, new confusion/lethargy/disorientation, or severe pain or distress; the client should not wait.

stem: At a mass-casualty scene, the nurse uses START triage. An adult victim is lying still and is not breathing. The nurse opens the airway with a head-tilt chin-lift, and the victim still does not breathe. Which tag should the nurse assign?
options: Red (immediate)
Yellow (delayed)
Green (minor)
Black (expectant/deceased)
rationales: Red is used if the victim starts breathing after the airway is opened. This victim did not.
Yellow is for victims who cannot walk but have normal breathing, perfusion, and mental status.
Green is for victims who can walk.
Correct. In START, an adult who does not breathe after airway repositioning is tagged black and the rescuer moves on.
takeaway: START: no breathing after opening the airway = black; breathing starts after opening the airway = red.

stem: During a mass-casualty incident, the nurse uses START triage on an adult victim who cannot walk. RR 24/min, radial pulse present, capillary refill less than 2 seconds. When the nurse says, "Squeeze my hand," the victim does not respond. Which tag should the nurse assign?
options: Green (minor)
Yellow (delayed)
Red (immediate)
Black (expectant/deceased)
rationales: Green is only for victims who can walk.
Yellow requires that the victim can follow simple commands. This victim cannot.
Correct. Breathing and perfusion are adequate, but inability to follow simple commands makes the victim red (immediate).
Black is for victims who do not breathe after the airway is opened. This victim is breathing.
takeaway: START checks RPM in order: Respirations (over 30 = red), Perfusion (no radial pulse or refill over 2 seconds = red), Mental status (cannot follow commands = red).

stem: The nurse is using START triage at a bus crash. Which victim should the nurse tag yellow (delayed)?
options: A victim who walks to the treatment area with a bleeding cut on the arm
A victim who cannot walk because of an open leg fracture; RR 22/min, radial pulse present, follows commands
A victim who cannot walk and has RR 36/min
A victim who cannot walk, has RR 20/min, and has no radial pulse
rationales: Any victim who can walk is tagged green (minor) first and is reassessed later.
Correct. The victim cannot walk, but respirations, perfusion, and mental status are all within START limits, so the tag is yellow.
A respiratory rate over 30/min is tagged red (immediate).
An absent radial pulse (poor perfusion) is tagged red (immediate).
takeaway: START yellow = cannot walk, but RR 30/min or less, radial pulse present, and follows simple commands.

stem: A hospital activates its disaster plan after a train crash and needs inpatient beds quickly. The charge nurse on a medical-surgical unit reviews four clients. Which client is most appropriate to discharge early?
options: A client 1 day after laparoscopic cholecystectomy who is eating, walking, and has pain controlled with oral medication
A client admitted 12 hours ago with pneumonia; temperature 39°C (102.2°F), SpO2 91% on 3 L/min oxygen
A client with diabetic ketoacidosis who was taken off an insulin infusion 2 hours ago
A client with new atrial fibrillation, HR 132/min, receiving a diltiazem infusion
rationales: Correct. This client is stable, has met discharge goals, and can safely continue recovery at home.
This client is febrile and hypoxemic and still needs inpatient care.
This client is in an early, unstable transition and needs close glucose and electrolyte monitoring.
This client has uncontrolled heart rate and a titrated IV infusion; this client is not stable for discharge.
takeaway: In a surge, discharge clients who are stable, predictable, and have met discharge goals; keep anyone unstable or on titrated infusions.

stem: The intensive care unit (ICU) needs a bed for an incoming trauma client. Which ICU client is most appropriate to transfer to a lower level of care?
options: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis on an insulin infusion; glucose 280 mg/dL, pH 7.29
A client extubated 2 hours ago after a COPD exacerbation; RR 26/min with accessory muscle use
A client 2 days after a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, chest-pain free for 36 hours, stable on oral medications, no dysrhythmias
A client with an upper GI bleed whose hemoglobin fell from 8.1 to 7.0 g/dL in 4 hours after 2 units of red blood cells
rationales: This client is still acidotic and needs an insulin infusion with hourly glucose checks, which requires ICU-level care.
Signs of increased work of breathing soon after extubation mean the client may need reintubation.
Correct. This client is stable and predictable, with no IV titration needs, and can safely move to a telemetry or step-down unit.
Hemoglobin falling despite transfusion means active bleeding; this client is unstable.
takeaway: Transfer to a lower level of care the client who is stable, predictable, and no longer needs titrated IV drugs or frequent intensive monitoring.

stem: The emergency department nurse is arranging admissions. Which client should the nurse expect to need an intensive care unit (ICU) bed?
options: A client with pneumonia who is alert; SpO2 94% on 2 L/min oxygen
A client with diabetic ketoacidosis; glucose 540 mg/dL, pH 7.10, needs a continuous insulin infusion with hourly glucose checks
A client with leg cellulitis who needs IV antibiotics; vital signs normal
A client with a hip fracture awaiting surgery; vital signs stable, pain controlled
rationales: This client is stable on low-flow oxygen and can be admitted to a medical unit.
Correct. Severe acidosis and a titrated insulin infusion with hourly monitoring need ICU-level care.
This client is stable and can be admitted to a medical-surgical unit.
This client is stable and can wait for surgery on an orthopedic or surgical unit.
takeaway: Clients with severe physiologic instability or titrated continuous infusions with hourly monitoring need an ICU bed.

stem: A client is ready to leave the hospital 5 days after an ischemic stroke with left-sided weakness. Before the stroke the client was independent. Now the client needs help to transfer from bed to chair but can take part in about 3 hours of therapy a day. Which discharge setting is most appropriate?
options: Home alone with outpatient physical therapy twice a week
An acute inpatient rehabilitation facility
Hospice care at home
Long-term custodial care in a nursing home
rationales: The client cannot transfer safely alone, so going home alone with limited therapy is unsafe.
Correct. The client has good rehabilitation potential and can tolerate intensive therapy (about 3 hours a day), which inpatient rehabilitation provides.
Hospice is for clients with a terminal prognosis of 6 months or less. This client is expected to improve.
Custodial care is for clients who need ongoing help without expected improvement. This client can still gain function.
takeaway: Match the discharge setting to the client's needs and rehabilitation potential: intensive therapy tolerated = inpatient rehabilitation.

stem: A 74-year-old client with heart failure is being discharged. The client lives alone, has a low fixed income, does not drive, and says, "Sometimes I skip my pills because they cost too much." Which actions should the nurse include in discharge planning? Select all that apply.
options: Refer the client to the social worker or case manager for medication assistance programs
Arrange home health nursing visits to monitor weight, symptoms, and medications
Refer the client to a home-delivered meal program that offers low-sodium meals
Schedule a follow-up visit within 7 days and arrange transportation
Tell the client to take the medications every other day so they last longer
Delay discharge until the client is able to drive again
rationales: Correct. Cost is causing missed doses; a social worker or case manager can find low-cost options or assistance programs.
Correct. Home health visits help find early signs of worsening heart failure and support medication use.
Correct. Low-sodium meals support heart failure management for a client who lives alone with limited resources.
Correct. Early follow-up (within about 7 days) lowers heart failure readmissions, and the client needs transportation to attend.
Changing the dose without a prescription is unsafe and outside nursing scope; it could cause heart failure to worsen.
Driving is not a discharge criterion; transportation can be arranged through community resources.
takeaway: Discharge planning addresses the barriers the client actually has (cost, transportation, food, monitoring) with referrals to community resources.

stem: The daughter of a client with end-stage lung cancer asks the nurse about hospice. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
options: "Your mother must sign a do-not-resuscitate form before she can receive hospice."
"Hospice is for people whose provider expects a life of 6 months or less if the illness follows its usual course."
"Once she starts hospice, she can never go back to treatment aimed at a cure."
"Hospice care is only provided in a hospital or an inpatient unit."
rationales: Medicare hospice rules do not require a do-not-resuscitate order to enroll.
Correct. Hospice eligibility requires a provider to certify a prognosis of 6 months or less if the disease runs its normal course.
A client may leave (revoke) hospice at any time and return to curative treatment.
Most hospice care is given where the client lives, such as at home or in a nursing home.
takeaway: Hospice = prognosis of 6 months or less, focus on comfort; the client can leave hospice at any time and no DNR is required to enroll.

stem: After a wrong-site surgery, the hospital performs a root cause analysis (RCA). Which statement by the nurse manager best describes the purpose of the RCA?
options: "We need to find out who made the error so they can be disciplined."
"We need to find the system and process failures that allowed this to happen, so we can fix them."
"We need to decide how much money the hospital should pay the client."
"We need to decide which nurse to report to the state board of nursing."
rationales: RCA is not designed to blame individuals; a blame focus discourages staff from reporting errors.
Correct. RCA looks for underlying system causes of a sentinel event and creates an action plan to prevent it from happening again.
Financial settlement is a risk management and legal issue, not the purpose of an RCA.
Board reporting is a separate process. RCA focuses on systems, not on punishing individuals.
takeaway: Root cause analysis looks for system and process causes of an adverse or sentinel event, not for someone to blame.

stem: Pharmacy sends a hydromorphone 10 mg/mL vial instead of the usual 1 mg/mL vial for a client prescribed hydromorphone 1 mg IV. The nurse notices the error before giving the drug, and the client is not harmed. After returning the vial to pharmacy, what should the nurse do?
options: Complete a safety event (incident) report describing the near miss
Take no further action because the client was not harmed
Write in the client's medical record that an incident report was completed
Ask the client to sign the incident report as a witness
rationales: Correct. Near misses should be reported so the organization can find and fix the system problem before a client is harmed.
Near misses show weak points in the system; not reporting them lets the same error reach a client later.
Incident reports are confidential quality documents and should not be mentioned in the client's record.
Clients do not sign incident reports; the report is completed by staff who saw or found the event.
takeaway: Report near misses just like errors that reach the client, and never mention the incident report in the medical record.

stem: The nurse is part of a unit team working to prevent central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSI). Which actions are part of evidence-based CLABSI prevention? Select all that apply.
options: Perform hand hygiene before touching the catheter or dressing
Scrub the needleless connector with an antiseptic before each access
Review the need for the central line every day and remove it promptly when it is no longer needed
Replace the central line routinely every 7 days
Apply antibiotic ointment to the insertion site at each dressing change
Change a transparent dressing if it becomes damp, loose, or soiled
rationales: Correct. Hand hygiene is the first step of every central line bundle.
Correct. "Scrub the hub" removes organisms that can enter the bloodstream through the catheter.
Correct. Infection risk rises each day the line stays in, so daily review of necessity is part of the bundle.
Routine replacement of central lines is not recommended; it adds insertion risk without reducing infection.
Topical antibiotic ointment is not recommended for most central lines because it can promote fungal infection and resistance.
Correct. A dressing that is not intact cannot protect the site and must be changed right away.
takeaway: CLABSI bundle: hand hygiene, chlorhexidine skin antisepsis, sterile barriers at insertion, scrub the hub, intact dressing, daily review of line need.

stem: The nurse observes an unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) caring for a client with an indwelling urinary catheter. Which action by the UAP requires the nurse to intervene?
options: Cleans the perineum and the catheter near the meatus with soap and water during daily hygiene
Keeps the tubing free of kinks and the bag below the level of the bladder
Disconnects the catheter from the drainage tubing to collect a urine specimen
Empties the drainage bag into a clean container used only for this client
rationales: Routine cleaning with soap and water is the correct way to care for the meatal area.
Unobstructed flow and keeping the bag below the bladder prevent urine backflow and infection.
Correct. Breaking the closed drainage system lets bacteria enter; specimens are taken from the sampling port with a sterile syringe.
Using a separate clean container for each client prevents cross-contamination.
takeaway: CAUTI prevention: keep the drainage system closed, the bag below the bladder, flow unobstructed, and remove the catheter as soon as it is not needed.

stem: The unit's quality improvement team uses the Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) model to reduce client falls. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Compare the fall rates before and after the change
Review fall data, set a goal, and design a change such as hourly purposeful rounding
Adopt the change on all units if falls decreased, or revise it and test again
Test hourly rounding on one unit for 6 weeks
rationales: Third (Study): the team checks the results of the test against the goal.
First (Plan): the team studies the problem and plans a specific change and how it will be measured.
Fourth (Act): the team spreads a successful change or adjusts it and begins a new cycle.
Second (Do): the change is tried on a small scale and data are collected.
takeaway: PDSA = Plan the change, Do a small test, Study the results, Act to adopt, adapt, or abandon.

stem: A nurse realizes she entered a pain assessment in the wrong client's electronic health record (EHR). What should the nurse do?
options: Delete the entry so the wrong information does not stay in the record
Follow facility policy to mark the entry as "entered in error," then document the assessment in the correct client's record
Ask a coworker with administrator access to remove the entry
Leave the entry as it is and only document in the correct client's record
rationales: Entries in a legal record must not be deleted; the original must remain traceable.
Correct. The EHR error-correction process keeps an audit trail while showing the entry is wrong, and the correct client still needs documentation.
Removing entries with someone else's access is improper and hides the change from the audit trail.
Leaving wrong data uncorrected in a client's record can lead to unsafe care decisions.
takeaway: Correct EHR errors with the facility's "entered in error" process; never delete or hide an entry.

stem: The nurse is giving medications using the electronic health record (EHR) and barcode medication administration (BCMA). Which actions show safe use of this technology? Select all that apply.
options: Scan the client's wristband and each medication at the bedside before giving it
Read the reason for an alert and resolve it before choosing to override
Scan medications for several clients at the medication cart and then give them
Copy yesterday's assessment note forward without changes to save time
Document medications and assessments after they are done, not before
Use a coworker's login when your own login is locked out
rationales: Correct. Scanning at the bedside confirms the right client and right drug at the point of care.
Correct. Alerts can signal a real error; overriding without review defeats the safety system.
Scanning away from the bedside skips the client check and is a known workaround that causes errors.
Copy-forward can record findings that are no longer true; each assessment must reflect current data.
Correct. Documenting before care is done is inaccurate and could mislead other staff.
Each user must use only their own login so the record shows who did what; sharing logins is a security violation.
takeaway: Use BCMA at the bedside, take alerts seriously, document only what you did after you did it, and never share logins.

stem: A client takes warfarin daily; this morning's INR is 2.8. A new prescription for sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim is entered, and the EHR shows a "major drug interaction" alert when the nurse scans the antibiotic. What is the nurse's best action?
options: Override the alert because the provider already prescribed the drug
Hold the antibiotic and contact the provider or pharmacist about the interaction before giving it
Give the antibiotic and hold today's warfarin dose
Give the antibiotic and ask for a repeat INR in 1 week
rationales: Overriding a major alert without review ignores the risk; the provider may not have seen the interaction.
Correct. Sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim can greatly increase warfarin's effect and bleeding risk, so the nurse clarifies first.
The nurse cannot independently change the warfarin plan; the provider must decide how to manage the interaction.
Waiting a week could allow a dangerous rise in INR and bleeding.
takeaway: Clinical decision-support alerts are a safety check: stop, review, and clarify with the provider or pharmacist before giving the drug.

stem: Which action by the nurse best shows cost-effective care without lowering safety?
options: Taking a full box of supplies into a contact-precautions room so they are close at hand
Asking the provider whether IV acetaminophen can be changed to oral acetaminophen now that the client is eating and drinking
Opening a sterile dressing kit to remove a peripheral IV catheter
Keeping the client on continuous pulse oximetry after the provider discontinued it, "just in case"
rationales: Unused supplies taken into an isolation room usually must be thrown away, which wastes resources.
Correct. Changing from IV to oral when the client can take oral drugs is equally effective, cheaper, and lowers IV-related risks.
Peripheral IV removal is a clean procedure; a sterile kit adds cost without benefit.
Continuing monitoring that is not prescribed or needed uses equipment and causes alarm fatigue without benefit.
takeaway: Cost-effective care uses the least costly option that is equally safe and effective, such as IV-to-oral conversion when appropriate.

stem: The unit has only one sitter (1:1 observer) available for the shift. Which client should the charge nurse assign the sitter to?
options: A client admitted after an overdose who says, "Next time I'll make sure it works."
An older client with dementia who wanders at night and has a working bed alarm
A client in alcohol withdrawal with a CIWA-Ar score of 6 who is calm
A client who pulls at the nasal cannula when sleepy
rationales: Correct. This client is expressing ongoing suicidal intent and needs constant 1:1 observation for safety.
Wandering risk can be managed with a bed alarm, frequent rounding, and a room near the nurses' station.
A low withdrawal score with a calm client needs routine monitoring, not 1:1 observation.
This can be managed with reorientation, securing the cannula, and checking oxygen saturation.
takeaway: When a resource is limited, give it to the client with the greatest risk of immediate harm, such as active suicidal intent.

stem: A provider writes a discharge prescription for a client 2 days after hip arthroplasty. The client still needs two staff members to walk to the bathroom and lives alone. Vital signs are stable. The nurse has already discussed the safety concern with the provider, who still wants the client discharged home today. What should the nurse do next?
options: Discharge the client as prescribed and document the concern
Notify the charge nurse or nursing supervisor, following the chain of command
Call the hospital's chief executive officer
Tell the client that the provider is making a mistake
rationales: Documentation alone does not protect the client from an unsafe discharge; the nurse must advocate further.
Correct. When a concern is not resolved with the provider, the nurse moves up the chain of command.
This skips several levels of the chain of command and is not the next step.
This damages trust and does not solve the problem; disagreements are handled through proper channels.
takeaway: If a safety concern is not resolved with the provider, go to the next level: charge nurse, then nursing supervisor, then medical leadership.

stem: A nurse tells the charge nurse that a night-shift coworker often leaves IV bags nearly empty and tasks unfinished at shift change. The nurse is becoming frustrated. What should the charge nurse advise first?
options: "Talk privately with your coworker, describe the specific problem, and try to agree on a solution together."
"Report your coworker to the state board of nursing."
"Write down each problem and present the list at the next staff meeting."
"Ask to change shifts so you do not have to follow this nurse."
rationales: Correct. Direct, private, respectful communication between the people involved is the first step in resolving staff conflict.
This is an extreme first step for a work-flow problem that has not been discussed yet.
Raising a personal conflict in public embarrasses the coworker and makes the conflict worse.
Avoidance does not solve the problem, and the unfinished work will still affect clients.
takeaway: Staff conflict is first handled directly and privately between the people involved, using specific facts; escalate only if it is not resolved.

stem: A nurse believes a newly prescribed medication dose is unsafe for a stable client. Place the steps of the chain of command in the correct order.
options: Notify the nursing supervisor if the issue is still not resolved
Hold the medication and discuss the concern with the prescribing provider using SBAR
Notify the charge nurse if the provider does not change the prescription
The supervisor contacts the medical director or chief of the department
rationales: Third: the house or nursing supervisor is the next level above the charge nurse.
First: the nurse goes directly to the prescriber and does not give a dose believed to be unsafe.
Second: the charge nurse is the first step up the nursing chain of command.
Fourth: medical leadership is involved when the issue cannot be resolved at the nursing supervisor level.
takeaway: Chain of command: prescriber, then charge nurse, then nursing supervisor, then medical leadership; never give a drug you believe is unsafe.

stem: An RN leads a team with one licensed practical nurse (LPN) and one unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP). Clients: (1) new admission with a COPD exacerbation, SpO2 89% on 2 L/min; (2) stable client with heart failure and type 2 diabetes who needs oral medications and scheduled subcutaneous insulin; (3) client receiving a first unit of packed red blood cells; (4) stable client 3 days after a stroke who needs help with bathing and walking to the chair. Which assignment is most appropriate?
options: RN: clients 1 and 3; LPN: clients 2 and 4; UAP: hygiene and walking for client 4 and vital signs for client 2
RN: clients 2 and 4; LPN: clients 1 and 3
RN: client 1; LPN: clients 3 and 4; UAP: client 2
RN: clients 3 and 4; LPN: clients 1 and 2
rationales: Correct. The RN takes the unstable new admission and the transfusion; the LPN takes stable clients with predictable care; the UAP does routine tasks for stable clients.
The unstable new admission needs RN assessment, and transfusion monitoring is RN responsibility in most facilities.
A UAP cannot be assigned a client who needs medications, and the transfusion should stay with the RN.
The LPN should not receive an unstable client who needs a full admission assessment.
takeaway: RN = unstable, new, or complex clients and initial assessments; LPN = stable clients with predictable outcomes; UAP = routine tasks for stable clients.

stem: The RN is planning care with a licensed practical nurse (LPN) for a stable client on a surgical unit. Which tasks can the RN assign to the LPN? Select all that apply.
options: Give scheduled oral and subcutaneous medications
Change a sterile dressing on a healing incision
Reinforce the incentive spirometer teaching the RN has already given
Complete the initial admission assessment
Develop the client's nursing plan of care
Give an IV push opioid dose for pain
rationales: Correct. Giving oral and subcutaneous medications to a stable client is within LPN scope.
Correct. Sterile dressing changes on a stable wound are within LPN scope.
Correct. LPNs can reinforce teaching that the RN has started.
Initial assessment is an RN responsibility; the LPN may collect data but not make the initial assessment.
Planning care and evaluating the plan are RN responsibilities.
In most states, IV push medications are outside LPN scope and are given by the RN.
takeaway: The RN keeps assessment, planning, evaluation, initial teaching, and most IV push drugs; the LPN can give oral/subcut/IM drugs, do dressings, and reinforce teaching.

stem: A client who speaks only Vietnamese needs discharge teaching about new insulin injections. The client's 14-year-old grandson speaks English well and offers to interpret. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept the grandson's offer because he is family and the client trusts him
Use a qualified medical interpreter in person, by phone, or by video
Give the client written instructions in English with pictures
Ask a bilingual housekeeping staff member to translate
rationales: Minors and family members should not interpret medical information; they may make errors, leave things out, or change the meaning.
Correct. A qualified medical interpreter gives accurate, private, complete communication, which the client has a right to receive.
The client cannot read English, and pictures alone cannot explain insulin safety.
Untrained staff are not qualified medical interpreters and may not know medical terms.
takeaway: Use a qualified medical interpreter for clients with limited English; do not use family members, especially children.

stem: The nurse is using a qualified medical interpreter to teach a Spanish-speaking client about warfarin. Which actions by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Look at and speak directly to the client, not to the interpreter
Use short sentences and pause so the interpreter can translate
Ask the client to explain the instructions back through the interpreter
Ask the interpreter to give a short summary instead of translating everything
Say to the interpreter, "Ask her if she understands."
Meet briefly with the interpreter before the session to explain the goals
rationales: Correct. Speaking directly to the client shows respect and keeps the client at the center of care.
Correct. Short phrases help the interpreter translate accurately and completely.
Correct. Teach-back confirms the client understood the teaching.
Summaries can leave out important safety information; the interpreter should translate everything that is said.
This speaks about the client in the third person and asks a yes/no question that does not check real understanding.
Correct. A short pre-session briefing helps the interpreter prepare for the topic and terms.
takeaway: With an interpreter: brief first, speak to the client in the first person, use short sentences, and confirm understanding with teach-back.

stem: A client on a ventilator after a severe brain injury has a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3. The provider plans to talk with the family tomorrow about withdrawing life support. What is the nurse's legal responsibility regarding organ donation?
options: Ask the family now whether they would like to donate the client's organs
Notify the organ procurement organization (OPO) promptly, according to hospital policy, before life support is withdrawn
Wait until the family brings up organ donation
Notify the OPO only after the client is declared dead
rationales: The donation request should be made by the organ procurement organization or a specially trained requester, not by any staff member.
Correct. Federal rules require hospitals to refer every imminent death and death to the OPO in a timely way so donation can be evaluated.
Referral is required regardless of whether the family asks about donation.
Waiting until after death may make donation impossible; imminent deaths must be referred in time for evaluation.
takeaway: Refer every imminent or actual death to the OPO promptly; the OPO or a trained requester, not the bedside nurse, asks the family about donation.

stem: A client has died in the hospital. Laws vary by state, but in which situations should the nurse expect the death to be reported to the medical examiner or coroner? Select all that apply.
options: A client who died from a head injury after a fall in the hospital
A child who died with injuries suspicious for abuse
A client who died by suicide
A client in hospice who died as expected from metastatic cancer
A client with end-stage heart failure and a do-not-resuscitate order who died as expected
A client who died unexpectedly during a surgical procedure
rationales: Correct. Deaths caused by injury or accident, including falls in the hospital, are reported to the medical examiner or coroner.
Correct. Suspected abuse or homicide is reported to the medical examiner or coroner.
Correct. Suicide is a violent, non-natural death and is reported.
An expected death from a known terminal illness is a natural death and usually does not need medical examiner review.
This is an expected natural death from a known disease and usually is not reported.
Correct. Unexpected deaths during surgery or procedures are reported for investigation.
takeaway: Deaths that are unexpected, violent, accidental, suspicious, or related to a procedure are reported to the medical examiner or coroner (exact rules vary by state); expected natural deaths usually are not.

stem: The nurse reviews restraint prescriptions for clients on the unit. Which prescription should the nurse question?
options: "Soft wrist restraints PRN if the client pulls at the endotracheal tube."
"Bilateral soft wrist restraints to prevent removal of the endotracheal tube; renew per hospital policy."
"Mitt restraint on the right hand to prevent pulling of the feeding tube; reassess need each shift."
"Four-point restraints for violent behavior that endangers staff, for up to 4 hours" for an adult client
rationales: Correct. Restraint prescriptions may never be written as PRN (as needed); each episode needs a specific, time-limited prescription.
This is a specific, non-PRN prescription for a non-violent (medical) restraint with a clear reason, which is acceptable.
Mitts used to protect a medical device are an acceptable, less-restrictive restraint with a clear reason.
For a violent adult, a time-limited prescription of up to 4 hours is consistent with federal (CMS) rules.
takeaway: Restraint prescriptions must be specific and time-limited and are never written as PRN.

stem: A client has soft wrist restraints to protect a central venous catheter. Which actions by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Tie the restraint to the bed frame with a quick-release knot
Check that two fingers fit under the restraint
Tie the straps to the side rails
Check skin, circulation, and offer fluids and toileting at the intervals required by policy
Remove the call light because the client cannot use the hands
Evaluate whether a less-restrictive alternative could be used
rationales: Correct. The bed frame moves with the bed, and a quick-release knot allows fast removal in an emergency.
Correct. This makes sure the restraint is not too tight and does not restrict circulation.
When the side rail is lowered or moved, the restraint can pull on the limb and cause injury.
Correct. Regular checks of circulation, skin, nutrition, hydration, and elimination are required for any client in restraints.
The client must always have a way to call for help; the call light should be placed within reach or the client checked often.
Correct. Restraints are used only as long as needed; the nurse keeps looking for ways to remove them.
takeaway: Restrained clients need a quick-release knot to the bed frame, a two-finger fit, regular circulation and needs checks, and ongoing review for removal.

stem: A provider calls with a telephone prescription for oral potassium chloride for a client whose potassium is 3.1 mEq/L. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.
options: Write down or enter the prescription while the provider is speaking
Read the complete prescription back to the provider
Receive the provider's confirmation that the prescription is correct
Document it as a telephone order with "read back," the provider's name, date, and time
Make sure the provider signs the prescription within the time required by policy
rationales: First: recording the prescription as it is given prevents relying on memory.
Second: read-back lets the provider catch any misunderstanding.
Third: the prescription is not acted on until the provider confirms it is correct.
Fourth: documentation records the source and the safety check.
Fifth: the provider must authenticate (sign) telephone prescriptions within the facility's time frame.
takeaway: Telephone orders: write it down, read it back, get confirmation, document, and have the provider sign within policy.

stem: A provider's prescription reads: "Metoprolol tartrate 25 mg PO." No frequency is written. The client's BP is 152/94 mm Hg and HR is 88/min. What should the nurse do?
options: Give 25 mg twice a day because that is the usual frequency
Ask the pharmacist to choose the frequency
Contact the provider to clarify the frequency before giving the drug
Give one dose now and ask the provider about the frequency at morning rounds
rationales: The nurse cannot assume or add missing parts of a prescription.
The pharmacist can help clarify but cannot complete the prescription for the provider.
Correct. An incomplete prescription must be clarified with the prescriber before it is carried out.
Giving a drug from an incomplete prescription is unsafe and not within nursing scope.
takeaway: A complete prescription has client, drug, dose, route, frequency, and prescriber signature; clarify any missing part with the prescriber before acting.
