stem: A client is admitted with a wound infected with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). No private rooms are available. Which client is the best roommate for this client?
options: A client with Clostridioides difficile diarrhea
A client with an MRSA urinary tract infection and no other infection
A client who had a colon resection yesterday
A client receiving chemotherapy with neutropenia
rationales: This is a different organism; cohorting two different resistant or spore-forming infections risks cross-infection.
Cohorting clients infected with the same organism is acceptable when a private room is not available.
A fresh surgical wound is at high risk for acquiring MRSA.
An immunosuppressed client must never be placed with a client who has an infection.
takeaway: If no private room is available, cohort clients who have the same organism and no other infection.

stem: A nurse sustains a needlestick injury with a used needle after giving a subcutaneous injection. What is the nurse's first action?
options: Squeeze the puncture site to force out blood
Wash the site right away with soap and water
Clean the site with a bleach solution
Complete an incident report before leaving the unit
rationales: Squeezing can cause more tissue damage and is not recommended.
Immediate washing with soap and water is the first step after a percutaneous exposure.
Caustic agents such as bleach damage tissue and are not recommended.
Reporting is required, but first aid to the site comes first; delays also delay post-exposure prophylaxis.
takeaway: After a needlestick: wash with soap and water, report right away, and get evaluated for post-exposure prophylaxis (ideally within hours).

stem: The nurse is caring for a client with Clostridioides difficile diarrhea on contact-plus (enteric) precautions. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Put on a gown and gloves before entering the room
Wash hands with soap and water after removing gloves
Keep a dedicated stethoscope and blood pressure cuff in the room
Clean room surfaces with an EPA-registered sporicidal (bleach-based) disinfectant
Wear an N95 respirator when giving care
Use alcohol-based hand rub as the only hand hygiene after care
rationales: Contact precautions require a gown and gloves on room entry because the environment is contaminated.
Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores; soap, water, and friction remove them.
Dedicated equipment prevents spores from spreading to other clients.
Spores survive on surfaces for months; a sporicidal agent such as bleach is needed.
C. difficile is not spread by the airborne route, so a respirator is not needed.
Alcohol-based rub alone does not remove C. difficile spores.
takeaway: C. difficile = gown and gloves, dedicated equipment, soap-and-water hand hygiene, and bleach-based (sporicidal) cleaning.

stem: A nurse is finishing care for a client on airborne and contact precautions and is wearing gloves, goggles, a gown, and a fit-tested N95 respirator. Place the steps for removing PPE in the correct order.
options: Remove the gown
Leave the room, close the door, and then remove the N95 respirator by the straps
Remove the gloves
Perform hand hygiene
Remove the goggles
rationales: The gown comes off after the gloves and goggles, rolling the contaminated outside inward.
For airborne precautions, the respirator is removed only after leaving the room, touching only the straps.
Gloves are the most contaminated item and come off first.
Hand hygiene is done right after all PPE is removed.
Goggles come off after gloves, handled by the ear pieces or headband.
takeaway: Doffing: gloves, goggles, gown, then the respirator outside the room, then hand hygiene.

stem: A client with suspected measles (rubeola) is placed in an airborne infection isolation room. Which nurse is the best choice to care for this client?
options: A nurse who is 12 weeks pregnant and unsure of her measles immunity
A nurse with documented receipt of two doses of measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine
A nurse with no measles immunity who has a current N95 fit test
A nurse who is also caring for a client with neutropenia
rationales: A pregnant staff member without proven immunity is at risk for serious measles complications.
Documented immunity makes this the safest assignment; the nurse still wears an N95 respirator.
Staff without immunity should not care for a client with measles when immune staff are available.
Caring for both clients raises the risk of carrying infection to an immunosuppressed client.
takeaway: Assign staff with proven measles immunity to a client with measles, and use an N95 respirator in an airborne infection isolation room.

stem: A client is admitted with pertussis (whooping cough). Which personal protective equipment must the nurse put on before entering the room?
options: A fit-tested N95 respirator
A surgical (face) mask
A gown and gloves only
No mask unless the nurse is within 1 meter (3 ft) of the client
rationales: Pertussis is spread by droplets, not the airborne route, so a respirator is not required.
Droplet precautions require a surgical mask when entering the room.
Gown and gloves are for contact precautions and do not protect against respiratory droplets.
Current CDC guidance is to put on the mask when entering the room, not based on distance.
takeaway: Droplet precautions (pertussis, influenza, mumps, meningococcus): surgical mask on room entry and a private room or cohort.

stem: Which actions by the nurse demonstrate correct use of standard precautions? Select all that apply.
options: Wearing a mask and eye protection while suctioning a tracheostomy
Performing hand hygiene after removing gloves
Holding soiled linen away from the uniform
Wearing gloves to empty a urinary drainage bag
Recapping a used needle with both hands
Wearing an N95 respirator for every client who has a fever
rationales: Suctioning can splash secretions, so face and eye protection are required.
Gloves can have tiny holes and hands can be contaminated during removal.
This prevents transfer of organisms to the nurse's clothing.
Contact with body fluids requires gloves under standard precautions.
Two-handed recapping is a leading cause of needlestick injuries; discard needles uncapped in a sharps container.
Fever alone does not require airborne precautions; PPE is chosen by the expected exposure and the suspected organism.
takeaway: Standard precautions apply to every client: choose PPE based on the expected contact with blood or body fluids.

stem: The nurse applies soft wrist restraints prescribed for a client who keeps pulling at a nasogastric tube. Which action is correct?
options: Tie the restraints to the side rails so they can be released quickly
Secure the restraints to the bed frame with a quick-release tie
Fasten the restraints tightly enough that a finger cannot fit underneath
Use a square knot so the client cannot untie it
rationales: Lowering the side rail with a restraint tied to it can injure the client's arm.
The bed frame moves with the client, and a quick-release tie allows fast removal in an emergency.
Restraints that are too tight impair circulation; two fingers should fit under the restraint.
A square knot cannot be released quickly in an emergency.
takeaway: Restraints: tie to the bed frame with a quick-release knot, allow two fingers underneath, and check circulation often.

stem: A 78-year-old client receives furosemide 40 mg twice daily and was started on zolpidem at bedtime. The client is at high risk for falls. Which intervention is most effective?
options: Raise all four side rails at night
Offer toileting every 2 hours while awake and before sleep, with the bed in low and locked position
Apply a vest restraint during the night
Turn off all room lights so the client sleeps well
rationales: Four raised side rails count as a restraint and increase injury when clients climb over them.
Scheduled toileting reduces urgent trips to the bathroom caused by the diuretic, the main fall trigger here.
Restraints are a last resort and increase the risk of injury and death.
Darkness raises fall risk; use a night light.
takeaway: Prevent falls by meeting needs before the client acts alone: scheduled toileting, low locked bed, call light in reach, and a night light.

stem: The nurse is about to give a scheduled antibiotic and notices the client's identification band was removed during IV insertion. The nurse has cared for this client all shift. What should the nurse do?
options: Give the medication because the nurse knows the client
Confirm the client's name and room number, then give the medication
Have a new identification band applied, then verify two identifiers before giving the medication
Give the medication and replace the band at the end of the shift
rationales: Familiarity is not a safe identifier; errors happen when staff rely on recognition.
A room number is never an acceptable identifier because clients change rooms.
Identity must be confirmed with two identifiers, such as name and date of birth, matched to the band and the medication record.
Delaying replacement leaves the client unidentified for other staff and procedures.
takeaway: Always use two client identifiers (such as name and date of birth) matched to the ID band and record; never use the room number.

stem: During screening before a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan, which client statement is most important to report to the provider before the scan?
options: "I get nervous in small spaces like elevators."
"I had a pacemaker put in 12 years ago."
"I am allergic to iodine contrast dye."
"I have several fillings in my teeth."
rationales: Claustrophobia should be addressed, for example with a prescribed anxiolytic, but it is not a safety contraindication.
Many older pacemakers are not MRI-safe; the magnet can cause device malfunction or heating.
MRI uses gadolinium-based contrast, not iodinated contrast.
Standard dental fillings are not ferromagnetic and are not a contraindication.
takeaway: Before MRI, screen for implanted devices and metal (pacemakers, pumps, metal fragments); a non-MRI-safe implant can be dangerous.

stem: A client has a sealed cervical radiation implant. The nurse finds the radioactive source lying in the bed. What should the nurse do?
options: Pick up the source with gloved hands and place it back in the vagina
Use long-handled forceps to place the source in the lead container in the room, then notify radiation oncology
Wrap the source in the bed linens and send it to the laundry
Leave the room and wait for the next scheduled visit by radiation oncology
rationales: Gloves do not shield radiation, and only the radiation oncology team reinserts a source.
Forceps increase distance and the lead container provides shielding; the radiation team must be told right away.
This spreads radiation exposure to other staff and is never acceptable.
The source must be contained promptly to limit exposure to the client and others.
takeaway: Dislodged radiation source: never touch it by hand; use long-handled forceps, put it in the lead container, and notify radiation oncology.

stem: The nurse prepares to give an IV antineoplastic (hazardous) drug. Which actions protect the nurse and others from exposure? Select all that apply.
options: Wear two pairs of chemotherapy-tested gloves
Wear a disposable, impermeable gown with long sleeves and closed back
Prime the IV tubing with a non-drug solution before attaching the drug bag
Place used tubing and bags in a designated hazardous drug waste container
Empty the client's urinal without gloves once the infusion is finished
Crush an oral antineoplastic tablet in an open medication cup if the client cannot swallow it
rationales: Double gloving reduces skin exposure if the outer glove is contaminated or torn.
A gown that resists permeation protects skin and clothing from drug splashes.
Priming with a compatible non-drug fluid prevents releasing hazardous drug into the air or onto surfaces.
Hazardous drug waste must be kept separate from regular trash and sharps.
Drug residue is excreted in body fluids for about 48 hours, so gloves (and a gown if splashing is likely) are needed.
Crushing hazardous tablets creates airborne particles; ask the pharmacy for another form.
takeaway: Hazardous drugs: double chemo gloves, impermeable gown, prime with non-drug fluid, separate hazardous waste, and gloves for body fluids for 48 hours.

stem: An IV bag of an antineoplastic drug leaks onto the floor of a client's room. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.
options: Put on PPE from the spill kit (double chemotherapy gloves, gown, eye protection, and respirator)
Clean the area with detergent and rinse with clean water
Secure the area and keep others away
Absorb the spill with pads from the spill kit, working from the outer edge toward the center
Place all waste in the hazardous drug waste container and report the spill
rationales: PPE is put on before any contact with the spilled drug.
Cleaning follows removal of the bulk spill to remove remaining drug residue.
Limiting access first prevents others from walking through or being exposed.
Working inward contains the spill and keeps it from spreading.
Proper disposal and reporting are done after the area is clean.
takeaway: Hazardous drug spill: secure the area, put on PPE, contain from outside in, clean, then dispose and report.

stem: A small fire starts in a wastebasket and the nurse prepares to use a fire extinguisher. Which action is correct?
options: Aim the nozzle at the top of the flames
Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire and sweep from side to side
Squeeze the handle before pulling the pin
Stand as close to the flames as possible
rationales: Spraying the top of the flames does not put out the fuel source.
PASS: Pull the pin, Aim at the base, Squeeze the handle, Sweep side to side.
The extinguisher will not discharge until the pin is pulled.
Stand about 6 to 8 feet (2 to 2.5 m) away to stay safe and spray effectively.
takeaway: Fire extinguisher = PASS: Pull, Aim at the base, Squeeze, Sweep.

stem: While adjusting an infusion pump, the nurse feels a slight tingling in the fingers. What is the nurse's best action?
options: Keep using the pump and report it at the end of the shift
Replace the pump, tag the faulty one "Do not use," and report it to biomedical engineering
Plug the pump into an extension cord on another outlet
Wrap the power cord with tape and continue the infusion
rationales: A faulty device can shock the client or staff; it must be removed from use right away.
Removing, labeling, and reporting faulty equipment prevents electrical injury to others.
Extension cords add hazard and do not fix a device fault.
Taping does not correct an electrical fault.
takeaway: Any shock, frayed cord, or damaged plug: take the equipment out of service, label it, and report it to biomedical engineering.

stem: The nurse is teaching an 82-year-old client who lives alone how to prevent injuries at home. Which recommendations should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Remove throw rugs from floors
Install grab bars in the shower and next to the toilet
Use night lights in the hallway and bathroom
Set the water heater no higher than 120°F (49°C)
Store often-used items on high shelves to keep counters clear
Wax the floors so they are easy to clean
rationales: Loose rugs are a common cause of trips and falls.
Grab bars give stable support during transfers in the bathroom.
Good lighting at night reduces falls on the way to the bathroom.
Older adults have thinner skin and slower reaction times, so lower water temperature prevents scalds.
Reaching up or using a step stool increases fall risk; keep items at waist to shoulder height.
Waxed floors are slippery and increase fall risk.
takeaway: Home safety for older adults: clear floors, grab bars, good lighting, and water heater at or below 120°F (49°C).

stem: The nurse teaches the parents of an 18-month-old about poisoning prevention. Which statement by a parent indicates a need for further teaching?
options: "I will keep cleaning products in a locked cabinet."
"I will keep syrup of ipecac at home to make my child vomit if needed."
"I will save the Poison Help number, 1-800-222-1222, in my phone."
"I will keep medicines in their original child-resistant containers."
rationales: Locked storage is correct because toddlers climb and open low cabinets.
Ipecac is no longer recommended; parents should call Poison Control instead.
This is the correct national number and should be easy to find.
Original labeled containers with child-resistant caps help prevent poisoning.
takeaway: For a suspected poisoning, call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222); do not induce vomiting.

stem: The nurse realizes a client received 10 units of insulin lispro instead of the prescribed 4 units 15 minutes ago. What is the nurse's first action?
options: Complete an incident (safety event) report
Check the client's blood glucose and assess for signs of hypoglycemia
Notify the charge nurse that a medication error occurred
Give the client a carbohydrate snack right away
rationales: Reporting is required, but client safety comes first.
Assessing the client is the first priority after a medication error so harm can be treated quickly.
The charge nurse should be told, but assessment of the client comes first.
Treatment should be based on the assessment; the nurse first checks glucose and the client's condition.
takeaway: After a medication error: assess the client first, then notify the provider, then report the event.

stem: Several workers exposed to a liquid chemical at a factory arrive at the emergency department. They are alert and breathing without difficulty. What is the priority action?
options: Bring them into the triage area for a full assessment
Remove their clothing and decontaminate them outside the department
Start IV access on each worker
Draw blood samples to identify the chemical
rationales: Bringing contaminated clients inside exposes staff and other clients.
Removing clothing removes most of the contaminant, and decontamination before entry protects the facility.
IV access is not the priority for stable clients who are still contaminated.
Lab testing does not prevent ongoing exposure and can wait.
takeaway: In a chemical exposure, decontaminate before entry (remove clothing first) unless a life-threatening problem needs immediate care.

stem: A client weighing 113 kg (250 lb) cannot bear weight but can follow directions. The client needs to move from bed to a chair. Which method is safest?
options: Three staff members lift the client using a draw sheet
Use a full-body mechanical lift with at least two caregivers
Use a gait belt and pivot the client to the chair
Ask the client to push up with the arms while one nurse pulls
rationales: Manual lifting of this weight puts staff at high risk of back injury.
A client who cannot bear weight needs a mechanical lift; safe client handling guidelines avoid manual lifts.
A stand-pivot transfer requires the client to bear weight.
This depends on upper body strength and puts both the client and nurse at risk.
takeaway: Clients who cannot bear weight are moved with a mechanical lift and at least two caregivers, not by manual lifting.

stem: The nurse sets up a sterile field for a sterile procedure. Which actions maintain surgical asepsis? Select all that apply.
options: Treating the outer 1 inch (2.5 cm) border of the sterile drape as nonsterile
Keeping sterile gloved hands above the waist
Reaching across the sterile field to get a supply
Discarding a sterile package that is torn or damp
Facing the sterile field at all times
Moistening the sterile drape with saline to keep it in place
rationales: The edge of the field is considered contaminated.
Items below waist level are out of view and considered contaminated.
Reaching over the field can drop particles or touch sterile items.
A torn or wet wrapper means the contents can no longer be considered sterile.
A field out of sight is considered contaminated.
A wet drape allows organisms to wick through from the nonsterile surface below.
takeaway: Sterile field: 1-inch border is nonsterile, stay above the waist, never turn your back or reach across, and keep it dry.

stem: The nurse opens a sterile kit wrapped in a paper cover on a bedside table. Which flap should the nurse open first?
options: The flap nearest the nurse
The flap farthest from the nurse
The right side flap
The flap that is easiest to reach
rationales: Opening the near flap first would require reaching over the sterile inside later.
Opening the far flap first avoids reaching across the exposed sterile area.
Side flaps are opened after the far flap.
Opening order is fixed to avoid reaching over the sterile area.
takeaway: Open a sterile package with the farthest flap first, then the sides, and the nearest flap last.

stem: Which clients require airborne precautions in an airborne infection isolation room? Select all that apply.
options: A client with measles (rubeola)
A client with suspected active pulmonary tuberculosis
A client with disseminated herpes zoster
A client with influenza A
A client with an MRSA wound infection
A client with mumps
rationales: Measles is spread by the airborne route.
Tuberculosis is spread by airborne droplet nuclei.
Disseminated zoster requires airborne and contact precautions until lesions are crusted.
Influenza requires droplet precautions.
MRSA requires contact precautions.
Mumps requires droplet precautions.
takeaway: Airborne precautions: measles, tuberculosis, and varicella or disseminated zoster ("My Chicken Hez TB").

stem: A client with vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE) is on contact precautions. The nurse needs to assess the client's lung sounds. Which action is correct?
options: Use the nurse's own stethoscope and wipe it with alcohol after use
Use a dedicated stethoscope that stays in the client's room
Skip the gown because the assessment is brief
Wear an N95 respirator for the assessment
rationales: Sharing personal equipment between rooms can spread resistant organisms.
Dedicated or disposable equipment prevents transmission to other clients.
Contact precautions require a gown and gloves for any contact with the client or room.
VRE is spread by contact, not by the airborne route.
takeaway: Contact precautions: gown and gloves on entry and dedicated equipment that stays in the room.

stem: A client with terminal pancreatic cancer says, "If I can just live until my daughter's wedding in June, I'll be ready to go." Which stage of grief is the client showing?
options: Denial
Anger
Bargaining
Acceptance
rationales: Denial involves refusing to accept the diagnosis, such as "The tests must be wrong."
Anger is shown by blaming or hostility toward others.
The client is trying to make a deal for more time, which is bargaining.
In acceptance the client is at peace and does not set conditions on dying.
takeaway: Bargaining = "If only... then..." statements that try to gain more time or change the outcome.

stem: A client comes to the emergency department after a home robbery. The client is shaking, pacing, and says, "I can't think. I don't know what to do." Which nursing approach is most appropriate?
options: Explore how the client's childhood affects the current reaction
Take a direct, active role and help the client focus on the immediate problem
Encourage the client to make major decisions about moving right away
Leave the client alone until the client calms down
rationales: Crisis intervention focuses on the present problem, not past history.
A client in crisis has trouble problem-solving, so the nurse is directive and focuses on immediate safety and needs.
Major decisions should not be made during a crisis when thinking is impaired.
Leaving an anxious client alone can increase anxiety and risk.
takeaway: Crisis intervention: ensure safety, be directive, focus on the immediate problem, and mobilize support; crises usually resolve within 4 to 6 weeks.

stem: A client was just told she has breast cancer. After the provider leaves, she says quietly, "I don't even know what to think right now." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?
options: "Breast cancer has a very high survival rate, so try not to worry."
"This is a lot to take in. I'm here to listen if you'd like to talk about it."
"Your oncologist is excellent and will take good care of you."
"You should call your family so they can support you."
rationales: This is false reassurance and dismisses the client's feelings.
Acknowledging the news and offering self encourage the client to share feelings at her own pace.
This changes the focus away from the client's feelings.
Giving advice is nontherapeutic and blocks the client from expressing feelings.
takeaway: After bad news, acknowledge the feelings and offer presence; avoid false reassurance, advice, and changing the subject.

stem: The nurse is evaluating stress management teaching for a client who cares for a parent with dementia. Which client statements indicate healthy coping? Select all that apply.
options: "I take a 20-minute walk most days."
"I practice slow, deep breathing when I start to feel tense."
"I joined a caregiver support group that meets weekly."
"I have a couple of glasses of wine every night to unwind."
"My sister stays with Mom one afternoon a week so I can rest."
"I skip meals so I have more time to get everything done."
rationales: Regular physical activity reduces stress hormones and improves mood.
Diaphragmatic breathing activates the relaxation response.
Social support is a key protective factor against caregiver burnout.
Using alcohol to cope is a maladaptive strategy that can lead to dependence.
Respite care prevents caregiver exhaustion.
Neglecting nutrition worsens stress and health.
takeaway: Healthy coping includes exercise, relaxation techniques, social support, and respite; substance use and self-neglect are maladaptive.

stem: A healthy term newborn had the state newborn screening blood sample collected at 18 hours of age and is being discharged home. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Tell the parents the screening is complete and no further testing is needed.
Arrange for a repeat newborn screen at the first follow-up visit.
Delay discharge until the infant is 72 hours old so the test can be repeated.
Ask the parents to bring a urine sample to the clinic in 1 week.
rationales: A sample taken before 24 hours of age can miss conditions such as phenylketonuria because the infant has had little protein feeding.
Samples collected before 24 hours of age are less reliable, so a repeat specimen is drawn after 24 hours of age per state protocol, often at the first follow-up visit.
Discharge does not need to be delayed; the repeat sample can be drawn at an outpatient visit.
Newborn screening for metabolic and genetic disorders uses a heel-stick blood spot, not urine.
takeaway: Newborn screening blood spots are best collected at 24 to 48 hours of age; a sample taken earlier must be repeated.

stem: The nurse is about to perform a well-child physical examination on a 20-month-old who is clinging to the parent. Which approach is best?
options: Ask the parent to wait outside so the toddler can focus on the nurse.
Examine the ears and mouth first while the toddler is still calm.
Examine the toddler on the parent's lap and leave the ears and mouth for last.
Explain each step in detail using a doll before starting.
rationales: Separation from the parent increases a toddler's fear; the parent should stay and help.
Invasive or uncomfortable parts of the exam cause crying and should be done last.
Keeping the toddler with the parent reduces stranger and separation anxiety, and saving invasive steps for the end keeps the child cooperative longer.
Detailed explanations are more useful for preschoolers; toddlers need brief, simple words and minimal handling.
takeaway: For toddlers, examine on the parent's lap when possible and do intrusive steps (ears, mouth) last.

stem: A 15-year-old comes to the clinic with a parent for a sports physical. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate when obtaining the health history?
options: Interview the adolescent and parent together for the entire visit.
Ask the parent to answer the questions about risk behaviors.
Interview the adolescent privately and explain the limits of confidentiality.
Promise the adolescent that nothing they say will be shared with anyone.
rationales: Adolescents are less likely to disclose sensitive information such as sexual activity or substance use in front of a parent.
The adolescent is the best source of information about their own behaviors.
Private time with the adolescent encourages honest answers, and explaining that safety concerns such as risk of harm must be shared builds trust.
Confidentiality has limits, such as risk of self-harm or abuse, so an absolute promise is not truthful.
takeaway: Interview adolescents alone for part of the visit and explain confidentiality and its limits up front.

stem: A 4-year-old is at the clinic for the scheduled fifth dose of DTaP vaccine. Which finding in the child's history is a contraindication to giving this vaccine?
options: A temperature of 37.8°C (100°F) with a runny nose today
Currently taking amoxicillin for an ear infection
Encephalopathy that began 3 days after the previous DTaP dose
Redness and swelling at the injection site after the previous dose
rationales: Mild illness with or without low-grade fever is not a reason to delay vaccination.
Antibiotic use does not affect the response to DTaP and is not a contraindication.
Encephalopathy within 7 days of a pertussis-containing vaccine, without another cause, is a contraindication to further pertussis vaccine doses.
Local reactions are common and expected and do not prevent further doses.
takeaway: True contraindications to DTaP are a severe allergic reaction to a prior dose or encephalopathy within 7 days of a prior dose; mild illness is not.

stem: A newborn is born to a client whose prenatal lab results show she is hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) positive. The newborn is stable and weighs 3,200 g. Which order should the nurse expect?
options: Hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth
Hepatitis B vaccine only at the 2-month well-child visit
HBIG only, with the vaccine series starting at 6 months
Testing the newborn for HBsAg before giving any treatment
rationales: Infants of HBsAg-positive mothers need both the vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours of birth to prevent perinatal transmission.
Waiting 2 months leaves the infant unprotected during the highest-risk period for infection.
The vaccine series must start at birth along with HBIG; HBIG alone gives only short-term protection.
Treatment is given within 12 hours without waiting for infant testing; infant testing is done after the vaccine series is complete.
takeaway: Infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers receive hepatitis B vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours of birth.

stem: A 25-year-old client with no history of abnormal results had a normal cervical cytology (Pap) test 2 years ago. The client asks how often she should have Pap testing. According to U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) guidance, which response by the nurse is correct?
options: Every year
Every 3 years
Every 5 years with cytology alone
Only if she develops symptoms such as abnormal bleeding
rationales: Annual cervical screening is no longer recommended for average-risk clients and leads to unnecessary procedures.
For average-risk clients aged 21 to 29, cervical cytology alone is recommended every 3 years.
A 5-year interval applies to HPV-based testing, not to cytology alone.
Screening is meant to find changes before symptoms appear.
takeaway: Cervical cancer screening for ages 21 to 29: cytology every 3 years.

stem: A pregnant client reports that the first day of her last menstrual period was March 10, 2026. Using Naegele's rule, which estimated date of birth should the nurse calculate?
options: December 3, 2026
December 10, 2026
December 17, 2026
January 17, 2027
rationales: This subtracts 7 days instead of adding them.
This subtracts 3 months but forgets to add 7 days.
Naegele's rule: first day of LMP minus 3 months plus 7 days plus 1 year gives December 17, 2026.
This subtracts only 2 months; the rule subtracts 3 months.
takeaway: Naegele's rule: first day of LMP − 3 months + 7 days + 1 year.

stem: The nurse measures fundal height for four prenatal clients. Which finding requires follow-up with the health care provider?
options: 22 weeks of gestation; fundal height 21 cm
30 weeks of gestation; fundal height 31 cm
34 weeks of gestation; fundal height 27 cm
20 weeks of gestation; fundus at the level of the umbilicus
rationales: Between about 20 and 36 weeks, fundal height in centimeters should be within 2 cm of the weeks of gestation; 21 cm is normal at 22 weeks.
This is within 2 cm of the gestational age and is expected.
A fundal height 7 cm less than the gestational age suggests possible fetal growth restriction or low amniotic fluid and needs further evaluation, such as ultrasound.
The fundus normally reaches the umbilicus at about 20 weeks.
takeaway: From 20 to 36 weeks, fundal height in cm ≈ weeks of gestation (±2 cm); a larger difference needs follow-up.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client at 30 weeks of gestation about warning signs during pregnancy. Which findings should the nurse instruct the client to report right away? Select all that apply.
options: Severe headache with blurred vision
A sudden gush or steady leak of fluid from the vagina
Fewer fetal movements than usual
Mild ankle swelling at the end of the day
Heartburn after large meals
Bright red vaginal bleeding
rationales: These can be signs of preeclampsia with severe features and need prompt evaluation.
This may mean rupture of membranes, which can lead to preterm labor or infection.
Decreased fetal movement can signal fetal compromise and needs same-day evaluation.
Dependent ankle edema that improves with rest is a common, expected finding in the third trimester.
Heartburn is common in later pregnancy due to hormonal relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter and pressure from the uterus.
Bleeding in the third trimester may indicate placenta previa or placental abruption.
takeaway: Teach pregnant clients to report headache with vision changes, fluid leakage, decreased fetal movement, and vaginal bleeding immediately.

stem: A client at 32 weeks of gestation asks when she will be tested for group B Streptococcus (GBS). Which response by the nurse is correct?
options: At your next visit, as soon as possible
Between 36 and 37 weeks of pregnancy
Only if you develop a fever during labor
When you are admitted in labor
rationales: Testing too early may not reflect colonization status at the time of birth.
Current guidance recommends a vaginal-rectal swab for GBS at 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks so results are valid for a term birth.
GBS screening is universal for pregnant clients, not based on symptoms.
Waiting until labor would not leave time to plan intrapartum antibiotics.
takeaway: Screen all pregnant clients for GBS with a vaginal-rectal swab at 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks.

stem: The nurse assesses a client 12 hours after an uncomplicated vaginal birth. Which finding is expected?
options: Fundus firm, midline, and at the level of the umbilicus with moderate lochia rubra
Fundus soft, 2 cm above the umbilicus, and displaced to the right
Lochia saturating a perineal pad in 1 hour
Oral temperature of 38.4°C (101.1°F)
rationales: In the first day after birth, the fundus is firm and near the umbilicus, and lochia rubra in moderate amounts is normal.
A boggy, displaced fundus suggests a full bladder and risk of hemorrhage; the client should void and the fundus be massaged.
Saturating a pad in 1 hour or less is excessive bleeding and needs immediate action.
A slight rise up to 38°C (100.4°F) can occur in the first 24 hours from dehydration, but 38.4°C needs evaluation for infection.
takeaway: On postpartum day 1, expect a firm, midline fundus at or near the umbilicus and moderate lochia rubra.

stem: The nurse is providing discharge teaching to a client on postpartum day 2. Which findings should the nurse instruct the client to report to the health care provider? Select all that apply.
options: Pain, warmth, and swelling in one calf
Soaking a pad within 1 hour
Pink-brown vaginal discharge on day 5
Cramping during breastfeeding
A headache that does not go away with acetaminophen
Temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher
rationales: These are signs of deep vein thrombosis; the postpartum period carries a higher risk of blood clots.
This indicates heavy bleeding that could be late postpartum hemorrhage.
Lochia serosa, which is pinkish brown, is expected from about day 4 to day 10.
Afterpains during breastfeeding are normal because oxytocin release causes uterine contraction.
A persistent headache can be a sign of postpartum preeclampsia, which can occur up to 6 weeks after birth.
Fever after the first 24 hours may indicate infection such as endometritis or mastitis.
takeaway: Postpartum clients should report calf pain, heavy bleeding, fever, and severe or persistent headache; lochia changes and afterpains are normal.

stem: The nurse is teaching the parents of a newborn about umbilical cord care. Which instruction is correct?
options: Clean the cord with rubbing alcohol at every diaper change.
Fold the top of the diaper down below the cord stump.
Give the baby a tub bath every day until the cord falls off.
Gently pull the cord off if it has not fallen off by day 7.
rationales: Current evidence supports dry cord care; routine alcohol does not prevent infection and may delay separation.
Keeping the diaper below the stump keeps it clean and dry and helps it fall off on its own.
Sponge baths are recommended until the stump falls off so it stays dry.
The stump should fall off on its own, usually in 10 to 14 days; pulling it can cause bleeding.
takeaway: Keep the cord stump clean and dry, fold the diaper below it, and sponge bathe until it falls off.

stem: The nurse is teaching the parents of a 3-week-old about safe sleep. Which practices should the nurse recommend? Select all that apply.
options: Place the infant on the back for every sleep.
Keep the crib in the parents' room but not share a bed with the infant.
Offer a pacifier at nap time and bedtime.
Use an inclined sleeper if the infant spits up often.
Line the crib with soft bumper pads to protect the head.
Place the infant on the side with a rolled blanket behind the back.
rationales: Back sleeping for naps and at night lowers the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).
Room-sharing without bed-sharing is recommended, ideally for at least the first 6 months.
Pacifier use at sleep time lowers SIDS risk; for breastfed infants it can be started once breastfeeding is well established.
Inclined sleep products are unsafe; infants should sleep on a firm, flat surface even with reflux.
Bumper pads increase the risk of suffocation and entrapment.
Side sleeping is unsafe because the infant can roll to the stomach, and loose blankets add suffocation risk.
takeaway: Safe sleep: back to sleep, firm flat surface, room-share without bed-share, and nothing soft in the crib.

stem: The nurse is reviewing car seat safety with the parents of a newborn. Which statement by a parent indicates understanding of the teaching?
options: "We can turn the car seat forward when the baby turns 1 year old and weighs 20 pounds."
"I will place the harness chest clip at the level of the baby's armpits."
"I will put the car seat in the front seat so I can watch the baby."
"In winter, I will buckle the baby in while wearing a thick snowsuit."
rationales: This is outdated advice; children should stay rear-facing as long as possible, until they reach the seat's top height or weight limit.
The chest clip at armpit level keeps the shoulder straps in place during a crash.
Infants should ride in the back seat; a rear-facing seat in front of an active airbag can cause fatal injury.
Bulky clothing compresses in a crash and leaves the harness too loose; use thin layers and place a blanket over the harness.
takeaway: Infants ride rear-facing in the back seat, with a snug harness and the chest clip at armpit level.

stem: A breastfeeding client plans to return to work and will pump and store breast milk. Which statement by the client indicates correct understanding?
options: "I can keep freshly pumped milk at room temperature for up to 12 hours."
"I will thaw frozen milk in the refrigerator overnight or in a bowl of warm water."
"I will warm the milk in the microwave and swirl it before feeding."
"If my baby does not finish a thawed bottle, I can refreeze it."
rationales: Freshly expressed milk should be used within about 4 hours at room temperature.
These are safe thawing methods that preserve nutrients and avoid hot spots.
Microwaving heats unevenly, can burn the infant's mouth, and can destroy some protective properties of the milk.
Thawed milk should not be refrozen; milk left over from a feeding should be used within 2 hours after the baby finishes or thrown away.
takeaway: Thaw breast milk in the refrigerator or warm water, never in the microwave, and never refreeze thawed milk.

stem: A client started a combined oral contraceptive pill 2 weeks ago. Which symptom should the nurse instruct the client to report immediately?
options: Light spotting between periods
Mild nausea after taking the pill
Pain and swelling in one calf
Mild breast tenderness
rationales: Breakthrough spotting is common in the first 3 months of use and usually resolves.
Nausea is a common, minor side effect that often improves if the pill is taken with food or at bedtime.
Estrogen increases the risk of blood clots; unilateral calf pain and swelling may be a deep vein thrombosis.
Breast tenderness is a common hormonal effect and is not dangerous.
takeaway: Teach ACHES for combined hormonal contraceptives: Abdominal pain, Chest pain, Headache, Eye problems, Severe leg pain.

stem: The nurse is using the 5 A's model with a client who smokes 1 pack of cigarettes per day. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.
options: Assist the client by helping set a quit date and discussing medication options.
Ask the client about tobacco use at this visit.
Arrange follow-up contact within the first week after the quit date.
Assess the client's willingness to try to quit in the next 30 days.
Advise the client clearly and personally to quit smoking.
rationales: Assisting comes after the client's readiness is known, so the plan matches the client's goals.
Asking about tobacco use at every visit is the first step; use must be identified before it can be addressed.
Arranging follow-up is the final step and supports the client through early relapse risk.
Assessing readiness follows advice and guides how much help to offer.
Clear, personal advice to quit follows identifying tobacco use.
takeaway: The 5 A's of tobacco cessation are Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, and Arrange.

stem: During an admission interview, the nurse uses the CAGE questionnaire. The client answers "yes" to feeling the need to cut down on drinking and to having a drink first thing in the morning. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Document that the screening result is negative.
Recognize a positive screen and complete a more detailed assessment of alcohol use.
Tell the client that the answers confirm alcohol dependence.
Ask the family whether the client's answers are honest.
rationales: Two or more "yes" answers on the CAGE is considered a positive screen.
A CAGE score of 2 or more suggests an alcohol use disorder and needs further assessment, including the timing of the last drink to anticipate withdrawal.
A screening tool identifies risk; it does not diagnose an alcohol use disorder.
Questioning the client's honesty with family damages trust and is not the next step.
takeaway: A CAGE score of 2 or more "yes" answers is a positive screen and calls for further assessment.

stem: The nurse is assessing a healthy 78-year-old client. Which finding is an expected age-related change?
options: New confusion that started yesterday
Difficulty hearing high-pitched sounds
Sudden loss of vision in one eye
Leaking urine whenever the client coughs
rationales: Acute confusion is not normal aging; it suggests delirium from causes such as infection, medication, or dehydration.
Presbycusis, a gradual loss of high-frequency hearing, is a common age-related change.
Sudden vision loss is an emergency, such as retinal detachment, stroke, or retinal artery occlusion.
Incontinence is common but is not a normal part of aging and should be evaluated and treated.
takeaway: Gradual high-frequency hearing loss is normal aging; acute confusion, sudden vision loss, and incontinence are not.

stem: The nurse has taught a client with heart failure to weigh daily and report weight gain. The client has limited health literacy. Which statement by the nurse best checks the client's understanding?
options: "Do you have any questions about weighing yourself?"
"Do you understand when to call the clinic?"
"I want to be sure I explained this well. Tell me how you will weigh yourself and when you will call us."
"Please read this handout and sign that you received it."
rationales: Clients with limited health literacy often say they have no questions even when they do not understand.
A yes-or-no question does not show what the client actually understood.
Teach-back asks the client to explain the plan in their own words and puts responsibility for clarity on the nurse.
A signature shows receipt, not understanding, and a handout may be too hard to read.
takeaway: Use teach-back: ask the client to explain or show the plan in their own words.

stem: The nurse is teaching parents about expected infant motor and social development. Place the milestones in the order in which they typically appear.
options: Walks independently
Smiles socially in response to a parent
Sits without support
Uses a pincer grasp to pick up small objects
Rolls from front to back
rationales: Walking alone typically appears around 12 to 15 months.
A social smile appears around 2 months, the earliest of these milestones.
Sitting without support develops around 6 to 9 months.
The pincer grasp develops around 9 to 12 months, after sitting and before independent walking.
Rolling over typically appears around 4 to 6 months, before sitting.
takeaway: Typical sequence: social smile (2 mo), rolling (4–6 mo), sitting (6–9 mo), pincer grasp (9–12 mo), walking (12–15 mo).

stem: Based on U.S. Preventive Services Task Force guidance, which clients should the nurse identify as eligible for annual low-dose CT lung cancer screening? Select all that apply.
options: 62-year-old with a 30 pack-year history who quit 5 years ago
55-year-old who currently smokes, with a 20 pack-year history
48-year-old who currently smokes, with a 25 pack-year history
70-year-old with a 40 pack-year history who quit 20 years ago
66-year-old who currently smokes, with a 10 pack-year history
78-year-old with a 25 pack-year history who quit 10 years ago
rationales: Eligible: aged 50 to 80, at least 20 pack-years, and quit within the past 15 years.
Eligible: meets the age range and the 20 pack-year minimum and currently smokes.
Not eligible: screening begins at age 50.
Not eligible: the client quit more than 15 years ago.
Not eligible: the history is below 20 pack-years.
Eligible: within the age range, at least 20 pack-years, and quit within 15 years.
takeaway: Annual low-dose CT screening: ages 50 to 80, at least 20 pack-years, and currently smoking or quit within 15 years.

stem: The nurse is reviewing clients who requested the live attenuated influenza vaccine (nasal spray). Which clients should not receive this vaccine? Select all that apply.
options: A 26-year-old client who is 28 weeks pregnant
A 3-year-old whose parent reports a wheezing episode 6 months ago
A 12-year-old taking daily aspirin for Kawasaki disease
A healthy 25-year-old nursing student
A 10-year-old with seasonal allergic rhinitis
rationales: Live vaccines, including the nasal influenza vaccine, are contraindicated in pregnancy; the injectable inactivated vaccine is recommended.
Children aged 2 to 4 years with asthma or wheezing in the past 12 months should not receive the nasal vaccine.
Children on aspirin therapy should not receive the live vaccine because of the risk of Reye syndrome.
Healthy, nonpregnant clients aged 2 to 49 years can receive the nasal vaccine.
Allergic rhinitis is not a contraindication to the nasal vaccine.
takeaway: The nasal live influenza vaccine is for healthy, nonpregnant people aged 2 to 49; avoid it in pregnancy, immunosuppression, young children with recent wheezing, and children on aspirin.

stem: The nurse is teaching a 68-year-old client with low bone density about preventing osteoporosis and fractures. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Walk briskly for 30 minutes on most days.
Include calcium- and vitamin D–rich foods in the diet.
Remove throw rugs and keep walkways well lit.
Swim daily, because it is the best exercise to build bone.
Take the full 1,500 mg calcium supplement in one dose.
Stop smoking.
rationales: Weight-bearing exercise such as walking stimulates bone formation and improves balance.
Calcium and vitamin D are needed to build and maintain bone mass.
Preventing falls is key to preventing fractures in clients with low bone density.
Swimming is not weight-bearing and does little to strengthen bone.
The body absorbs calcium best in doses of 500 mg or less, so supplements should be split through the day.
Smoking speeds bone loss and increases fracture risk.
takeaway: Osteoporosis prevention: weight-bearing exercise, calcium and vitamin D, fall prevention, and no smoking.

stem: A client with osteoarthritis of the right hip is learning to walk with a single-point cane. Which observation indicates the client is using the cane correctly?
options: The client keeps the elbow fully straight while bearing weight on the cane.
The client holds the cane in the left hand and moves it forward at the same time as the right leg.
The top of the cane is level with the client's waist.
The client holds the cane in the right hand and moves it forward with the right leg.
rationales: The elbow should be flexed about 15 to 30 degrees; a locked elbow means the cane is too long and reduces support.
Correct. The cane is held on the stronger side and advanced together with the weaker leg to widen the base of support and share the load.
The handle should be level with the wrist crease or greater trochanter; waist height is too tall.
The cane belongs on the strong side; holding it on the affected side does not unload the painful hip.
takeaway: Hold the cane on the strong side and move it with the weak leg.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client to use axillary crutches after an ankle fracture. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: "The pads should be about two to three finger widths below my armpits."
"When I get tired, I can rest my weight on the pads under my arms."
"My elbows should be slightly bent when I hold the hand grips."
"I will remove throw rugs from the floors at home."
rationales: This is correct fitting and protects the axillary nerves.
Correct answer. Leaning on the axillary pads compresses the brachial plexus and can cause crutch palsy; weight goes through the hands.
Correct teaching; about 20 to 30 degrees of elbow flexion lets the arms bear weight.
Correct teaching; removing loose rugs reduces fall risk.
takeaway: Crutch users bear weight on the hands, never on the axillary pads.

stem: An older client is using a standard (non-wheeled) walker after hip surgery. Which action by the client requires the nurse to intervene?
options: The client pulls on the walker frame to rise from the chair.
The client steps into the walker, leading with the affected leg.
The client keeps all four legs of the walker on the floor before stepping.
The client lifts the walker and places it about one step length ahead.
rationales: Correct answer. A walker can tip when pulled on; the client should push up from the chair armrests, then grasp the walker.
This is correct; the weaker leg moves into the walker first, followed by the stronger leg.
This is correct; all four legs must be stable before weight is shifted.
This is correct technique for a standard walker.
takeaway: Push up from the chair armrests; never pull on a walker to stand.

stem: An older adult client in a long-term care facility has frequent episodes of fecal incontinence. Which intervention should the nurse include in a bowel training program?
options: Apply adult briefs and check them every 4 hours.
Offer the bedpan only when the client asks for it.
Limit fluid intake to 1,000 mL per day to make stool firmer.
Assist the client to the toilet about 30 minutes after breakfast each day.
rationales: Containment products manage incontinence but do not retrain bowel function.
Waiting for a request does not build a routine and often results in accidents.
Fluid restriction causes hard stool and constipation; 1,500 to 2,000 mL daily is usually encouraged unless restricted.
Correct. A consistent time after a meal uses the gastrocolic reflex to establish a predictable bowel pattern.
takeaway: Bowel training uses a consistent toileting time, usually after a meal, to use the gastrocolic reflex.

stem: While receiving a large-volume tap water enema, a client reports abdominal cramping after about 300 mL has been instilled. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Raise the enema container higher to finish the instillation quickly.
Ask the client to bear down to relieve the pressure.
Remove the tubing and end the procedure.
Clamp the tubing or lower the container and wait until the cramping eases.
rationales: Raising the container increases flow pressure and worsens cramping.
Bearing down will expel the solution; the client should take slow, deep breaths instead.
Cramping is common and expected; stopping completely is not needed unless the client cannot tolerate it after pausing.
Correct. Slowing or pausing the flow lets the bowel relax; instillation resumes once cramping subsides.
takeaway: For cramping during an enema, slow or pause the flow, then resume.

stem: The nurse assesses a client on the second day after colostomy surgery. Which stoma finding should the nurse report to the health care provider immediately?
options: Stoma is mildly swollen.
Stoma bleeds slightly when cleaned.
Stoma appears dark purple and dry.
Stoma is moist and beefy red.
rationales: Edema is expected for several weeks after surgery and gradually decreases.
The stoma is very vascular; minor bleeding with gentle cleaning is common.
Correct. A dusky, purple, or black stoma suggests poor blood supply and possible necrosis, which needs urgent evaluation.
A moist, pink to red stoma is normal and shows good blood supply.
takeaway: A dusky, purple, or black stoma means ischemia; report it right away.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client who has a new ileostomy. Which client statement indicates understanding of the teaching?
options: "I will drink less water so the output becomes thicker."
"I will chew my food well and limit foods like popcorn, nuts, and corn."
"I will irrigate my ileostomy every morning."
"After a few weeks my output will become formed like normal stool."
rationales: Ileostomy output is high in fluid and sodium; limiting fluids increases the risk of dehydration. Clients need extra fluids.
Correct. High-fiber, poorly digested foods can cause food blockage at the narrow ileal stoma.
Ileostomies are not irrigated; output is continuous and liquid to pasty.
Ileostomy output stays liquid to pasty because the colon is bypassed.
takeaway: Ileostomy clients chew well, limit high-fiber foods that can block the stoma, and drink extra fluids.

stem: A client receiving hemodialysis has a serum potassium of 5.6 mEq/L. The client asks for a snack. Which choice is best?
options: A glass of orange juice
A banana
A baked potato with the skin
Apple slices
rationales: Orange juice is high in potassium and adds to fluid intake.
Bananas are high in potassium.
Potatoes, especially with skin, are very high in potassium.
Correct. Apples are a low-potassium fruit suitable for a renal diet.
takeaway: Renal diets limit high-potassium foods such as bananas, oranges, potatoes, and tomatoes.

stem: A client with heart failure is prescribed a 2-gram sodium diet. Which lunch selection shows the client understands the diet?
options: Turkey deli sandwich with a dill pickle
A slice of cheese pizza
Grilled fresh chicken breast, steamed broccoli, and a baked sweet potato
Canned chicken noodle soup with saltine crackers
rationales: Processed deli meats and pickles are major sources of sodium.
Cheese, pizza crust, and sauce are all high in sodium.
Correct. Fresh, unprocessed foods prepared without added salt are naturally low in sodium.
Canned soups and salted crackers are very high in sodium.
takeaway: Low-sodium diets favor fresh foods and avoid canned, processed, cured, and pickled items.

stem: A client with a flare of Crohn's disease is prescribed a low-residue diet. Which breakfast choice indicates understanding of the diet?
options: Whole-grain cereal with sliced strawberries
Oatmeal with raisins
Scrambled eggs, white toast, and canned peaches
A bran muffin and an apple with the peel
rationales: Whole grains and seeded berries add fiber and residue.
Raisins and whole grains are high in fiber and residue.
Correct. Eggs, refined white bread, and peeled canned fruit are low in fiber and residue.
Bran and fruit peels are high in fiber.
takeaway: Low-residue diets use refined grains, tender proteins, and peeled cooked or canned fruits and vegetables.

stem: A client has a nasogastric tube for intermittent feedings. Placement was confirmed by x-ray when the tube was inserted. Which action should the nurse take before the next feeding?
options: Place the end of the tube in a cup of water and watch for bubbles.
Check that the external tube marking is unchanged and test the pH of aspirated contents.
Inject 30 mL of air and listen over the stomach for a whooshing sound.
Ask the client to speak to confirm the tube is not in the trachea.
rationales: This method is unsafe and unreliable; the client could aspirate water if the tube is in the airway.
Correct. An unchanged external length plus an acidic aspirate (pH 5 or less) supports gastric placement between x-rays.
Auscultation is unreliable; air can be heard over the stomach even when the tube is in the lung or esophagus.
The ability to speak does not rule out a small-bore tube in the airway.
takeaway: Before each feeding, check the tube's external mark and the aspirate pH; never rely on air auscultation.

stem: A 78-year-old client reports trouble falling asleep at night. Which recommendation should the nurse give?
options: "If you cannot fall asleep in about 20 minutes, get up and do something quiet until you feel sleepy."
"Have a glass of wine at bedtime to help you relax."
"Take a 2-hour nap in the afternoon to make up for lost sleep."
"Do vigorous exercise right before going to bed."
rationales: Correct. This stimulus-control technique links the bed with sleep rather than with lying awake.
Alcohol may cause drowsiness but fragments sleep and causes early waking.
Long daytime naps reduce sleep drive at night; short naps under 30 minutes are preferred, if any.
Exercise is helpful earlier in the day; close to bedtime it is stimulating.
takeaway: Sleep hygiene: consistent schedule, no late caffeine or alcohol, and get up if unable to sleep after about 20 minutes.

stem: A client twisted an ankle 2 hours ago. The ankle is swollen and painful. Which comfort measure should the nurse use?
options: Apply an ice pack wrapped in a towel for 15 to 20 minutes.
Apply an ice pack directly on the skin for 45 minutes.
Apply a warm moist compress for 30 minutes.
Place a heating pad on low under the ankle overnight.
rationales: Correct. Cold causes vasoconstriction, reducing swelling and pain; a cloth barrier and time limit prevent tissue injury.
Direct, prolonged cold can cause frostbite and rebound vasodilation.
Heat increases blood flow and swelling during the first 24 to 48 hours after injury.
Continuous heat worsens acute swelling and risks burns.
takeaway: Acute injury: cold for 15 to 20 minutes with a cloth barrier during the first 24 to 48 hours.

stem: A client with chronic low back pain asks to try guided imagery. Which nursing action best reflects this technique?
options: Asking the client to picture a peaceful place and describe its sights, sounds, and smells while breathing slowly.
Turning on a television program the client enjoys.
Giving the client a back massage with lotion.
Asking the client to tense and then relax each muscle group from the feet upward.
rationales: Correct. Guided imagery uses the client's imagination of a calming scene, engaging the senses, to promote relaxation and reduce pain.
This is distraction, a different nonpharmacological method.
This is cutaneous stimulation, not guided imagery.
This describes progressive muscle relaxation.
takeaway: Guided imagery uses a detailed, sensory mental image of a calming place.

stem: The nurse needs to assess pain in a 4-year-old client after a tonsillectomy. The child is alert and talks easily. Which pain scale is most appropriate?
options: 0 to 10 numeric rating scale
Wong-Baker FACES scale
CRIES scale
FLACC scale
rationales: Numeric scales require an understanding of numbers and are usually used for children about 8 years and older.
Correct. FACES is a self-report tool suitable for children about 3 years and older.
CRIES is designed for neonates.
FLACC is a behavioral tool for infants and children who cannot self-report; a verbal 4-year-old can self-report.
takeaway: Use self-report when possible: FACES for young verbal children, numeric scale for older children and adults.

stem: A client with advanced dementia cannot speak. The nurse notices moaning and grimacing during repositioning. Which pain assessment tool is most appropriate?
options: 0 to 10 numeric rating scale
Wong-Baker FACES scale
Verbal descriptor scale
Pain Assessment in Advanced Dementia (PAINAD) scale
rationales: The client cannot understand or answer a numeric scale.
FACES is a self-report tool; the client cannot point to or choose a face reliably.
This requires the client to choose words such as mild or severe, which is not possible here.
Correct. PAINAD scores observable behaviors such as breathing, vocalization, facial expression, body language, and consolability.
takeaway: Use a behavioral tool such as PAINAD for adults with advanced dementia who cannot self-report.

stem: A client who is actively dying has noisy, gurgling respirations. The family is upset by the sound. Which nursing action is best?
options: Perform deep nasotracheal suctioning every hour.
Place the client flat on the back.
Increase the IV fluid rate.
Turn the client onto the side with the head of the bed raised, and explain that the sound is not usually distressing to the client.
rationales: Deep suctioning is uncomfortable, often ineffective for these secretions, and can increase distress.
Supine positioning lets secretions pool in the throat and makes the sound worse.
Extra fluids can increase secretions and worsen the gurgling.
Correct. Side-lying and elevation help secretions drain; explaining the cause supports the family.
takeaway: For end-of-life noisy breathing, reposition side-lying with head raised and educate the family; avoid routine deep suctioning.

stem: A client in the final days of life refuses food and coughs when given liquids. The client's daughter insists on feeding full meals. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Keep encouraging her to finish each meal so she keeps her strength."
"Feeding her could harm her, so please stop."
"Decreased hunger is a normal part of dying. You can offer small sips or ice chips if your mother wants them, and help with mouth care."
"I will ask the provider about placing a feeding tube."
rationales: Forcing food causes discomfort and increases the risk of aspiration.
This is true in part but dismissive; it does not explain or offer the daughter another way to help.
Correct. This educates the family, respects the client's wishes, and gives the daughter a meaningful way to provide comfort while reducing aspiration risk.
Artificial nutrition at the end of life does not usually improve comfort or survival and is not the first response.
takeaway: At the end of life, offer food and fluids only for comfort, provide mouth care, and teach the family that loss of appetite is expected.

stem: The nurse is caring for a client who just had a plaster cast applied to the forearm. Which action is correct while the cast dries?
options: Rest the cast on a hard surface to keep its shape.
Handle the cast with the palms of the hands.
Cover the cast with a blanket to keep the arm warm.
Use a heat lamp to speed drying.
rationales: Hard surfaces can flatten the wet cast; it should rest on a pillow.
Correct. Palms spread pressure evenly; fingertips can make dents that press on the skin underneath.
Covering traps heat and slows drying; the cast should be left open to air.
External heat can burn the skin under the cast and causes uneven drying.
takeaway: Handle a wet plaster cast with palms only, support it on pillows, and leave it uncovered to dry.

stem: A client with a femur fracture is in balanced skeletal traction. The nurse finds that the traction weights are resting on the floor. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Reposition the client up toward the head of the bed so the weights hang freely.
Shorten the rope by tying a knot near the pulley.
Lift the weights and set them on the bed frame.
Remove the weights until the client is repositioned.
rationales: Correct. The client has slid down; moving the client up restores the countertraction and free-hanging weights.
Knots can catch in the pulley and changing the rope alters the prescribed traction setup.
Weights must hang freely to provide continuous pull.
Removing weights releases traction and can cause pain and fragment movement; weights stay on unless prescribed otherwise.
takeaway: Traction weights must hang freely at all times; reposition the client rather than moving the weights.

stem: A client who takes warfarin tells the nurse about several supplements the client uses. Which supplement is the nurse's greatest concern?
options: Ginkgo biloba
Probiotic capsules
Topical aloe vera gel
Calcium carbonate
rationales: Correct. Ginkgo inhibits platelet function and can increase the risk of bleeding with warfarin.
Probiotics are not known to have a significant interaction with warfarin.
Topical aloe on the skin is not expected to affect anticoagulation.
Calcium carbonate does not significantly affect warfarin's anticoagulant effect.
takeaway: Ginkgo, garlic, and ginseng can increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants; ask every client about supplements.

stem: The nurse is performing passive range-of-motion exercises for a client with left-sided hemiplegia. Which technique is correct?
options: Move each joint past the point of resistance to increase flexibility.
Perform the exercises once a week.
Support the limb above and below the joint and move it slowly to the point of resistance.
Perform fast repetitions so the exercise can be completed quickly.
rationales: Forcing beyond resistance can injure joints, muscles, and ligaments.
Range of motion should be done at least two to three times daily to prevent contractures.
Correct. Supporting the limb and moving smoothly to resistance, not pain, protects the joint.
Rapid movement can increase spasticity and cause injury; movements should be slow and smooth.
takeaway: Passive ROM: support the joint, move slowly and smoothly, and stop at resistance or pain.

stem: The nurse is reviewing care for a client with an indwelling urinary catheter. Which actions help prevent catheter-associated urinary tract infection? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the drainage bag below the level of the bladder.
Secure the catheter to the client's upper thigh.
Clean the urinary meatus with soap and water during daily hygiene.
Disconnect the catheter from the tubing to collect a urine specimen.
Irrigate the catheter daily to keep it open.
Rest the drainage bag on the floor so it drains well.
rationales: Correct. This prevents backflow of urine into the bladder.
Correct. Securing the catheter prevents movement and urethral trauma.
Correct. Routine hygiene is recommended; antiseptic cleaning is not needed.
Breaking the closed system lets bacteria enter; specimens are taken from the sampling port.
Routine irrigation is not recommended and opens the closed system.
The bag must not touch the floor because of contamination risk.
takeaway: Prevent CAUTI: closed system, bag below bladder and off the floor, catheter secured, daily hygiene.

stem: The nurse is teaching foot care to a client with diabetes and peripheral neuropathy. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Inspect your feet every day, using a mirror for the soles.
Dry carefully between your toes after washing.
Wear well-fitting shoes and socks, and do not walk barefoot.
Soak your feet in warm water for 20 minutes each day.
Apply lotion between your toes to prevent dryness.
Cut off corns with a razor blade.
rationales: Correct. Loss of sensation means injuries may go unnoticed; daily inspection finds them early.
Correct. Moisture between the toes promotes fungal infection and skin breakdown.
Correct. This protects numb feet from injury.
Soaking dries and macerates skin, and the client may not feel water that is too hot.
Lotion between the toes keeps the area moist and promotes infection; apply it to the tops and soles only.
Self-treating corns can cause wounds and infection; a podiatrist should treat them.
takeaway: Diabetic foot care: inspect daily, keep feet clean and dry, wear shoes, no soaking or self-treating corns.

stem: A client is on bed rest after a stroke. Which interventions should the nurse include to prevent complications of immobility? Select all that apply.
options: Reposition the client at least every 2 hours.
Apply high-top sneakers or foot boots on a schedule.
Encourage deep breathing and coughing every 1 to 2 hours while awake.
Encourage fluid intake of 2 to 3 L daily unless restricted.
Massage reddened areas over bony prominences.
Keep a pillow under the knees at all times.
rationales: Correct. Regular turning relieves pressure on bony prominences.
Correct. Keeping the foot at 90 degrees prevents plantar flexion contracture (footdrop).
Correct. This helps prevent atelectasis and pneumonia.
Correct. Fluids help prevent constipation, urinary stasis, and kidney stones.
Massaging reddened skin can damage underlying tissue and is not recommended.
Constant knee flexion promotes knee contractures and slows venous return.
takeaway: Immobility affects every system: turn, prevent footdrop, deep breathe, and hydrate; never massage reddened bony areas.

stem: A client receiving palliative care for advanced cancer has ongoing nausea. Which nonpharmacological measures should the nurse use? Select all that apply.
options: Offer small, frequent meals of bland, cool foods.
Remove the meal tray cover outside the room and limit strong odors.
Provide oral care before meals.
Have the client lie flat after eating.
Encourage the client to eat three large meals each day.
rationales: Correct. Small portions and cool foods with less odor are better tolerated.
Correct. Strong smells can trigger nausea.
Correct. A clean mouth reduces unpleasant tastes and improves appetite.
Lying flat after meals can increase nausea and reflux; keep the head raised.
Large meals stretch the stomach and worsen nausea.
takeaway: Non-drug nausea relief: small cool bland meals, limit odors, mouth care, and stay upright after eating.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client who is going home with a new fiberglass arm cast. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Keep your arm raised above heart level for the first 24 to 48 hours.
Use a hair dryer on the cool setting if the skin under the cast itches.
Call your provider for numbness, tingling, or pain that gets worse.
Slide a ruler under the cast to scratch an itch.
Sprinkle powder inside the cast to keep it dry.
It is fine to let the cast get wet in the shower.
rationales: Correct. Elevation reduces swelling under the cast.
Correct. Cool air can relieve itching safely.
Correct. These can be signs of nerve or circulation problems such as compartment syndrome.
Objects inside the cast can break the skin and cause infection.
Powder can clump and irritate the skin.
Standard cast padding holds moisture and can cause skin breakdown; the cast should be kept dry unless it has a waterproof liner.
takeaway: Cast care: elevate, keep it dry, nothing inside the cast, and report numbness, tingling, or increasing pain.

stem: Which interventions should the nurse use to promote sleep for a hospitalized client? Select all that apply.
options: Cluster care at night to allow longer periods of uninterrupted sleep.
Dim the lights and reduce noise at night.
Support the client's usual bedtime routine, such as reading.
Offer a cup of coffee with the evening snack.
Leave the television on all night for company.
rationales: Correct. Grouping tasks lets the client complete full sleep cycles.
Correct. A dark, quiet environment supports sleep.
Correct. Familiar routines signal the body to prepare for sleep.
Caffeine is a stimulant and interferes with sleep.
Light and noise from a television disrupt sleep.
takeaway: Promote sleep by clustering care, limiting light and noise, and supporting the client's routines.

stem: A client with dysphagia after a stroke is prescribed thickened liquids. Which actions should the nurse include to prevent aspiration? Select all that apply.
options: Seat the client upright at 90 degrees for meals.
Have the client tuck the chin down when swallowing.
Keep the client upright for at least 30 minutes after eating.
Give liquids at the thickness prescribed by the speech-language pathologist.
Offer liquids through a straw.
Encourage the client to wash down solid food with sips of thin water.
rationales: Correct. An upright position uses gravity to help food move into the esophagus.
Correct. Chin tuck helps protect the airway during swallowing.
Correct. This reduces the risk of reflux and aspiration after meals.
Correct. Thickened liquids move more slowly and are easier to control.
Straws make liquid flow faster and harder to control, which increases aspiration risk.
Mixing consistencies and thin liquids increases aspiration risk for clients with dysphagia.
takeaway: Dysphagia: sit upright, chin tuck, prescribed liquid thickness, no straws, and stay upright 30 minutes after meals.

stem: The nurse is providing oral care to an unconscious client. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Turn the client to the side with the head turned toward the nurse.
Have suction equipment ready at the bedside.
Use a soft toothbrush or swab moistened with a small amount of fluid.
Place the client flat on the back during care.
Rinse the mouth with a large amount of mouthwash.
Use lemon-glycerin swabs to moisten the mouth.
rationales: Correct. Side-lying lets fluid drain out of the mouth instead of into the airway.
Correct. Suction removes pooled fluid and reduces aspiration risk.
Correct. Small amounts of fluid clean the mouth safely.
Supine positioning allows fluid to flow into the airway.
Large amounts of fluid increase aspiration risk.
Lemon-glycerin dries the mucosa and can damage tooth enamel.
takeaway: Oral care for unconscious clients: side-lying, suction ready, small amounts of fluid.

stem: The nurse is giving a cleansing enema to an adult client. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Insert the lubricated tip 7.5 to 10 cm (3 to 4 in) toward the umbilicus while the client breathes out slowly.
Verify the prescription, explain the procedure, and perform hand hygiene.
Lubricate the tip of the tubing just before inserting it.
Raise the container 30 to 45 cm (12 to 18 in) above the anus and let the solution flow in slowly.
Place a waterproof pad, help the client into the left side-lying (Sims) position with the right knee flexed, and put on clean gloves.
rationales: This follows positioning and lubrication; exhaling relaxes the anal sphincter.
This comes first to confirm the order, gain cooperation, and begin infection control.
Lubrication is done immediately before insertion, after the client is positioned, to ease entry and reduce trauma.
Instillation is the last step after the tube is in place; slow flow reduces cramping.
Left side-lying follows the natural curve of the sigmoid colon and rectum; gloves are put on once the client is positioned.
takeaway: Enema: verify and explain, left Sims position and gloves, lubricate, insert 7.5 to 10 cm, then instill slowly from 30 to 45 cm high.

stem: The nurse is changing a client's colostomy pouching system. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Measure the clean, dry stoma with a measuring guide.
Gently remove the old pouch, pushing the skin away from the barrier.
Apply the barrier and hold a hand over it for 30 to 60 seconds.
Clean the skin around the stoma with warm water and pat it dry.
Cut the barrier opening about 1.5 to 3 mm (1/16 to 1/8 in) larger than the stoma.
rationales: Measuring after cleaning ensures an accurate size for the barrier opening.
Removal comes first; pushing the skin away reduces trauma.
Body heat helps the adhesive seal, which is the final step.
Clean, dry skin is needed before measuring and for a good seal.
Done after measuring; a slightly larger opening protects the stoma without exposing much skin.
takeaway: Pouch change: remove, clean and dry, measure, cut to fit, apply and hold.

stem: The nurse is helping a client with right-sided weakness move from the bed to a chair. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Apply a gait belt and help the client stand while bracing the client's weak knee with the nurse's knee.
Pivot the client on the stronger left leg toward the chair.
Before getting the client up, place the chair at the client's left side at a 45-degree angle and lock the bed and chair wheels.
Have the client reach back for the armrests and lower slowly into the chair.
Raise the head of the bed and help the client sit on the edge with feet flat on the floor.
rationales: Standing comes after sitting and dangling; the gait belt gives a secure hold and bracing the weak knee prevents buckling.
The client turns on the strong leg once standing.
Setting up the equipment comes first; the chair goes on the strong side.
This is the last step, giving a controlled sit.
Sitting and dangling first allows the client to adjust and reduces orthostatic dizziness.
takeaway: Transfer toward the strong side: set up and lock, sit and dangle, stand, pivot on the strong leg, sit.

stem: A client is scheduled for a CT scan with IV contrast this afternoon. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider before the scan?
options: The client takes metformin and has a serum creatinine of 2.6 mg/dL.
The client's BUN is 15 mg/dL.
The client's hemoglobin is 13.5 g/dL.
The client says a previous contrast injection caused a brief warm, flushed feeling.
