stem: A nurse reviews new postoperative prescriptions for a 72-year-old opioid-naive client who weighs 60 kg. Which prescription should the nurse clarify before giving any dose?
options: Hydromorphone 10 mg IV every 3 hours as needed for severe pain
Morphine 2 mg IV every 2 hours as needed for severe pain
Oxycodone 5 mg orally every 4 hours as needed for moderate pain
Acetaminophen 650 mg orally every 6 hours
rationales: Hydromorphone is about five to seven times more potent than morphine; usual IV starting doses for an opioid-naive adult are about 0.2 to 1 mg, so 10 mg is a potentially fatal dose and a classic hydromorphone–morphine mix-up.
This is a conservative, appropriate IV morphine dose for an older opioid-naive adult.
This is a usual starting oral dose of oxycodone for an opioid-naive adult.
This totals 2,600 mg per day, well under the maximum daily dose, and is an appropriate opioid-sparing analgesic.
takeaway: Hydromorphone is several times more potent than morphine. A dose in the morphine range (for example, 10 mg IV) is a high-alert error that must be clarified.

stem: A client with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m²) has been receiving morphine every 4 hours for 3 days. The client has become increasingly drowsy and has new myoclonic jerking. Which explanation best accounts for these findings?
options: The client has developed tolerance and needs a higher dose of morphine.
Active morphine metabolites are accumulating because the kidneys cannot excrete them.
The client is experiencing opioid withdrawal.
Morphine is causing an allergic reaction affecting the nervous system.
rationales: Tolerance produces less effect, not increasing sedation; raising the dose would worsen the toxicity.

Morphine-6-glucuronide (sedating) and morphine-3-glucuronide (neuroexcitatory, causing myoclonus) are cleared by the kidneys and accumulate when kidney function is poor, which is why morphine is avoided or reduced in significant kidney disease.
Withdrawal causes agitation, yawning, rhinorrhea and diarrhea while opioid is stopped; this client is receiving regular doses and is drowsy.
True opioid allergy presents with urticaria, facial swelling or anaphylaxis, not sedation and myoclonus.
takeaway: Morphine's active metabolites accumulate in kidney impairment, causing sedation and myoclonus. Older adults and clients with reduced kidney function need lower doses or another opioid.

stem: A client in the emergency department with a migraine takes methadone daily for opioid use disorder. The provider prescribes butorphanol nasal spray. What is the nurse's priority concern?
options: Butorphanol will cause much stronger respiratory depression than methadone alone.
The nasal spray is likely to cause severe nasal bleeding.
Butorphanol may precipitate acute opioid withdrawal in a client who is physically dependent on opioids.
Butorphanol must not be used for headache because it has no analgesic effect.
rationales: Mixed agonist-antagonists have a ceiling on respiratory depression; the main danger in an opioid-dependent client is precipitated withdrawal, not additive depression.
Nasal irritation can occur but significant bleeding is not a typical concern and is not the priority.
Butorphanol is a mixed agonist-antagonist; its mu-receptor antagonist activity can displace methadone and trigger abrupt withdrawal, so it should be avoided in opioid-dependent clients.
Butorphanol does provide analgesia through kappa-receptor agonism and has been used for migraine; its problem here is the interaction with methadone.
takeaway: Mixed agonist-antagonists (butorphanol, nalbuphine) can precipitate withdrawal in clients who are physically dependent on full opioid agonists such as methadone.

stem: A client who had a total hip arthroplasty yesterday is scheduled for physical therapy at 10:00. The client has a prescription for oral oxycodone as needed for pain and reports pain of 4/10 at rest. At what time should the nurse give the oxycodone?
options: 10:00, when therapy begins
After therapy, when the pain is at its worst
07:00, three hours before therapy
rationales: Giving the dose at the start of therapy means the drug is not yet effective during the most painful activity.

Oral oxycodone begins to work in about 10 to 30 minutes and peaks at about 30 to 60 minutes, so giving it 30 to 60 minutes before therapy provides peak relief during the session and supports participation.
Treating pain only after it becomes severe is less effective than preventing it; pain is best managed before predictable painful activity.
By 10:00 the drug will be past its peak and wearing off, so relief during therapy will be limited.
takeaway: Time oral analgesics so peak effect coincides with painful activity. For immediate-release oral opioids, give them about 30 to 60 minutes beforehand.

stem: A nurse finds the spouse of a client who is using an IV morphine PCA pump pressing the dose button while the client sleeps. What is the nurse's priority action?
options: Thank the spouse for helping keep the client comfortable during sleep.
Tell the spouse that only the client may press the button, then assess the client's sedation level and respirations.
Increase the lockout interval so that the spouse cannot give doses as often.
Remove the PCA pump and give morphine by intermittent IV push instead.
rationales: Encouraging PCA by proxy bypasses the built-in safety mechanism and can lead to respiratory depression.

PCA is safe because a client who becomes sedated stops pressing the button; when others press it (PCA by proxy), this safeguard is lost and oversedation can occur, so the nurse stops the practice and checks the client.
Changing pump settings requires a prescription and does not address the unsafe practice of someone other than the client pressing the button.
Stopping PCA is not necessary; education about who may press the button and assessment of the client are the appropriate first steps.
takeaway: Only the client should press the PCA button. Stop PCA by proxy right away and assess sedation and breathing.

stem: A client using an IV morphine PCA pump has the following settings: 1 mg per dose, 10-minute lockout, no basal rate. In the past hour the pump recorded 18 attempts and 6 doses delivered. The client is alert, rates pain 8/10, and has respirations of 18/min. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Tell the client to press the button more often to get more medication.
Report the findings to the provider and request a review of the PCA dose.
Explain that the client is pressing the button too often and may be developing an addiction.
Press the button for the client during the lockout period to deliver an extra dose.
rationales: The pump is already delivering every dose the lockout allows; additional presses will not deliver more drug.

Six doses in an hour is the maximum possible with a 10-minute lockout; frequent unsuccessful attempts and severe pain in an alert client with normal breathing show the current dose is inadequate and needs adjustment.
Frequent demands with uncontrolled pain reflect undertreated pain, not addiction; labeling the client this way is inaccurate and harmful.
The pump will not deliver during lockout, and nurses do not press the button for the client except under a specific authorized-agent protocol.
takeaway: Many attempts with maximum doses delivered and persistent pain in an alert client mean the PCA settings are inadequate. Report it so the dose can be adjusted.

stem: A client with osteoarthritis has taken ibuprofen 800 mg three times daily for several months. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?
options: Mild morning stiffness lasting 20 minutes
Black, tarry stools for the past 2 days
Occasional mild heartburn after meals
Knee pain rated 3/10 after walking
rationales: Brief morning stiffness is typical of osteoarthritis and is not an NSAID adverse effect needing urgent action.
Melena suggests upper gastrointestinal bleeding, a serious and potentially life-threatening complication of long-term NSAID use.
Mild dyspepsia is common with NSAIDs and should be monitored, but it is less urgent than signs of active bleeding.
Mild activity-related pain is consistent with osteoarthritis and does not indicate an adverse drug effect.
takeaway: Long-term NSAID use can cause gastrointestinal bleeding. Black, tarry stools or coffee-ground vomit need prompt reporting.

stem: A 79-year-old client with heart failure takes lisinopril and furosemide. The client begins taking naproxen 500 mg twice daily for shoulder pain. Which laboratory value should the nurse monitor most closely?
options: Serum amylase
Hemoglobin A1C
Thyroid-stimulating hormone
Serum creatinine
rationales: Amylase is used to assess the pancreas and is not affected in a clinically important way by this drug combination.
A1C reflects long-term blood glucose control and is unrelated to the main risk of this combination.
TSH evaluates thyroid function and is not affected by NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors or diuretics.
Combining an NSAID with an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic reduces kidney perfusion and can cause acute kidney injury; a rising creatinine (normal about 0.6 to 1.3 mg/dL) is the key warning sign.
takeaway: An NSAID plus an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) plus a diuretic can cause acute kidney injury, especially in older adults. Monitor creatinine and urine output.

stem: The parent of an 8-year-old with influenza asks whether aspirin can be given for the child's fever and body aches. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Aspirin is safe if you give it with food to protect the stomach.”
“Use a low-dose baby aspirin, which is safe for children.”
“Aspirin is fine once the fever is above 102°F (38.9°C).”
“Do not give aspirin; it is linked to Reye syndrome in children with viral illnesses. Acetaminophen or ibuprofen can be used instead.”
rationales: Giving aspirin with food reduces stomach upset but does not reduce the risk of Reye syndrome.
Low-dose aspirin is still a salicylate and still carries the risk of Reye syndrome in a child with a viral infection.
The degree of fever does not change the risk; aspirin should be avoided in children and teenagers with viral illnesses.

Aspirin and other salicylates given to children and teenagers during viral illnesses such as influenza or chickenpox are associated with Reye syndrome, which causes acute encephalopathy and liver failure.
takeaway: Avoid aspirin and other salicylates in children and teenagers with viral illnesses because of Reye syndrome.

stem: A client with chronic low back pain is starting daily meloxicam. Which instruction about the drug's boxed warning should the nurse include?
options: “Expect your urine to turn reddish-orange while taking this drug.”
“Seek emergency care right away for chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness on one side of your body, or slurred speech.”
“Stop the drug if you develop a dry cough.”
“Take the drug only at bedtime because it causes drowsiness.”
rationales: Meloxicam does not change urine color; this effect is associated with drugs such as rifampin or phenazopyridine.
NSAIDs carry a boxed warning for increased risk of heart attack and stroke, which can occur early in treatment and is higher with long-term use and existing heart disease.
Dry cough is a typical adverse effect of ACE inhibitors, not NSAIDs.
Meloxicam is not notably sedating; the important warnings concern cardiovascular events and GI bleeding.
takeaway: NSAIDs (except low-dose aspirin) carry boxed warnings for heart attack, stroke and GI bleeding. Teach clients the warning signs that need emergency care.

stem: A client discharged with hydrocodone-acetaminophen tablets asks about treating a cold at home. Which client statement indicates understanding of the teaching?
options: “Cold medicines never contain acetaminophen, so I can take any of them.”
“I can take extra-strength acetaminophen with my pain pills, since they are different drugs.”
“If a product says APAP, it means it is aspirin-free and safe to combine.”
“I will check the ingredient list of any cold medicine for acetaminophen or APAP before I take it.”
rationales: Many multi-symptom cold and flu products contain acetaminophen; this belief could lead to overdose.
The prescription tablet already contains acetaminophen; adding more increases the total daily dose and the risk of liver injury.
APAP is an abbreviation for acetaminophen (N-acetyl-para-aminophenol), not a label for an aspirin-free safe product.
Many combination opioid tablets and over-the-counter cold, flu and sleep products contain acetaminophen (sometimes listed as APAP), so reading labels prevents accidental overdose.
takeaway: Acetaminophen hides in combination opioids and OTC cold, flu and sleep products, sometimes labeled as APAP. Teach clients to read every label.

stem: A client who began taking allopurinol 3 weeks ago for chronic gout calls the clinic and reports a new red rash on the trunk and a fever. What should the nurse instruct the client to do?
options: Continue allopurinol and apply hydrocortisone cream to the rash.
Take an extra dose of allopurinol, because the fever means a gout flare is starting.
Take ibuprofen for the fever and call back if the rash lasts longer than 2 weeks.
Stop taking allopurinol and come in to be evaluated today.
rationales: Continuing the drug after a rash appears risks progression to a life-threatening hypersensitivity reaction.
Fever with rash points to a drug reaction, not gout; more allopurinol could worsen the reaction.
Waiting 2 weeks could allow a severe cutaneous reaction to progress; the client needs prompt evaluation.

Allopurinol should be stopped at the first sign of rash because it can be an early sign of a severe hypersensitivity reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome or DRESS, which usually appears within the first months of therapy.
takeaway: Stop allopurinol at the first sign of rash, especially with fever, because it may signal a severe hypersensitivity reaction.

stem: A client with gout who could not tolerate allopurinol is prescribed febuxostat. Which medication on the client's list should the nurse report to the provider?
options: Azathioprine
Omeprazole
Amlodipine
Docusate sodium
rationales: Febuxostat is contraindicated with azathioprine and mercaptopurine because xanthine oxidase inhibition sharply increases their levels, causing severe bone marrow suppression.
Omeprazole does not have a clinically significant interaction with febuxostat.
Amlodipine does not interact meaningfully with febuxostat.
A stool softener has no interaction with febuxostat.
takeaway: Febuxostat (and allopurinol) block xanthine oxidase. Azathioprine and mercaptopurine then accumulate, so febuxostat is contraindicated with them.

stem: A client who has been taking ergotamine-caffeine tablets frequently for migraines calls the clinic. Which reported finding requires immediate evaluation?
options: Mild nausea after taking the tablets
Cold, pale, numb fingers and toes with aching leg muscles
Feeling jittery after a dose
Headache relief within an hour of the dose
rationales: Nausea is a common side effect of ergotamine and is not by itself dangerous.
These are signs of ergotism, peripheral ischemia from ergot-induced vasoconstriction, which can lead to gangrene; the drug should be stopped and the client evaluated right away.
Mild jitteriness is expected from the caffeine component and is not an emergency.
This is the intended therapeutic effect.
takeaway: Overuse of ergotamine can cause ergotism, with cold, numb, pale extremities and muscle pain. Stop the drug and seek urgent evaluation.

stem: A client with spinal cord injury has an implanted intrathecal baclofen pump and missed the scheduled refill appointment. The client now has severe itching, markedly increased muscle spasticity, a temperature of 101.8°F (38.8°C), and new confusion. What should the nurse do?
options: Give acetaminophen for the fever and recheck the temperature in 1 hour.
Notify the provider immediately of possible baclofen withdrawal.
Apply warm packs to the spastic muscles and reposition the client.
Reassure the client that spasticity often fluctuates in spinal cord injury.
rationales: Treating the fever alone delays recognition of a life-threatening withdrawal syndrome.

Abrupt interruption of intrathecal baclofen causes high fever, altered mental status, rebound spasticity and pruritus, which can progress to rhabdomyolysis, multiple organ failure and death; it requires emergency treatment and restoration of baclofen.
Comfort measures do not address the cause, which is loss of baclofen delivery.
Fever, confusion and severe rebound spasticity together are not a normal fluctuation and must be reported urgently.
takeaway: Intrathecal baclofen withdrawal (fever, altered mental status, rebound spasticity, itching) is a medical emergency. Report it immediately.

stem: A client who takes oxycodone 10 mg every 6 hours for cancer pain is started on gabapentin for neuropathic pain. Which nursing action is the priority after the first doses?
options: Check serum potassium every morning.
Measure blood glucose before each dose.
Monitor sedation level and respiratory rate closely.
Assess for pinpoint pupils as the main sign of toxicity.
rationales: Gabapentin does not affect potassium, and potassium monitoring is not part of this drug combination.
Gabapentin does not cause clinically important changes in blood glucose.
Gabapentinoids taken with opioids increase the risk of serious respiratory depression and oversedation, an FDA warning that applies especially to older adults and clients with lung disease.
Miosis is expected with opioids and is not a reliable sign of dangerous toxicity; sedation and respiratory status are the key assessments.
takeaway: Gabapentin or pregabalin added to an opioid increases the risk of respiratory depression. Monitor sedation and respirations closely, especially at first.

stem: A client who began taking pregabalin for diabetic peripheral neuropathy 1 week ago calls the clinic. Which reported symptom requires immediate action?
options: Mild dizziness when standing up
Dry mouth
Gaining 2 lb (0.9 kg) over the week
Swelling of the lips and tongue
rationales: Dizziness is a common, expected side effect that is managed with caution and slow position changes.
Dry mouth is a common, minor side effect of pregabalin.
Modest weight gain and mild peripheral edema can occur with pregabalin; they are monitored but are not emergencies.
Pregabalin can cause swelling of the face, mouth and throat that may compromise the airway; the client should stop the drug and seek emergency care.
takeaway: Pregabalin can cause serious allergic-type swelling. Swelling of the face, lips or tongue needs emergency care; dizziness and sleepiness are common and expected.

stem: A client who takes duloxetine for diabetic neuropathic pain was prescribed tramadol 2 days ago for a knee injury. Which finding should the nurse report immediately?
options: Temperature of 102.6°F (39.2°C), agitation, tremor, and muscle twitching
Mild nausea after taking duloxetine
Dry mouth
Slight drowsiness in the evening
rationales: Duloxetine (an SNRI) and tramadol both increase serotonin; hyperthermia, agitation, tremor and myoclonus or hyperreflexia indicate serotonin syndrome, which can be fatal.
Nausea is a common duloxetine side effect, especially early in therapy, and is not an emergency.
Dry mouth is a common, minor side effect of both drugs.
Mild drowsiness is expected with tramadol and does not suggest serotonin syndrome.
takeaway: SNRIs or SSRIs combined with tramadol (or other serotonergic drugs) can cause serotonin syndrome: hyperthermia, agitation, tremor, clonus and hyperreflexia.

stem: A client with chronic low back pain asks the nurse what can be done besides medication. Which recommendation is most appropriate?
options: Stay on bed rest until the pain is completely gone.
Wear a lumbar brace at all times, including during sleep.
Take part in a regular exercise program such as yoga or tai chi.
Avoid any activity that causes even mild discomfort.
rationales: Prolonged bed rest leads to deconditioning and slower recovery; staying active is recommended.
Continuous bracing weakens core muscles and is not supported for chronic low back pain.
Exercise-based therapies such as yoga and tai chi, along with mindfulness and cognitive behavioral approaches, are recommended first-line nonpharmacologic treatments for chronic low back pain.
Avoiding all activity promotes fear-avoidance and disability; gradual, guided activity is encouraged.
takeaway: For chronic low back pain, stay active. Exercise, yoga, tai chi and mind-body therapies come before medication, and bed rest is avoided.

stem: A client with diabetic peripheral neuropathy wants to use a warm pack for an aching shoulder. Which instruction is most important?
options: “Check the pack's temperature on skin with normal feeling, place a cloth between the pack and your skin, and limit use to about 20 minutes.”
“Use the highest setting, since your nerves will not feel the heat well.”
“Fall asleep with the heating pad on the low setting to keep the muscles relaxed overnight.”
“Place the warm pack directly on your skin so the heat penetrates better.”
rationales: Reduced sensation means the client may not feel a burn developing; testing temperature on skin with normal sensation, using a barrier and limiting the time prevent thermal injury.
Higher heat greatly increases the risk of burns in a client who cannot sense excessive temperature.
Prolonged heat application, even on low, can cause burns, especially when the client is asleep and has reduced sensation.
Direct contact without a barrier increases the risk of burns.
takeaway: Heat is a useful comfort measure, but clients with reduced sensation need a barrier, a time limit (about 20 minutes) and a temperature check on skin with normal feeling.

stem: A nurse is assessing pain in a 5-year-old who had a tonsillectomy this morning. The child is awake and talking. Which pain assessment tool is most appropriate?
options: 0-to-10 numeric rating scale
FLACC (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability) scale
Wong-Baker FACES Pain Rating Scale
CRIES neonatal pain scale
rationales: Numeric scales require an understanding of numbers and proportion and are generally used for children about 8 years and older.
FLACC is a behavioral scale for infants, toddlers and children who cannot self-report; a verbal 5-year-old should be asked to self-report.
The FACES scale is validated for children about 3 years and older who can point to the face that matches how they feel, so it is appropriate for a verbal preschooler.
CRIES is designed for postoperative pain in neonates, not preschool children.
takeaway: Match the pain tool to the child's development: FLACC for preverbal children, FACES for about age 3 and up, and numeric scales for about age 8 and up.

stem: A nurse is preparing to perform a heel stick on a 2-day-old newborn. Which intervention is most effective for reducing procedural pain?
options: Give oral acetaminophen immediately before the heel stick.
Apply a topical lidocaine-prilocaine cream to the heel right before the stick.
Give oral sucrose solution on a pacifier about 2 minutes before the heel stick.
Wait until the newborn is in deep sleep so the newborn will not feel the stick.
rationales: Acetaminophen has not been shown to reduce the pain of heel lance in newborns and is not used for this purpose.
Topical anesthetic cream needs about an hour to work and has not been shown to reduce heel lance pain; applying it right before the procedure has no effect.

Oral sucrose with non-nutritive sucking given about 2 minutes before a brief painful procedure is an evidence-based way to reduce newborn pain; skin-to-skin contact, swaddling and breastfeeding also help.
Newborns feel pain whether asleep or awake; waking a sleeping infant with a painful procedure does not prevent pain.
takeaway: For brief newborn procedures, use oral sucrose with a pacifier, skin-to-skin contact, swaddling or breastfeeding. Newborns feel pain even when asleep.

stem: A client 2 days after a laminectomy is laughing with visitors and tells the nurse, “My back pain is 8 out of 10.” The client has a prescription for an as-needed analgesic and is alert with normal respirations. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept the client's rating, give the prescribed analgesic, and reassess its effect.
Withhold the analgesic because the client's behavior does not match the rating.
Ask the visitors to leave so the client will report a more accurate rating.
Document that the client appears to be exaggerating the pain.
rationales: Pain is what the client says it is; self-report is the most reliable indicator, and behaviors such as laughing or distraction do not rule out severe pain.
Clients cope with pain in many ways, including humor and distraction; withholding analgesia based on behavior leads to undertreated pain.
This implies the client's report is unreliable and isolates the client without addressing the pain.
This judgment is biased and unsupported; the nurse should document the client's own rating and the response to treatment.
takeaway: Self-report is the gold standard for pain. Behaviors such as laughing, sleeping or normal vital signs do not disprove a client's pain rating.

stem: A nurse reviews prescriptions for an 84-year-old client with reduced kidney function who has hip fracture pain. Which prescription should the nurse question?
options: Acetaminophen 650 mg orally every 6 hours
Oxycodone 2.5 mg orally every 4 hours as needed
Senna 8.6 mg orally at bedtime
Meperidine 50 mg IM every 4 hours as needed
rationales: Scheduled acetaminophen within the daily maximum is a recommended first-line analgesic for older adults.
A low starting dose of oxycodone is appropriate for an older adult with moderate to severe pain, with monitoring.
A stimulant laxative is appropriate to prevent opioid-induced constipation.

Meperidine is on the Beers Criteria list of drugs to avoid in older adults; its metabolite normeperidine accumulates, especially with reduced kidney function, causing tremors, delirium and seizures, and it is a poor analgesic.
takeaway: Avoid meperidine, especially in older adults and in kidney impairment, because normeperidine accumulates and can cause seizures.

stem: A client has received ketorolac 15 mg IV every 6 hours for 4 days after abdominal surgery. A new prescription continues IV ketorolac for 3 more days. Which action by the nurse is appropriate?
options: Give the drug as prescribed, since the IV route avoids stomach irritation.
Change to oral ketorolac to continue the 3-day course.
Contact the provider, because the total course of ketorolac should not exceed 5 days.
Give the drug and monitor only the client's pain rating.
rationales: NSAID GI toxicity is systemic, from prostaglandin inhibition, so the IV route does not prevent GI bleeding.
Oral ketorolac counts toward the same 5-day total limit, and the nurse cannot change the route without a prescription.
Ketorolac (IV, IM and oral combined) is limited to 5 days because the risk of GI bleeding and acute kidney injury rises with longer use; 7 days total exceeds this limit.
Even within the limit, ketorolac requires monitoring of kidney function, bleeding and GI symptoms; here the duration itself must be clarified.
takeaway: Ketorolac is limited to 5 days in total by all routes combined because of GI bleeding and kidney injury risk.

stem: Thirty minutes after receiving morphine 4 mg IV for the first time, a postoperative client asks to walk to the bathroom. What should the nurse do first?
options: Tell the client to walk alone to promote independence.
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter so the client does not need to get up.
Give a PRN antiemetic before the client stands up.
Have the client sit on the side of the bed for a few minutes, then assist the client to walk.
rationales: Walking unassisted soon after the first IV opioid dose puts the client at risk of falling from dizziness or orthostatic hypotension.
Catheterization requires a prescription, increases infection risk and is not needed to manage this situation.
An antiemetic does not prevent orthostatic hypotension and is not indicated without nausea.
Opioids can cause orthostatic hypotension and dizziness; dangling first and assisting the client help prevent a fall.
takeaway: After opioid doses, especially the first, change position slowly and assist with ambulation to prevent falls from orthostatic hypotension and dizziness.

stem: A nurse is identifying postoperative clients at increased risk for opioid-induced respiratory depression. Which client factors increase this risk? Select all that apply.
options: Obstructive sleep apnea
No opioid use before surgery
Takes lorazepam at bedtime
Age 78 years
Has taken a stable dose of opioid for chronic pain for 2 years
Pain rated 8/10
rationales: Correct. Clients with sleep apnea already have airway obstruction during sleep, and opioids further blunt arousal and respiratory drive.
Correct. Opioid-naive clients have not developed tolerance to respiratory depression and are at higher risk, especially in the first 24 hours.
Correct. Benzodiazepines add to opioid central nervous system and respiratory depression.
Correct. Older adults have reduced drug clearance and greater sensitivity to opioid sedation.
Incorrect. Long-term opioid use produces tolerance to respiratory depression, so this is not a risk factor compared with opioid-naive clients (although dose increases still need monitoring).
Incorrect. Pain stimulates respiration; severe pain itself is not a risk factor for respiratory depression, although it does require careful dose titration.
takeaway: High risk for opioid respiratory depression: opioid-naive, older age, sleep apnea or obesity, lung disease, and other sedatives such as benzodiazepines or gabapentinoids.

stem: A nurse is teaching a client who is starting naproxen for osteoarthritis. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Take each dose with food or milk.
Take the tablets on an empty stomach so they work faster.
Report black stools or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Do not take over-the-counter ibuprofen along with naproxen.
Swelling of the ankles and weight gain are harmless and can be ignored.
rationales: Correct. Taking NSAIDs with food reduces gastric irritation.
Incorrect. Taking NSAIDs on an empty stomach increases GI irritation and the risk of ulcers.
Correct. These are signs of GI bleeding, a serious NSAID adverse effect.
Correct. Combining NSAIDs adds GI, kidney and cardiovascular risk without added benefit.
Incorrect. NSAIDs cause sodium and fluid retention, which can worsen hypertension or heart failure; edema and weight gain should be reported.
takeaway: NSAID teaching: take with food, use only one NSAID at a time, and report GI bleeding, edema, weight gain and cardiovascular warning signs.

stem: A client is taking prescribed acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours. The nurse teaches the client to avoid duplicating acetaminophen. Which products contain acetaminophen? Select all that apply.
options: Oxycodone-acetaminophen (Percocet)
NyQuil Cold & Flu
Naproxen sodium (Aleve)
Excedrin Migraine
Ibuprofen (Advil)
Tylenol PM
rationales: Correct. This combination opioid contains acetaminophen in every tablet.
Correct. This nighttime multi-symptom product contains acetaminophen along with dextromethorphan and doxylamine.
Incorrect. Naproxen is an NSAID and contains no acetaminophen.
Correct. This product combines acetaminophen, aspirin and caffeine.
Incorrect. Ibuprofen is an NSAID and does not contain acetaminophen.
Correct. This sleep product contains acetaminophen and diphenhydramine.
takeaway: Acetaminophen is found in many combination opioids, cold and flu remedies, migraine products and 'PM' sleep aids. Teach clients to count every source toward the daily limit.

stem: A client is receiving a continuous peripheral nerve block infusion of ropivacaine after shoulder surgery. Which findings should the nurse recognize as early signs of local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)? Select all that apply.
options: Numbness around the mouth
Metallic taste
Pinpoint pupils
Ringing in the ears
Numbness of the operative arm
rationales: Correct. Circumoral numbness is a classic early central nervous system sign of LAST.
Correct. A metallic taste is an early neurologic warning sign of rising local anesthetic levels.
Incorrect. Miosis is associated with opioids, not local anesthetic toxicity.
Correct. Tinnitus is an early sign of local anesthetic toxicity that may progress to seizures and cardiac dysrhythmias.
Incorrect. Numbness in the blocked extremity is the intended effect of a peripheral nerve block.
takeaway: Early LAST signs include circumoral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, dizziness and agitation; it can progress to seizures and cardiac arrest. Stop the infusion and get help.

stem: A nurse is teaching a client with chronic cancer pain who uses transdermal fentanyl. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Avoid heating pads, electric blankets, hot tubs and saunas.
Replace the patch every 24 hours.
Fold a used patch in half with the sticky sides together before disposal.
Call the provider if you develop a fever.
Cut the patch in half on days when your pain is less.
Store patches where children and pets cannot reach them.
rationales: Correct. Heat increases blood flow to the skin and fentanyl absorption, which can cause an overdose.
Incorrect. Most fentanyl patches are changed every 72 hours; changing every 24 hours could cause overdose.
Correct. Used patches still contain fentanyl; folding them and disposing of them as directed (such as flushing, per FDA guidance) prevents accidental exposure.
Correct. Fever raises skin temperature and can increase fentanyl absorption.
Incorrect. Cutting a fentanyl patch damages the controlled release and can cause a rapid, dangerous dose.
Correct. Even one patch can cause fatal respiratory depression in a child or pet.
takeaway: Fentanyl patch safety: no heat, report fever, never cut, change on schedule (usually every 72 hours), and store and discard so children and pets cannot be exposed.

stem: A nurse uses the PAINAD scale to assess pain in a client with advanced dementia who cannot give a self-report. Which observations suggest the client is in pain? Select all that apply.
options: Grimacing
Moaning when repositioned
Absence of crying, so the client has no pain
Clenched fists and rigid body posture
Heart rate of 92/min as the main proof of pain
rationales: Correct. Facial grimacing is a key behavioral indicator of pain in nonverbal clients.
Correct. Negative vocalizations such as moaning or groaning indicate possible pain.
Incorrect. Lack of crying does not mean lack of pain; clients with dementia often show pain in other ways.
Correct. Rigid or tense body language and clenched fists are PAINAD indicators of pain.
Incorrect. Vital signs are unreliable indicators of pain and should not be used alone to confirm or rule it out.
takeaway: In nonverbal clients, look at behavior (face, vocalizations, body language, breathing, consolability). Vital signs are not reliable pain indicators.

stem: A nurse is planning nonpharmacologic pain relief for a client 1 day after an open abdominal surgery. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Teach the client to splint the incision with a pillow when coughing.
Use nonpharmacologic methods in place of prescribed analgesics.
Offer music or guided imagery the client enjoys.
Keep the client flat and still to avoid stretching the incision.
Reposition the client and support the body with pillows.
Apply a heating pad directly to the incision.
rationales: Correct. Splinting supports the incision and lessens pain during coughing and deep breathing.
Incorrect. Nonpharmacologic methods add to, but do not replace, analgesics for moderate to severe postoperative pain.
Correct. Distraction and relaxation techniques reduce pain perception and anxiety.
Incorrect. Immobility increases the risk of complications such as pneumonia and thrombosis; early ambulation with pain control is encouraged.
Correct. Regular repositioning with support reduces muscle tension and pressure discomfort.
Incorrect. Heat on a fresh incision can increase swelling and bleeding and risks burns; cold may be used if prescribed.
takeaway: Nonpharmacologic measures (splinting, positioning, distraction, relaxation) complement analgesics; they do not replace them.

stem: A nurse is assessing pain in a client with severe dementia who cannot reliably answer questions. Place the steps of the pain assessment hierarchy for nonverbal clients in the correct order.
options: Try an analgesic and watch for a change in pain behaviors.
Observe pain behaviors using a validated tool.
Attempt to obtain a self-report, even a simple yes or no or a pointed answer.
Ask family members or caregivers who know the client well about changes in behavior.
Search for potential causes of pain, such as recent surgery, fractures, or pressure injuries.
rationales: Step 5. An analgesic trial is the final step; a reduction in pain behaviors after treatment confirms that pain was likely the cause.
Step 3. Behaviors such as grimacing, moaning or guarding provide evidence of pain when self-report is not possible.
Step 1. Self-report is always attempted first because it is the most reliable indicator, and many cognitively impaired clients can give a simple answer.
Step 4. Surrogates can describe the client's usual behavior and recognize changes that may signal pain.
Step 2. If a painful condition or procedure is present, pain should be assumed present.
takeaway: Hierarchy for nonverbal clients: self-report, causes of pain, behaviors, surrogate report, then an analgesic trial.

stem: A nurse is teaching a client how to use lidocaine 5% topical patches prescribed for postherpetic neuralgia. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Cut the patch to fit the painful area, if needed, before removing the release liner.
Remove the patch after 12 hours.
Inspect the painful area to make sure the skin is intact.
Leave the skin uncovered for 12 hours before applying the next patch.
Remove the release liner and apply the patch to the most painful area.
rationales: Step 2. Patches may be cut to size, and cutting before removing the liner keeps the adhesive manageable.
Step 4. Lidocaine 5% patches are worn for up to 12 hours in a 24-hour period.
Step 1. Lidocaine patches are applied only to intact skin, because broken skin increases absorption and the risk of toxicity.
Step 5. A 12-hour patch-free period limits systemic absorption and skin irritation.
Step 3. The patch is then placed directly over the area of neuropathic pain.
takeaway: Lidocaine 5% patches: intact skin only, cut before removing the liner, wear up to 12 hours, then 12 hours off.

stem: A client with community-acquired pneumonia has a documented history of throat swelling and low blood pressure after taking amoxicillin 5 years ago. The new prescription is amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg orally every 12 hours. What is the nurse's best action?
options: Give the first dose and observe the client closely for 30 minutes.
Withhold the medication and contact the prescriber for an alternative antibiotic.
Give diphenhydramine 30 minutes before the first dose.
Give the dose with food to lower the risk of a reaction.
rationales: Amoxicillin-clavulanate contains amoxicillin, the exact drug that caused a prior anaphylactic reaction; observation does not make giving it safe.
Throat swelling and hypotension describe anaphylaxis. Giving the same penicillin again risks a life-threatening reaction, so the nurse holds the dose and clarifies the order.
Antihistamine premedication does not prevent an IgE-mediated anaphylactic reaction and can mask early warning signs.
Food reduces gastrointestinal upset from amoxicillin-clavulanate; it has no effect on allergic reactions.
takeaway: Always compare a new prescription with the client's allergy history. A penicillin combination product (such as amoxicillin-clavulanate or piperacillin-tazobactam) is still a penicillin.

stem: A client receives vancomycin every 12 hours, and the next dose is due at 2100. The prescriber orders a trough level. When should the nurse arrange for the blood sample to be drawn?
options: 30 minutes after the 2100 infusion is finished
Within 30 minutes before the 2100 dose
As soon as the 2100 infusion is started
At any time during the shift, as long as the time is recorded
rationales: A sample drawn shortly after the infusion reflects a level near the peak, not the trough.
A trough is the lowest concentration and is drawn just before the next dose (usually within 30 minutes). Many facilities now use AUC-based dosing with timed levels; the nurse follows the protocol.
Once the infusion starts, the serum level begins to rise, so the result would not be a true trough.
Vancomycin levels are only interpretable when drawn at the correct time in relation to the dose.
takeaway: Draw a trough immediately before the next dose. Hold the dose until the sample is drawn, and follow the facility's vancomycin protocol.

stem: Ms. Okafor, 66, has received IV vancomycin and IV piperacillin-tazobactam for 4 days for an infected diabetic foot ulcer. Which finding should the nurse report to the prescriber immediately?
options: WBC 10,800/mm³, down from 16,000/mm³ on admission
Fingerstick blood glucose of 168 mg/dL before lunch
Serum creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, up from a baseline of 0.9 mg/dL
Mild nausea after breakfast
rationales: A falling WBC count suggests that the infection is responding to treatment; it is an expected, favorable trend.
Mild hyperglycemia is common during infection in a client with diabetes. It needs follow-up but is not as urgent as a rising creatinine.

Creatinine has doubled (normal about 0.6–1.2 mg/dL), indicating acute kidney injury. Vancomycin is nephrotoxic, and adding piperacillin-tazobactam increases the risk. The prescriber may need to adjust or change therapy.
Mild nausea is a common, minor effect of antibiotics and does not need immediate reporting.
takeaway: Monitor creatinine and urine output during vancomycin therapy, especially with other nephrotoxic drugs. A rising creatinine is reported promptly.

stem: A client is receiving vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV every 12 hours for osteomyelitis. Which assessments should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Serum creatinine and urine output
Client reports of ringing in the ears or hearing changes
Flushing, itching or rash on the face, neck and upper body during the infusion
Serum vancomycin levels at the times set by protocol
Daily INR
Serum amylase
rationales: Correct. Vancomycin can cause nephrotoxicity, so kidney function is monitored throughout therapy.
Correct. Ototoxicity is a known, though less common, adverse effect, especially with high levels or other ototoxic drugs.
Correct. These signs suggest vancomycin infusion reaction, which is managed by stopping or slowing the infusion.
Correct. Levels (trough or AUC-based) guide dosing to balance effectiveness against toxicity.
Incorrect. Vancomycin does not affect clotting factors; INR is not routinely needed.
Incorrect. Pancreatitis is not a recognized adverse effect of vancomycin that requires routine monitoring.
takeaway: Vancomycin monitoring centers on the kidneys, hearing, the infusion rate and drug levels.

stem: A client receiving IV gentamicin for Pseudomonas pneumonia has several new prescriptions. Which medication requires the closest monitoring because it adds to gentamicin's risk of ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity?
options: Pantoprazole 40 mg IV daily
Furosemide 40 mg IV every 12 hours
Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily
Acetaminophen 650 mg orally every 6 hours as needed
rationales: Pantoprazole does not increase the risk of aminoglycoside ototoxicity or nephrotoxicity.
Loop diuretics are ototoxic, and the volume loss they cause can concentrate aminoglycosides and harm the kidneys. The nurse monitors hearing, creatinine, urine output and drug levels closely.
Enoxaparin raises the risk of bleeding but does not add to aminoglycoside toxicity. Its dose may need adjustment if kidney function declines.
Acetaminophen at this dose is not ototoxic or nephrotoxic and does not interact with gentamicin.
takeaway: Loop diuretics with aminoglycosides increase the risk of hearing loss and kidney injury. Monitor hearing, creatinine and levels closely.

stem: Mr. Delgado, 74, takes prednisone 10 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica. He started levofloxacin 3 days ago for pneumonia and now reports sudden pain and swelling just above his right heel. What should the nurse do first?
options: Apply a heating pad and encourage him to keep walking.
Give ibuprofen and reassess the pain in 1 hour.
Hold the next levofloxacin dose, have him rest the leg and notify the prescriber.
Teach him calf-stretching exercises to relieve the tightness.
rationales: Heat and walking could worsen a damaged Achilles tendon and increase the risk of rupture.
An analgesic may hide symptoms without dealing with the cause, which is suspected fluoroquinolone tendinitis.

Fluoroquinolones carry a boxed warning for tendinitis and tendon rupture, and the risk is higher in adults over 60 and in clients taking corticosteroids. The drug should be stopped and the tendon rested.
Stretching puts stress on an inflamed tendon and could cause it to rupture.
takeaway: Tendon pain during fluoroquinolone therapy: hold the drug, rest the limb and report it. The risk is higher with age over 60 and with corticosteroids.

stem: The nurse reviews the history of a client who has been prescribed levofloxacin. Which findings increase the client's risk of a serious adverse reaction to this drug? Select all that apply.
options: Age 78 years
Takes prednisone 5 mg daily
Hypothyroidism controlled with levothyroxine
History of myasthenia gravis
Lactose intolerance
Appendectomy 20 years ago
rationales: Correct. Adults over 60 have a higher risk of fluoroquinolone-associated tendinitis and tendon rupture.
Correct. Corticosteroid use further increases the risk of tendon rupture with fluoroquinolones.
Incorrect. Treated hypothyroidism is not a recognized risk factor for serious fluoroquinolone reactions.
Correct. Fluoroquinolones can worsen myasthenic weakness, including respiratory muscle weakness (boxed warning).
Incorrect. Lactose intolerance does not affect fluoroquinolone safety.
Incorrect. A remote abdominal surgery has no bearing on fluoroquinolone risk.
takeaway: Major fluoroquinolone risk flags: age over 60, corticosteroids, organ transplant, myasthenia gravis and QT-prolonging conditions or drugs.

stem: A 70-year-old client receiving IV azithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia also takes citalopram for depression. Which finding should the nurse report immediately?
options: QTc of 528 ms on today's ECG, up from 440 ms at admission
Two loose stools since yesterday
Mild nausea after the morning dose
Slight discomfort at the IV site during the infusion
rationales: Azithromycin and citalopram both prolong the QT interval. A QTc above 500 ms (normal is below about 450 ms in men and 460 ms in women) greatly increases the risk of torsades de pointes and must be reported at once.
Mild diarrhea is a common effect of macrolides. It should be monitored but is not as urgent as a dangerously long QTc.
Nausea is a common, minor effect of macrolides.
IV azithromycin can cause discomfort at the infusion site. This is minor and is managed by checking the site and following the dilution and rate instructions.
takeaway: Macrolides can prolong the QT interval, especially when given with other QT-prolonging drugs. Report a QTc above 500 ms or a large increase from baseline.

stem: Which client's prescription for oral tetracycline should the nurse question?
options: A 45-year-old with rosacea
A 50-year-old receiving bismuth quadruple therapy for Helicobacter pylori
A 22-year-old man with moderate inflammatory acne
A 24-year-old with acne who is 14 weeks pregnant
rationales: Tetracyclines are commonly used for inflammatory rosacea in nonpregnant adults.
Tetracycline is a standard part of bismuth quadruple therapy for H. pylori.
Tetracyclines are appropriate for moderate inflammatory acne in nonpregnant adults.
Tetracyclines are avoided in pregnancy, especially after the first trimester, because they deposit in developing teeth and bone, causing permanent tooth discoloration and impaired bone growth.
takeaway: Avoid tetracyclines in pregnancy and in children under 8 years (short courses of doxycycline are an exception), because they stain developing teeth and affect bone growth.

stem: On day 9 of sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim therapy, Ms. Nguyen, 34, reports fever, burning eyes and painful mouth sores. She has a dusky red rash with small blisters spreading across her trunk. What should the nurse do first?
options: Apply hydrocortisone cream to the rash.
Give diphenhydramine and continue the antibiotic.
Hold the next dose and notify the provider immediately.
Encourage saltwater mouth rinses and reassess tomorrow.
rationales: Topical steroids do not treat a severe systemic drug reaction and would delay the essential step of stopping the drug.
Continuing the suspected cause allows a potentially fatal reaction to progress.
Fever, mucosal involvement and a blistering, dusky rash suggest Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Stopping the drug at once is the most important factor in outcome, and urgent evaluation is needed.
Supportive mouth care may help later, but waiting to act on a possible Stevens-Johnson syndrome is unsafe.
takeaway: A blistering rash with fever and mucosal sores during sulfonamide therapy suggests Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Stop the drug and report it immediately.

stem: An 81-year-old client with chronic kidney disease takes lisinopril daily and has been taking sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim for 5 days. Which laboratory result is the priority to report?
options: Sodium 137 mEq/L
Potassium 6.2 mEq/L
Fasting glucose 112 mg/dL
WBC 9,200/mm³
rationales: This is within the normal range of 135–145 mEq/L.

This is above the normal range of 3.5–5 mEq/L. Trimethoprim blocks potassium excretion in the kidney, much like amiloride, and with an ACE inhibitor, chronic kidney disease and older age it can cause dangerous hyperkalemia and dysrhythmias.
This is slightly above the normal fasting range of 70–99 mg/dL, but it is not an urgent problem.
This is within the normal range of about 5,000–10,000/mm³ and suggests that the infection is controlled.
takeaway: Trimethoprim can raise potassium. Watch for hyperkalemia in older adults, clients with kidney disease and clients taking ACE inhibitors, ARBs or potassium-sparing diuretics.

stem: Mr. Brooks, 62, has taken oral clindamycin for 6 days for a dental abscess. He now reports five watery stools in 24 hours, lower abdominal cramping and a temperature of 100.6 °F (38.1 °C). Which action is most appropriate?
options: Give loperamide to slow the diarrhea.
Encourage a high-fiber diet to firm up the stools.
Tell him that diarrhea is an expected side effect and to keep taking the medicine.
Notify the provider, anticipate a stool test for C. difficile and start contact precautions.
rationales: Antimotility drugs are avoided in suspected C. difficile infection because they can keep the toxin in the colon and raise the risk of toxic megacolon.
Dietary fiber does not treat C. difficile infection and delays appropriate evaluation.
Watery diarrhea with fever and cramping after clindamycin is not a minor side effect. It suggests C. difficile infection, which needs testing.
Clindamycin is strongly linked to C. difficile infection. Three or more unformed stools in 24 hours with fever and cramping call for testing, contact precautions and review of the antibiotic.
takeaway: New watery diarrhea during or after antibiotics (especially clindamycin) suggests C. difficile. Test, isolate, avoid antimotility drugs and report it.

stem: A client with Clostridioides difficile infection is discharged. Which instruction should the nurse give environmental services for cleaning the room?
options: Use an EPA-registered sporicidal disinfectant, such as a bleach-based product.
Wipe surfaces with alcohol-based wipes.
Use the standard quaternary ammonium cleaner used in other rooms.
Do routine cleaning only, because the client's diarrhea had stopped before discharge.
rationales: C. difficile forms spores that resist many routine disinfectants. Sporicidal agents, such as chlorine-based products, are needed to kill them on surfaces.
Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores.
Most quaternary ammonium products are not sporicidal and will not reliably remove C. difficile spores.
Spores survive on surfaces for months whether or not the client still has symptoms, so enhanced cleaning is still needed.
takeaway: C. difficile spores need soap-and-water hand washing and sporicidal (for example, bleach-based) environmental cleaning. Alcohol does not kill them.

stem: The nurse is caring for a client with C. difficile infection. Which infection-control measures are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Wash hands with soap and water after removing gloves.
Put on a gown and gloves when entering the room.
Use a dedicated stethoscope and blood pressure cuff for this client.
Use alcohol-based hand rub alone when leaving the room.
Wear a fit-tested N95 respirator during care.
Place the client in a private room or with another client who has C. difficile.
rationales: Correct. Scrubbing with soap and running water physically removes spores, which alcohol-based rubs do not kill.
Correct. Contact precautions require a gown and gloves for all room entries.
Correct. Dedicated equipment prevents spores from being carried to other clients.
Incorrect. Alcohol-based rubs do not kill C. difficile spores.
Incorrect. C. difficile is spread by contact, not through the air; a respirator is not required.
Correct. A private room or cohorting reduces spread to other clients.
takeaway: C. difficile: contact precautions, a private room, dedicated equipment and soap-and-water hand hygiene.

stem: Mrs. Lindqvist, 78, has taken nitrofurantoin nightly for 6 months to prevent recurrent urinary tract infections. She reports a new dry cough and shortness of breath when walking, and the nurse hears fine crackles in both lung bases. What should the nurse do?
options: Reassure her that the cough is probably from seasonal allergies.
Encourage her to increase her fluid intake.
Report the findings promptly, because nitrofurantoin can cause pulmonary reactions.
Suggest an over-the-counter cough suppressant at bedtime.
rationales: Attributing new respiratory symptoms to allergies could delay recognition of a serious drug reaction.
Fluids do not address the possibility of drug-induced lung injury.

Long-term nitrofurantoin can cause chronic pulmonary reactions, such as interstitial pneumonitis or fibrosis, especially in older adults. The drug may need to be stopped, so the findings must be reported promptly.
Suppressing the cough hides an important symptom and does not treat the cause.
takeaway: New cough, dyspnea or crackles in a client on long-term nitrofurantoin may be a pulmonary reaction. Report it promptly.

stem: A client who takes sertraline for depression is started on IV linezolid for a VRE wound infection. Which findings should the nurse recognize as possible signs of serotonin syndrome? Select all that apply.
options: Agitation and restlessness
Temperature of 102.4 °F (39.1 °C)
Hyperreflexia with clonus in the ankles
Heavy sweating
Bradycardia and lethargy
Flaccid muscles with absent reflexes
rationales: Correct. Changes in mental status, such as agitation, anxiety or confusion, are common in serotonin syndrome.
Correct. Hyperthermia reflects autonomic instability and increased muscle activity.
Correct. Neuromuscular hyperactivity, especially clonus and hyperreflexia, is a key feature.
Correct. Diaphoresis is a sign of autonomic overactivity.
Incorrect. Serotonin syndrome usually causes tachycardia and agitation, not bradycardia and sedation.
Incorrect. Serotonin syndrome causes increased muscle tone and reflexes, not flaccidity.
takeaway: Linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor. With SSRIs, watch for agitation, fever, sweating, tachycardia, hyperreflexia and clonus.

stem: A client being discharged on oral linezolid is choosing meals from a menu. Which selection indicates a need for further teaching?
options: Grilled chicken breast with rice and green beans
Scrambled eggs with whole-wheat toast
Baked fresh salmon with a garden salad
An aged cheddar and salami sandwich with a draft (tap) beer
rationales: Fresh poultry, rice and vegetables are low in tyramine and safe to eat with linezolid.
Fresh eggs and bread are low in tyramine.
Fresh fish and fresh vegetables are low in tyramine.
Aged cheese, cured meats and tap beer are high in tyramine. Because linezolid inhibits monoamine oxidase, large amounts of tyramine can cause a sudden rise in blood pressure.
takeaway: Linezolid inhibits MAO. Teach the client to limit high-tyramine foods (aged cheese, cured meats, tap beer, soy sauce) and to report severe headache.

stem: A client whose INR has been stable at 2.4 on warfarin is started on oral fluconazole for esophageal candidiasis. What is the priority nursing consideration?
options: Expect the INR to fall, and anticipate an increase in the warfarin dose.
Teach the client to eat more leafy green vegetables to balance the medications.
Monitor the INR closely and watch for bleeding, because fluconazole increases warfarin's effect.
Give fluconazole 2 hours apart from warfarin to avoid the interaction.
rationales: Fluconazole raises warfarin levels rather than lowering them, so the INR is expected to rise, not fall.
Changing vitamin K intake makes anticoagulation less predictable and does not deal with the drug interaction.
Fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9, the main enzyme that breaks down warfarin. This can raise the INR sharply and cause bleeding, so closer INR checks and bleeding assessment are needed.
This interaction occurs in the liver, not in the gut, so separating the doses does not prevent it.
takeaway: Azole antifungals (such as fluconazole) increase warfarin's effect. Monitor the INR closely and watch for bleeding.

stem: A client with herpes simplex encephalitis is to start acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours. Which nursing action is most important to prevent a serious adverse effect?
options: Give each dose by IV push over 2 minutes so it reaches the brain quickly.
Infuse each dose over at least 1 hour and keep the client well hydrated.
Restrict fluids to prevent cerebral edema.
Refrigerate the diluted solution until it is time to give it.
rationales: Rapid IV push increases the risk of crystals forming in the kidney tubules and of local tissue injury. Acyclovir is never given by bolus.
Acyclovir can crystallize in the renal tubules and cause acute kidney injury. Infusing over at least 1 hour with adequate hydration and urine output reduces this risk.
Fluid restriction concentrates the urine and increases the risk of crystal nephropathy.
Refrigerating diluted acyclovir can cause it to precipitate. The label advises against refrigeration.
takeaway: IV acyclovir: infuse over at least 1 hour, keep the client well hydrated and monitor creatinine and urine output.

stem: A healthy 35-year-old developed influenza symptoms yesterday and is prescribed oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily for 5 days. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?
options: "Now that I'm on this medicine, I won't need my yearly flu shot."
"I can stop taking it once my fever goes away."
"It works best because I'm starting it within 2 days of when I got sick."
"I can go back to work tomorrow even if I still have a fever."
rationales: Oseltamivir is not a substitute for annual influenza vaccination.
The full 5-day course should be completed.
In outpatients, oseltamivir is most effective when started within 48 hours of symptom onset, when it can shorten the illness.
Oseltamivir does not make the client immediately noncontagious. People should stay home until they have been fever-free for at least 24 hours without antipyretics.
takeaway: Oseltamivir works best when started within 48 hours of flu symptoms. It does not replace the annual vaccine.

stem: A client is starting daily oral HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) with emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: "You need a negative HIV test before starting, and you'll be tested again about every 3 months."
"Your kidney function will be checked while you take this medicine."
"Taking it every day gives you the best protection."
"You won't need condoms anymore, because this protects you from all sexually transmitted infections."
"You can stop taking it after 30 days, once you're protected."
rationales: Correct. PrEP alone is not a complete HIV treatment, so taking it with undiagnosed HIV can lead to resistance. Regular testing is required.
Correct. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate can affect the kidneys, so creatinine clearance is monitored.
Correct. The effectiveness of daily oral PrEP depends closely on adherence.
Incorrect. PrEP prevents HIV only. Condoms still reduce the risk of gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis and other infections.
Incorrect. Protection lasts only while the drug is taken consistently, for as long as the client is at risk.
takeaway: PrEP requires a negative HIV test first, testing every 3 months, kidney monitoring and daily adherence. It does not prevent other STIs.

stem: While disposing of a used needle, a nurse sustains a needlestick injury after giving an injection to a client who has HIV. What should the nurse do first?
options: Wash the puncture site with soap and water.
Squeeze the wound to make it bleed, then soak it in bleach.
Wait for the client's latest viral load before deciding on treatment.
Finish the shift and then complete an incident report.
rationales: Immediate first aid is to wash the wound with soap and water. Next, the nurse reports the exposure right away so that post-exposure prophylaxis can be started, ideally within hours and no later than 72 hours.
Squeezing the wound and applying caustic agents such as bleach are not recommended and can damage the tissue.
Post-exposure prophylaxis should not be delayed while waiting for source results. The sooner it starts, the better it works.
Waiting until the end of the shift delays evaluation and post-exposure prophylaxis, which works best when started as soon as possible.
takeaway: After a needlestick: wash with soap and water, then report immediately. HIV PEP works best when started within hours (no later than 72 hours).

stem: A client is scheduled to start sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for chronic hepatitis C. Before the first dose, which test result should the nurse confirm is in the record?
options: Hepatitis A IgM antibody
Fasting lipid panel
Hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody
Tuberculin skin test
rationales: IgM anti-HAV detects acute hepatitis A. It is not a required safety screen before hepatitis C treatment.
A lipid panel is not required before starting hepatitis C direct-acting antivirals.

Direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis C carry a boxed warning about hepatitis B reactivation, which can cause fulminant hepatitis. Every client is screened for current or past hepatitis B infection before starting treatment.
TB screening is required before some immunosuppressive therapies, but not before hepatitis C antivirals.
takeaway: Screen for hepatitis B (HBsAg and anti-HBc) before starting hepatitis C antivirals, because hepatitis B can reactivate.

stem: The nurse is screening adults at an immunization clinic. Which clients should NOT receive the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine today? Select all that apply.
options: A 26-year-old who is 10 weeks pregnant
A 40-year-old receiving chemotherapy for leukemia
A 33-year-old with HIV whose CD4 count is 150 cells/mm³
A breastfeeding mother of a 3-month-old
A client who lives with a pregnant woman
A client with a mild cold and a temperature of 99.1 °F (37.3 °C)
rationales: Correct. MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy. It is given after delivery, and pregnancy should be avoided for 4 weeks after vaccination.
Correct. Live vaccines are contraindicated in severe immunosuppression, such as during chemotherapy.
Correct. MMR is contraindicated in HIV with severe immunosuppression (CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ in adults).
Incorrect. Breastfeeding is not a contraindication to MMR.
Incorrect. Vaccinated people do not transmit MMR vaccine viruses in a way that endangers household contacts; vaccinating them is recommended.
Incorrect. A mild illness, with or without a low-grade temperature, is not a reason to delay vaccination.
takeaway: Live vaccines (such as MMR and varicella) are contraindicated in pregnancy and in severe immunosuppression. A mild illness, breastfeeding and a pregnant household member are not contraindications.

stem: A 40-year-old client who gets hives after eating eggs asks for an influenza vaccine. Which action by the nurse is appropriate?
options: Explain that people with egg allergy cannot receive any influenza vaccine.
Give an egg-free recombinant vaccine only, and observe the client for 30 minutes.
Refer the client to an allergist for the vaccine to be given in a medical setting.
Give any age-appropriate influenza vaccine with the same precautions as for any vaccine.
rationales: This is false. People with egg allergy can safely receive influenza vaccine.
Current CDC/ACIP guidance does not limit people with egg allergy to egg-free products or require a longer observation period.
Since the 2023–2024 season, ACIP no longer recommends extra precautions for egg allergy alone, including special settings.
ACIP recommends that people with egg allergy receive any licensed, age-appropriate influenza vaccine. No additional safety measures are needed beyond those for any vaccine.
takeaway: Egg allergy alone is not a reason to withhold or change influenza vaccine. Use any age-appropriate vaccine with standard precautions.

stem: Several infants are due for oral rotavirus vaccine. For which infant should the nurse withhold the vaccine and consult the provider?
options: A 4-month-old who had intussusception at 3 months of age
A 2-month-old with a runny nose and no fever
A 2-month-old who was born at 36 weeks of gestation
A 4-month-old whose mother is pregnant
rationales: A history of intussusception is a contraindication to rotavirus vaccine, because the vaccine carries a small risk of intussusception.
A mild illness without fever is not a reason to delay vaccination.
Preterm infants are vaccinated according to chronological age, using the same schedule.
A pregnant household member is not a contraindication to rotavirus vaccine. Good hand hygiene after diaper changes is advised.
takeaway: Rotavirus vaccine is contraindicated after a history of intussusception or with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).

stem: A 13-month-old received the MMR vaccine today, but the varicella vaccine was not in stock. The parent asks when the child can receive the varicella vaccine. What is the earliest correct time?
options: 7 days from today
At least 28 days from today
At least 3 months from today
At least 6 months from today
rationales: Seven days is too soon. When two live injectable vaccines are not given on the same day, the immune response to the first can interfere with the second.
Live injectable vaccines that are not given on the same day must be separated by at least 28 days (4 weeks), or the second dose may not work as well.
Three months is longer than required; the minimum interval is 28 days.
Six months is unnecessarily long and would leave the child unprotected for longer.
takeaway: Give live injectable vaccines on the same day, or separate them by at least 28 days.

stem: A client at 22 weeks of gestation received Tdap during her previous pregnancy 2 years ago. She asks whether she needs it again. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: "No. Tdap protects you for 10 years, so you don't need another dose."
"Yes. You should receive it today, at 22 weeks."
"Yes. It's recommended in every pregnancy, ideally between 27 and 36 weeks."
"You should wait and receive it right after delivery."
rationales: Tdap is recommended in every pregnancy, whatever the timing of earlier doses, so that antibodies pass to the newborn.
The recommended window is 27 to 36 weeks, which gives the best antibody transfer to the fetus.
CDC recommends one dose of Tdap in each pregnancy, preferably in the early part of weeks 27 to 36, to protect the newborn from pertussis.
Postpartum vaccination does not provide antibodies to the newborn during the highest-risk first months of life.
takeaway: Give Tdap in every pregnancy, at 27 to 36 weeks, to protect the newborn from pertussis.

stem: A 62-year-old client asks about the recombinant zoster (shingles) vaccine. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
options: "Because it's a live vaccine, you can't get it if your immune system is weak."
"One dose protects you for life."
"You don't need it if you had chickenpox as a child."
"It's two doses, given 2 to 6 months apart, and you can get it even if you've had shingles before."
rationales: Recombinant zoster vaccine is not live. It is recommended for immunocompromised adults aged 19 years and older.
The vaccine is a 2-dose series.
A history of chickenpox is the reason shingles can occur, since the virus stays dormant. Adults aged 50 and older are vaccinated regardless.
Recombinant zoster vaccine is recommended for adults aged 50 and older as 2 doses, 2 to 6 months apart, including people who have already had shingles.
takeaway: Recombinant zoster vaccine: not live, 2 doses 2 to 6 months apart, for adults 50 and older (and immunocompromised adults 19 and older).

stem: A 15-month-old has just received the varicella vaccine. Which instruction is most important for the nurse to give the parent?
options: "Avoid giving aspirin or other salicylate products, such as bismuth subsalicylate, for 6 weeks."
"Keep your child home from childcare for 2 weeks."
"Give ibuprofen before each meal for the next 3 days."
"Apply a warm compress to the injection site for 24 hours."
rationales: The varicella vaccine label advises avoiding salicylates for 6 weeks after vaccination because of the risk of Reye syndrome, which has been linked to aspirin use during wild-type varicella.
Children do not need to be excluded after vaccination. Spread of the vaccine virus is rare and occurs only if a rash develops.
Routine scheduled analgesics are not needed. Fever reducers are given only for discomfort or fever, and never aspirin.
Cool compresses are generally used for injection-site soreness. This is not the most important safety teaching.
takeaway: After varicella vaccination, avoid salicylates (aspirin, bismuth subsalicylate) for 6 weeks because of the risk of Reye syndrome.

stem: A college student admitted with meningococcal meningitis is placed on droplet precautions. IV ceftriaxone was started at 1000 today. When may droplet precautions be discontinued?
options: When the cerebrospinal fluid culture comes back negative
After 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy
After the full course of antibiotics is completed
When the client has been fever-free for 12 hours
rationales: Repeat cultures are not the criterion. Precautions are based on the length of effective therapy.
CDC recommends droplet precautions for Neisseria meningitidis until the client has received 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy.
Continuing precautions for the whole course is unnecessary, because transmission risk falls sharply after 24 hours of effective therapy.
Fever is not the criterion for ending meningococcal droplet precautions.
takeaway: Meningococcal disease: droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy have been given.

stem: The nurse is assigning rooms on a medical unit. Which clients require droplet precautions? Select all that apply.
options: A client with confirmed influenza A
A client with Neisseria meningitidis meningitis who started antibiotics 6 hours ago
A client with mumps
A client with measles (rubeola)
A client with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis
A client with an MRSA-infected leg wound
rationales: Correct. Influenza spreads by large respiratory droplets, so droplet precautions are required.
Correct. Droplet precautions continue until 24 hours of effective therapy have been given.
Correct. Mumps spreads by respiratory droplets and saliva; droplet precautions are used.
Incorrect. Measles is airborne and requires an airborne infection isolation room and a fit-tested N95 respirator.
Incorrect. Tuberculosis is airborne and requires airborne precautions.
Incorrect. MRSA requires contact precautions, not droplet precautions.
takeaway: Droplet precautions: influenza, meningococcal disease, mumps and pertussis. Airborne precautions: measles, varicella and TB.

stem: The emergency department has one airborne infection isolation room available. Which client should the charge nurse place in this room?
options: A client with MRSA cellulitis of the forearm
A client with confirmed influenza A
A client with a productive cough, night sweats and a cavitary lesion on chest x-ray
A client with C. difficile diarrhea
rationales: MRSA is spread by contact and needs contact precautions, not a negative-pressure room.
Influenza needs droplet precautions. A standard private room is enough.
These findings suggest pulmonary tuberculosis, which is airborne and needs a negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room.
C. difficile needs contact precautions and soap-and-water hand hygiene, not airborne isolation.
takeaway: Save airborne infection isolation rooms for airborne diseases: TB, measles, varicella and disseminated zoster.

stem: The nurse is about to enter the room of a client on contact and droplet precautions. Place the steps for putting on PPE in the order recommended by the CDC.
options: Put on gloves, extending them over the gown cuffs.
Perform hand hygiene.
Put on a surgical mask.
Put on the gown and tie it at the neck and waist.
Put on goggles or a face shield.
rationales: Last: gloves go on last so they cover the gown cuffs and stay clean for client contact.
First: clean hands before touching clean PPE.
Third: the mask goes on after the gown and is secured before the eye protection.
Second: the gown goes on first among the PPE items.
Fourth: eye protection goes on after the mask so it fits over it.
takeaway: Donning: hand hygiene, gown, mask or respirator, eye protection, gloves.

stem: The nurse is leaving the room of a client on contact and droplet precautions and is wearing a gown, surgical mask, goggles and gloves. Place the steps for removing PPE in the order recommended by the CDC.
options: Remove the gown, pulling it away from the body and rolling it inside out.
Remove the gloves.
Remove the goggles by the earpieces or headband.
Remove the mask by the ties or ear loops without touching the front.
Perform hand hygiene.
rationales: Third: the gown is removed after the eye protection, touching only the inside.
First: gloves are the most contaminated item and are removed first.
Second: eye protection is removed by the clean back parts after the gloves are off.
Fourth: the mask is removed last, touching only the ties or loops.
Last: hand hygiene after removing all PPE removes any contamination picked up along the way.
takeaway: Doffing (CDC sequence): gloves, eye protection, gown, mask or respirator, then hand hygiene.

stem: A client in the emergency department meets criteria for sepsis, with a serum lactate of 3.8 mmol/L. One IV line is in place, and a second is being inserted. Prescriptions include blood cultures x2, cefepime 2 g IV over 30 minutes, vancomycin 1.75 g IV over 3 hours and a repeat lactate. Place the nurse's actions in order.
options: Start the vancomycin infusion.
Obtain two sets of blood cultures from separate sites.
Recheck the serum lactate level.
Infuse cefepime.
rationales: Third: vancomycin takes hours to infuse, so starting it after the short cefepime infusion avoids delaying the broad-spectrum beta-lactam.
First: cultures are drawn before antibiotics when this causes no significant delay, so the organism can be identified.
Last: the Surviving Sepsis bundle calls for remeasuring lactate (usually within 2 to 4 hours) when the first level is above 2 mmol/L, to assess the response to treatment.
Second: the broad-spectrum beta-lactam infuses quickly, so all antibiotics are started as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour of recognizing sepsis.
takeaway: Sepsis: cultures first if they cause no delay, antibiotics within the hour (the fastest broad-spectrum agent first), then remeasure an elevated lactate.

stem: Mr. Asante, 69, has suspected septic shock from pneumonia: BP 84/46 mm Hg, HR 122/min and lactate 4.6 mmol/L. Two attempts to draw blood cultures have failed, and phlebotomy cannot arrive for 90 minutes. Piperacillin-tazobactam is at the bedside, and a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus is infusing. What should the nurse do?
options: Hold the antibiotic until phlebotomy obtains the blood cultures.
Draw the blood cultures from the IV line that is infusing the crystalloid.
Continue the fluid bolus only, and start antibiotics after the blood pressure improves.
Give the piperacillin-tazobactam now, notify the provider and obtain cultures as soon as possible.
rationales: A 90-minute delay in antibiotics during septic shock increases mortality. Cultures should not substantially delay antibiotics.
Samples drawn from a line with fluids running are diluted and contaminated, and the results would be unreliable.
Fluids and antibiotics are both time-critical. Antibiotics should start within 1 hour of recognizing septic shock, not after the blood pressure improves.

Surviving Sepsis guidance is to draw cultures before antibiotics only when this does not substantially delay treatment. In septic shock, antibiotics are given within 1 hour, so the nurse gives the dose and obtains cultures as soon as possible.
takeaway: Draw cultures before antibiotics only when doing so causes no significant delay. In septic shock, antibiotics within 1 hour come first.

stem: A 7-year-old with streptococcal pharyngitis took the first dose of amoxicillin at 0800 today. The parent asks when the child can go back to school. What is the nurse's best response?
options: "Your child can go back this afternoon, since treatment has started."
"Your child can return after at least 12 hours of antibiotics, once there's no fever."
"Your child needs to stay home for 5 days."
"Your child must stay home until all 10 days of the antibiotic are finished."
rationales: A few hours of antibiotics are not enough to make the child noncontagious.
CDC advises that children with strep throat can return to school once they no longer have a fever and have taken antibiotics for at least 12 hours.
A fixed 5-day exclusion is not required for strep pharyngitis that is being treated.
The full course is needed to prevent complications, but the child is no longer contagious long before the course ends.
takeaway: Children with strep throat may return to school after at least 12 hours of antibiotics, once they are fever-free.
