Agree to float but tell the NICU staff that the nurse will not accept any infants
rationales: Nurses must accept assignments within their competence; telling the charge nurse lets the unit assign safe tasks and supports client safety.
Leaving without a safe handoff of responsibility may be considered abandonment and leaves the facility short-staffed.
Taking on care beyond one's competence puts clients at risk and is a breach of the standard of care.
Refusing all work does not help the unit; the nurse should work with the charge nurse to find safe tasks.
takeaway: When floated to an unfamiliar area, tell the charge nurse about your limits and accept only tasks you are competent to do.

stem: A night-shift nurse's shift ended 30 minutes ago, and the day-shift nurse assigned to the nurse's clients has not arrived. The nurse has a family commitment. What should the nurse do?
options: Leave a written report at the nurses' station and go home
Ask the assistive personnel to watch the clients until the day nurse arrives
Call the day-shift nurse at home to find out when she will arrive, then leave
Notify the charge nurse and stay with the clients until care is handed off to another nurse
rationales: A written report without a person accepting responsibility does not transfer care and may be abandonment.
AP cannot take over RN responsibilities for a group of clients.
Knowing when the nurse will arrive does not provide safe coverage now.
Leaving clients without handing off their care to another nurse can be considered client abandonment; the charge nurse is responsible for finding coverage.
takeaway: Do not leave clients until care has been handed off to another qualified nurse; notify the charge nurse when relief is late.

stem: During interprofessional rounds, the team discusses a client who had a stroke 3 days ago. Which statement by the nurse best contributes to the team's plan of care?
options: "She's doing about the same as yesterday."
"I'll leave the plan up to the provider."
"Since yesterday she has needed 2 more liters of oxygen, and she coughs after thin liquids. I'd like speech-language pathology to evaluate her swallowing today."
"She seems confused, but she's always like that."
rationales: This gives the team no useful data for planning.
Nurses are full members of the team and should share their assessments and recommendations.
This shares specific nursing assessment data, links it to a possible aspiration risk, and requests the right team member, which is effective collaboration.
This is vague and assumes a baseline without data; a change in mental status after stroke must be described clearly.
takeaway: In interprofessional collaboration, share specific assessment data and make clear recommendations, including referrals to the right discipline.

stem: An RN tells the nurse manager that a coworker often makes belittling remarks about her in front of other staff. Which action should the manager encourage the RN to take first?
options: Speak with the coworker privately and describe the behavior and its effect using "I" statements
Make the same kind of remarks about the coworker so she understands how it feels
Avoid the coworker and ask never to be scheduled on the same shift
Post about the coworker's behavior in the unit's group chat
rationales: Addressing lateral (horizontal) violence directly and privately, with calm "I" statements, is the first step in resolving the conflict.
Retaliation makes the conflict worse and is unprofessional.
Avoidance does not resolve the conflict, and the behavior may continue with others.
Public discussion is unprofessional and escalates the conflict.
takeaway: Address workplace incivility early, directly and privately using "I" statements; involve the manager if it continues.

stem: The charge nurse is helping two nurses resolve a conflict about sharing break coverage. Place the steps of the conflict resolution process in the correct order.
options: Agree on a plan and a time to check how it is working
Meet with both nurses privately at a time when they can talk without interruption
Identify a shared goal and work together on possible solutions
Have each nurse describe the problem from their own point of view
rationales: Last: a clear agreement and follow-up help make the solution last.
First: a private, calm setting allows open discussion.
Third: focusing on a common goal (safe client coverage) supports a collaborative, win-win solution.
Second: each person must feel heard, and the real issue becomes clear before solutions are discussed.
takeaway: Conflict resolution: meet privately, let each person be heard, look for a shared goal and options, then agree on a plan and follow up.

stem: An 86-year-old client 1 day after hip fracture repair rates her pain 8/10, is grimacing, and will not move in bed. Her current pain plan has not helped. When the nurse calls, the provider says, "Older clients always complain. Just reposition her." What should the nurse do next?
options: Reposition the client and reassess at the end of the shift
Give the provider the assessment findings again, explain the risks of poorly controlled pain, and request a change in the pain plan; use the chain of command if the concern is not addressed
Tell the client that the provider believes she is overreacting
Ask the family to call the provider and complain
rationales: Repositioning alone does not address severe pain, and waiting until the end of the shift leaves the client suffering.
The nurse advocates for the client with objective data; uncontrolled pain after hip surgery can delay walking and increase the risk of delirium, pneumonia and clots.
This is unprofessional, harms trust, and does not help the client.
Advocacy is the nurse's professional responsibility and should not be passed to the family.
takeaway: Advocate with objective data when a client's needs are dismissed; use the chain of command if the problem is not resolved.

stem: Which actions by the nurse show client advocacy? Select all that apply.
options: Asking for a qualified medical interpreter when a client does not speak English well
Supporting a client's informed decision even when the nurse would choose differently
Encouraging the client to accept the treatment that the family prefers
Questioning a plan that conflicts with the client's documented wishes
Making decisions for a competent client who seems overwhelmed
Making sure the client's questions are answered before a procedure
rationales: Correct. Advocacy includes making sure the client can understand and take part in care.
Correct. Advocacy means protecting the client's right to make his or her own choices.
Incorrect. The nurse advocates for the client's wishes, not the family's.
Correct. Speaking up when a plan goes against the client's wishes is a key advocacy action.
Incorrect. This is paternalism; the nurse should support the client in making decisions, not make them for the client.
Correct. Advocacy includes making sure the client is informed.
takeaway: Advocacy means protecting the client's rights, wishes and understanding, even when others, including the nurse, would choose differently.

stem: Mr. Okafor, a 67-year-old client with COPD, has been to the emergency department three times in 6 weeks. The hospital assigns him a nurse case manager. Which action best describes the case manager's role?
options: Giving all of his direct bedside care during each hospital stay.
Coordinating services among the hospital, his clinic and home care, and following his progress after discharge to prevent gaps.
Changing his home oxygen flow rate based on his clinic oxygen readings.
Approving or denying each future emergency department visit on behalf of his insurer.
rationales: Staff nurses give direct bedside care; the case manager's job is to coordinate care across settings, not to replace the bedside nurse.
Case management is a collaborative process that links the client to services across settings over time to improve outcomes, prevent readmissions and use resources well.
Oxygen is prescribed; changing the flow rate requires a provider's prescription and is not a case management function.
A case manager does not block emergency care; federal law (EMTALA) requires a medical screening exam for anyone who comes to an emergency department.
takeaway: A case manager coordinates care across settings and over time (continuity of care) to improve outcomes and reduce readmissions; it is not direct bedside care.

stem: Mrs. Haddad, 81, is being transferred from the hospital to a skilled nursing facility (SNF) after treatment for pneumonia. Which action by the hospital nurse best supports continuity of care?
options: Sending only the provider's discharge summary with the ambulance crew.
Asking the client's daughter to explain the client's care needs to the SNF staff.
Waiting for the SNF nurse to call if there are questions after the client arrives.
Giving a verbal report to the SNF nurse and sending a written transfer summary with current status, care needs, allergies, code status and pending test results.
rationales: The provider's summary does not cover current nursing needs such as skin status, mobility, diet and the last assessment; nursing information is lost.
Family input is helpful, but the professional handoff is the nurse's responsibility; family members may not know or remember clinical details.
A passive approach leaves gaps; important information should be given before the client arrives, not only if the receiving nurse thinks to ask.
A two-way verbal handoff with a complete written transfer record lets the receiving nurse ask questions and continue care without gaps.
takeaway: Transfers between settings are high-risk handoffs: give a two-way verbal report and a complete written summary, including pending results and code status.

stem: A nurse case manager is planning the move of Daniel Kim, 34, who has a new spinal cord injury, from the acute care unit to an acute rehabilitation facility. Which actions are part of the case manager's role? Select all that apply.
options: Confirm that the client's insurance has authorized the rehabilitation admission.
Arrange a care conference with the client, his family and the interdisciplinary team.
Choose the rehabilitation facility for the client without discussing options with him.
Document the client's own goals and preferences for rehabilitation.
Stop the client's bowel program on the day of transfer to make the move simpler.
Share the plan of care with the receiving facility before the client arrives.
rationales: Correct. Verifying coverage and obtaining authorization is a core case management task that prevents delays and unexpected costs.
Correct. Case managers bring the team and family together so everyone agrees on goals and the plan.
Incorrect. The client has the right to choose among available post-acute providers; the case manager presents options and supports his choice.
Correct. Client-centered goals guide the plan and are shared with the receiving team.
Incorrect. Ongoing care such as a bowel program must continue without interruption; stopping it can cause complications.
Correct. Sending information before arrival supports continuity of care.
takeaway: Case managers verify coverage, bring the team together, center the plan on the client's goals and choices, and share the plan with the next setting.

stem: Mr. Alvarez, 71, is going home after surgery to repair a hip fracture. He can walk about 20 feet with a walker, needs help to leave the house, lives with his wife, and has a surgical wound that needs assessment. Which referral is most appropriate?
options: Hospice care.
An outpatient cardiac rehabilitation program.
Home health care for skilled nursing and physical therapy.
An adult day program.
rationales: Hospice is for clients with a terminal illness and a life expectancy of about 6 months or less; this client is recovering.
Cardiac rehabilitation is for clients after heart events or surgery; it does not address his hip or wound, and he has trouble leaving home.
He is homebound (leaving home takes major effort) and needs skilled care (wound assessment and therapy), which are the conditions for home health services.
Adult day programs provide supervision and social activity outside the home; they do not provide skilled wound care or physical therapy at home.
takeaway: Home health is for clients who are homebound and need intermittent skilled care such as nursing assessment or physical therapy.

stem: Mr. Brennan, 76, is enrolled in hospice for end-stage heart failure. He tells the nurse, "A heart center has a new treatment I want to try, but I'm afraid I'm stuck in hospice now." Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: "You can leave hospice at any time to seek that treatment, and you can choose hospice again later if you still qualify."
"Once you choose hospice, you cannot change your decision."
"You must wait until the end of your current 90-day benefit period before you can leave."
"You will need a court order to leave hospice."
rationales: Under the Medicare hospice benefit, a client may revoke the hospice election at any time to pursue curative treatment and may re-elect hospice later if still eligible.
This is false; enrolling in hospice is voluntary and can be revoked at any time.
No waiting period is required; the client can revoke at any time (unused days in that benefit period are given up).
No legal proceeding is needed; the client signs a revocation statement.
takeaway: Hospice is a voluntary choice: a client can revoke hospice at any time to pursue curative care and can re-elect it later if eligible.

stem: A nurse is reviewing discharge planning practices with a new nurse on a medical unit. Which practices support a safe discharge? Select all that apply.
options: Begin discharge planning when the client is admitted.
Assess the client's home setting, support people and ability to manage care.
Use teach-back to check the client's understanding of self-care instructions.
Make or confirm follow-up appointments before the client leaves.
Start all teaching on the morning of discharge so it is fresh in the client's mind.
Give a client with limited English proficiency written instructions in English only.
rationales: Correct. Starting at admission gives time to identify needs, arrange services and teach.
Correct. Knowing the home situation identifies needs for equipment, services or referrals.
Correct. Teach-back confirms understanding and finds gaps before the client leaves.
Correct. Scheduled follow-up reduces missed visits and readmissions.
Incorrect. Last-minute teaching is rushed and stressful; teaching should be spread across the stay.
Incorrect. Instructions should be given in the client's preferred language with a qualified interpreter or translated materials.
takeaway: Discharge planning starts at admission and includes a home assessment, teach-back in the client's language, and confirmed follow-up.

stem: Mrs. Nwosu, 63, is recovering from a stroke. She has trouble buttoning her blouse, brushing her hair and holding a fork. Which referral should the nurse discuss with the provider?
options: Physical therapy.
Occupational therapy.
Speech-language pathology.
Respiratory therapy.
rationales: Physical therapy focuses mainly on mobility, gait, balance and strength of large muscle groups rather than fine motor tasks of daily living.
Occupational therapy helps clients regain the ability to perform activities of daily living such as dressing, grooming and eating, including fine motor skills and adaptive equipment.
Speech-language pathologists treat speech, language, cognition-communication and swallowing problems, not use of the hands for dressing or grooming.
Respiratory therapy manages breathing treatments and airway support; nothing in the scenario points to a breathing problem.
takeaway: Occupational therapy addresses activities of daily living (dressing, grooming, eating); physical therapy addresses mobility; speech therapy addresses speech and swallowing.

stem: Two nurses are giving bedside handoff for Mrs. Lindqvist, 58, in a semi-private room. Her roommate has two visitors in the room. Today Mrs. Lindqvist received a new diagnosis of breast cancer that she has not shared with anyone. Which action by the nurses is best?
options: Give the whole report at the nurses' station instead, without seeing the client
Give the full report at the bedside at normal volume, because HIPAA allows information to be shared for treatment
Do the bedside check with the client, speak quietly, and share the new diagnosis away from the visitors or after asking the client how she would like it discussed
Ask the roommate's visitors to leave the hospital until the handoff is finished
rationales: Skipping the bedside part loses the benefits of bedside handoff, such as checking the client, lines and safety together and involving the client.
HIPAA permits sharing for treatment but still requires reasonable safeguards; announcing a new diagnosis in front of visitors is an avoidable disclosure.
This keeps the safety benefits of bedside handoff while using reasonable safeguards (lower voices, privacy for sensitive details) and respects the client's choice about who learns her diagnosis.
Visitors may be asked to step out briefly, but sending them out of the hospital is unnecessary; the nurses can protect privacy with simpler measures.
takeaway: Bedside handoff should include the client but still protect privacy: lower voices and discuss sensitive information away from others or as the client prefers.

stem: A transporter arrives to take Mr. Petrov, 58, to radiology for a CT scan. He is on fall precautions, has a latex allergy and is receiving a continuous IV infusion of normal saline. Which action by the nurse best ensures a safe transfer?
options: Give a brief handoff to the radiology staff about the latex allergy, fall risk and IV line, and confirm they received it.
Rely on the allergy and fall-risk wristbands to communicate the risks.
Send the paper chart and let radiology staff read about his risks.
Tell the transporter about the risks and ask him to remember to pass them on.
rationales: Handoff communication is needed whenever responsibility moves to another department; telling the receiving staff directly about key risks prevents harm.
Wristbands are helpful reminders but are easily missed; they do not replace a direct handoff to the people taking over care.
Busy staff may not read the record before acting; key risks must be communicated directly.
Relying on a third person to relay information adds a step where details can be lost; the nurse should hand off to the staff who will care for the client.
takeaway: Any time care moves to another department, give a direct handoff of key safety risks (allergies, fall risk, lines) to the receiving staff.

stem: A post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) nurse gives handoff to the surgical unit nurse for a client who had an open bowel resection. Which information should the PACU nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: The procedure performed and the type of anesthesia used.
Vital sign trends and airway status in the PACU.
Estimated blood loss and intake and output.
The names of every staff member who was in the operating room.
Status of the dressing and any drains.
rationales: Correct. The procedure and anesthesia type guide monitoring for complications.
Correct. Trends show whether the client is stable or changing.
Correct. Fluid balance information helps detect bleeding or fluid deficit after surgery.
Incorrect. The full staff list is not clinically needed for ongoing care; it is recorded in the operative record.
Correct. The receiving nurse needs a baseline for the dressing and drain output to recognize bleeding or leakage.
takeaway: Post-operative handoff covers the procedure, anesthesia, vital sign trends, airway, fluid balance, and dressings and drains.

stem: A unit uses the I-PASS handoff tool. Place the parts of the handoff in the order the I-PASS tool presents them.
options: Action list: the tasks to be done and who is responsible.
Synthesis by the receiver: the oncoming nurse summarizes and asks questions.
Illness severity: stable, "watcher," or unstable.
Situation awareness and contingency planning: what might happen and what to do if it does.
Summary of the client: diagnosis, events leading to admission and current course.
rationales: Action list is the third element, listing what must be done, by when and by whom.
Synthesis by the receiver comes last, closing the loop and confirming shared understanding.
Illness severity comes first so the receiver knows at once how closely to watch the client.
Situation awareness and contingency planning is fourth, preparing the receiver for likely changes.
The client summary is the second element, giving the background needed to understand the plan.
takeaway: I-PASS order: Illness severity, client (Patient) summary, Action list, Situation awareness and contingency planning, Synthesis by the receiver.

stem: Mr. Farouk, 52, reads his visit note in the clinic's online portal. He calls the nurse and says, "Your note says I drink six beers a day. I told you six beers a week. Please delete that line." What is the nurse's best response?
options: "I'll delete the line for you right now so the record is correct."

"I can't delete a record entry, but you have the right to ask for a correction. I'll help you submit an amendment request, and the note can be corrected or your statement added according to our process."
"Once a note is signed, it can never be changed, so there is nothing we can do."
"Only your lawyer can ask us to change your medical record."
rationales: Entries in a legal health record are never deleted; deleting it would remove the original entry and the audit trail.

Under HIPAA, clients have the right to request an amendment to their records; the facility reviews the request, and corrections are added without erasing the original entry. If the request is denied, the client may file a statement of disagreement.
This is inaccurate; records can be corrected or amended through a formal process, even though the original is kept.
Clients may request amendments themselves; a lawyer is not needed.
takeaway: Clients have a HIPAA right to request amendment of their health record; errors are corrected through the facility's process without deleting the original entry.

stem: The electronic health record (EHR) stops working without warning, and the information technology department says it may be down for several hours. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Keep notes in a personal notebook and shred them after the system is back up.
Delay routine assessments until the EHR is working so they can be charted properly.
Send provider prescriptions and updates by text message on a personal phone.
Use the facility's downtime forms and procedures, then enter or scan the information into the EHR when it is restored, according to policy.
rationales: Personal notes are not part of the legal record and are a privacy risk; destroying them leaves care undocumented.
Care must continue during downtime; delaying assessments puts clients at risk.
Personal text messaging is not a secure or approved way to transmit prescriptions or protected health information.
Facilities have downtime procedures so that care and documentation continue; paper records are added to the EHR afterward as the policy directs.
takeaway: During EHR downtime, follow the facility's downtime procedures and paper forms, then reconcile the information into the EHR when it is restored.

stem: A coworker's electronic health record (EHR) login is locked. She asks the nurse, "Can I just chart under your login until IT resets mine?" What is the nurse's best response?
options: "I can't share my login. Every entry must be under your own account. Let's call the IT help desk now."
"Yes, but I'll stay next to you while you chart."
"I'll tell you my password, and then I'll change it at the end of the shift."
"Go ahead, and just type your name at the end of each note."
rationales: Each user is accountable for every entry made under their credentials; sharing logins breaks security and makes the record inaccurate. The correct fix is to have the account reset.
Standing nearby does not change that the entries would be recorded under the wrong person's name.
Sharing a password at any time violates security policy; changing it later does not fix the false entries.
The audit trail would still show the nurse as the author; typed names do not make the entries valid.
takeaway: Never share EHR credentials: the person logged in is legally responsible for every entry made under that account.

stem: A nurse educator is reviewing safe documentation in the electronic health record (EHR). Which practices are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Document care as soon as possible after it is given.
Lock or log out of the workstation when stepping away.
Correct errors using the EHR's amendment function so the original entry is kept.
Copy and paste the previous shift's assessment and change it only if something looks very different.
Document scheduled care before giving it to save time later in the shift.
Use only abbreviations approved by the facility.
rationales: Correct. Timely documentation keeps the record accurate and available to the team.
Correct. This protects client information and prevents others from making entries under your login.
Correct. Corrections must preserve the original entry and show who changed it and when.
Incorrect. Copying forward without a fresh assessment can carry outdated or false information into the record.
Incorrect. Charting care before it is done is inaccurate and dangerous if the care is delayed or not given.
Correct. Unapproved abbreviations can be misread and cause errors.
takeaway: Document promptly and personally, protect your login, amend instead of deleting, never pre-chart or copy forward unchecked, and use approved abbreviations.

stem: An electronic health record (EHR) alert flags Mr. Delgado, 69, as meeting sepsis screening criteria: temperature 101.8°F (38.8°C), heart rate 112/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and WBC 14,500/mm³. The nurse has already dismissed several false sepsis alerts this shift. What should the nurse do?
options: Dismiss the alert, since this alert has been unreliable all shift.
Recheck vital signs at the next scheduled time and decide then.
Assess the client promptly and notify the provider or rapid response team per the sepsis protocol.
Ask the information technology department to turn off the sepsis alert for the unit.
rationales: Alert fatigue is a known safety risk; this client's data truly meet screening criteria and need follow-up.
Waiting delays recognition of sepsis, in which every hour of delay in treatment increases risk of death.
Fever, tachycardia, tachypnea and a high WBC (normal about 5,000–10,000/mm³) suggest possible sepsis; prompt bedside assessment and escalation follow the protocol.
Alert settings may need review through quality channels, but that does not address this client's urgent findings.
takeaway: Clinical decision support alerts must be checked against the client; real findings that meet sepsis criteria need prompt assessment and escalation, despite alert fatigue.

stem: A nurse is reviewing safety events from the past month. According to The Joint Commission, which event is a sentinel event?
options: A client had nausea after general anesthesia that resolved with treatment.
A client fell while getting out of bed alone and fractured her hip.
A dietary aide brought the wrong meal tray, but the nurse caught it before the client ate.
A client's IV site infiltrated and the mild swelling resolved after the IV was removed and the arm elevated.
rationales: Postoperative nausea is a common, expected effect; it did not cause death or serious harm.
A fall in a hospital that results in a fracture is listed by The Joint Commission as a sentinel event because it causes severe harm.
This is a near miss (the error did not reach the client); it should be reported but is not a sentinel event.
This is a minor complication without severe or permanent harm.
takeaway: A sentinel event is a safety event resulting in death, permanent harm or severe temporary harm (for example, a fall with fracture); it requires a root cause analysis.

stem: After a client dies from an unrecognized internal bleed, the hospital begins a root cause analysis (RCA). Place the RCA steps in the correct order.
options: Develop and carry out an action plan to fix the system problems found.
Bring together an interdisciplinary team that includes people familiar with the process involved.
Describe what happened by building a detailed timeline of the event.
Measure whether the changes worked over time.
Identify contributing factors and the underlying root causes.
rationales: The action plan is created once root causes are known, so it is the fourth step.
An RCA starts by forming a team with the needed expertise.
The team first gathers facts and builds a timeline before looking for causes.
The final step is to monitor outcomes to check that the actions reduced risk.
After the timeline is clear, the team asks why the event happened, looking for system causes rather than individual blame.
takeaway: RCA sequence: form a team, describe what happened, find the root causes, act on them, then measure the results.

stem: Before sending blood samples to the lab, the nurse notices a tube is labeled with another client's name. The error was caught before the sample left the unit. What should the nurse do?
options: Peel off the wrong label, apply the correct label and send the sample.
Send the sample and call the lab to tell them the label is wrong.
Discard the sample and recollect it, without reporting, because the error did not reach the client.
Discard the sample, recollect it with correct labeling at the bedside, and file a safety event report for the near miss.
rationales: Relabeling a specimen is never acceptable because there is no way to prove whose blood is in the tube.
A sample with the wrong label could cause results to be filed under the wrong client and lead to harmful treatment.
Near misses should be reported; they show system weaknesses before harm occurs.
The mislabeled specimen must not be used; recollection with bedside labeling is safe, and reporting the near miss helps the organization find and fix the cause.
takeaway: Never relabel a specimen; recollect it and report near misses, because they reveal system problems before anyone is harmed.

stem: A nurse turned off a client's bed-exit alarm because "it kept going off for no reason." The client got up alone and fell but was not injured. The nurse says many staff on the unit do this. Using a just culture approach, what is the nurse manager's best response?
options: Coach the nurse about the risk of disabling alarms and look into why staff on the unit are turning them off.
Fire the nurse because the client could have been seriously hurt.
Take no action because the client was not injured.
Report the nurse to the state board of nursing.
rationales: In a just culture, at-risk behavior (a choice whose risk is not recognized or is believed justified) is managed with coaching, and a widespread practice points to a system problem such as alarm design or settings.
Punishment is reserved for reckless behavior (consciously ignoring a substantial and unjustifiable risk); this is at-risk behavior common on the unit.
Outcome does not decide the response; the behavior and the system issue still need to be addressed.
A board report is not appropriate for an at-risk behavior that reflects a unit-wide practice; coaching and system fixes are the right response.
takeaway: Just culture: console human error, coach at-risk behavior, and discipline reckless behavior, while fixing the system problems behind common workarounds.

stem: Only one airborne infection isolation room (negative-pressure room) is open on a medical unit. Four clients need admission. Which client should be placed in this room?
options: A client with a wound infected with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).
A client with influenza.
A client with suspected active pulmonary tuberculosis.
A client with Clostridioides difficile diarrhea.
rationales: MRSA in a wound requires contact precautions, which can be provided in a standard private room.
Influenza requires droplet precautions, which do not need a negative-pressure room.
Pulmonary tuberculosis spreads by the airborne route and requires an airborne infection isolation room; this is the best use of the limited resource.
C. difficile requires contact precautions in a private room, not negative pressure.
takeaway: Allocate scarce resources to the client who specifically needs them: negative-pressure rooms go to airborne infections such as tuberculosis.

stem: A nurse on a step-down unit receives an assignment she believes is unsafe because of the number and acuity of her clients. She has already discussed it with the charge nurse, who cannot change it. What should the nurse do next?
options: Leave the unit and inform the supervisor by phone that she will not work under these conditions.
Accept the assignment, complete the facility's assignment-despite-objection (staffing concern) form, and notify the nursing supervisor.
Accept the assignment without saying anything more, to avoid conflict.
Refuse the two most complex clients and let the charge nurse decide who will care for them.
rationales: Leaving after accepting responsibility for clients, without a proper handoff, can be client abandonment.
The nurse provides care while formally documenting the concern and escalating through the chain of command; this protects clients and the nurse.
Silence does not protect clients or allow leaders to act; the concern should be documented and escalated.
Refusing selected clients without an agreed plan leaves those clients without a nurse and does not address the staffing problem.
takeaway: For an unsafe assignment: discuss with the charge nurse, document the objection in writing, escalate up the chain of command, and do not abandon clients.

stem: A nurse manager is introducing a new early-warning score in the electronic health record to help nurses recognize clients who are getting worse. Several experienced nurses say, "Our old way works fine." Which approach is most likely to help the change succeed?
options: Tell the staff that the new score is required and that nurses who do not use it will be disciplined
Start using the score without explanation, because it was approved by hospital leadership
Share the unit's data on missed deterioration, involve staff in planning, train unit champions, and ask for feedback during a trial period
Postpone the change until every nurse on the unit agrees with it
rationales: Threats may produce short-term compliance but increase resistance and do not build understanding or buy-in.
Change without explanation leaves staff unsure why it matters and makes resistance more likely.
Showing why change is needed (unfreezing), involving staff, providing peer champions and inviting feedback build ownership and support lasting change.
Waiting for complete agreement can delay a safety improvement indefinitely; resistance is managed through involvement and support, not unanimity.
takeaway: Change is most successful when staff understand why it is needed, help plan it, have peer champions, and can give feedback.

stem: During the surgical time-out, the circulating nurse sees that the signed consent lists the left knee, but the site marked on the client is the right knee. The surgeon says, "I know which side it is. Let's go." What should the nurse do?
options: Proceed, because the surgeon is responsible for choosing the operative site.
Note the discrepancy in the record after the procedure.
Ask the anesthesia provider to decide which side is correct.
Stop the procedure until the discrepancy is resolved, and use the chain of command if the surgeon will not wait.
rationales: Every team member shares responsibility for the time-out; proceeding with an unresolved discrepancy risks wrong-site surgery.
Documenting afterward does not prevent the harm; the discrepancy must be resolved before the incision.
One person's opinion does not resolve the conflict; the source documents and client must be checked.
Under the Universal Protocol, any team member can and should halt the procedure when the time-out finds a discrepancy; escalate if needed.
takeaway: Any team member can stop a procedure when the time-out reveals a discrepancy; resolve it before incision and escalate if needed.

stem: Ana has just finished a 12-hour night shift. The manager asks her to stay for another 8 hours because two nurses called in sick. Ana feels too tired to think clearly. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Stay, because declining extra hours would be client abandonment.
Stay but avoid taking any clients with complex needs.
Decline, explaining that her level of fatigue would make it unsafe for her to care for clients.
Stay and drink extra caffeine to stay alert.
rationales: Abandonment applies when a nurse leaves clients she has accepted without a handoff; declining an extra shift after giving report is not abandonment.
Fatigue impairs judgment for all care, not only complex care; working while impaired is still unsafe.
Nurses have an ethical responsibility to judge their own fitness to practice; fatigue increases error risk, and declining extra hours for safety reasons is appropriate.
Caffeine does not reverse the effects of prolonged wakefulness on judgment and reaction time.
takeaway: Fatigue is a safety risk; a nurse should decline extra hours when too tired to practice safely, and doing so is not abandonment.

stem: On a medical unit, the census rises from 22 to 28 clients and three clients now need more frequent assessment. The charge nurse thinks staffing is no longer safe. What should the charge nurse do first?
options: Ask the nurses to skip their breaks until the next shift arrives.
Close the unit to new admissions on her own authority.
Tell the staff to provide only essential care until the shift ends.
Use the unit's acuity tool to document the workload and notify the nursing supervisor or staffing office to request more staff.
rationales: Skipping breaks increases fatigue and errors and does not solve the staffing gap.
Decisions about closing a unit are usually made by administration; the charge nurse should escalate through the proper channels.
Reducing care without a plan may leave needed care undone and does not address the cause.
Objective acuity data supports a request through the chain of command so leaders can provide resources such as float, on-call or agency staff.
takeaway: When census or acuity rises, the charge nurse documents workload with an acuity tool and escalates to the supervisor or staffing office for more resources.

stem: A nurse is off duty at home when the local news reports a major bus crash, and the nurse's hospital activates its emergency operations plan. Which actions by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Follow the hospital's staff call-in plan and report to the assigned area or labor pool when called
Drive straight to the emergency department and begin caring for victims without checking in
Bring the hospital ID badge, because access to the building may be restricted
Post updates on social media about the injured clients as they arrive
Make sure the nurse's own family emergency plan is in place so the nurse can work when called
Call the emergency department to ask how many victims are expected
rationales: Correct. The incident command system assigns staff where they are most needed; reporting as directed keeps the response organized.
Incorrect. Self-deploying without checking in (freelancing) disrupts the incident command structure and staff accountability.
Correct. During a disaster, hospitals often lock down entrances; staff identification allows entry.
Incorrect. Posting about clients breaches privacy; information is released only by the public information officer.
Correct. Personal and family preparedness lets staff report for duty without worrying about dependents.
Incorrect. Personal calls tie up phone lines needed for the response; staff wait for official call-in information.
takeaway: In a disaster, staff follow the call-in plan, check in through incident command, bring ID, keep client information private, and have a family plan ready.

stem: During a mass casualty incident, a staff nurse working in the hospital's triage area is approached by a television reporter who asks how many victims have died. What is the best response?
options: Give the number of deaths she knows of, without any names.
Refer the reporter to the hospital's public information officer.
Ask a family member of a victim to speak with the reporter instead.
Let the reporter stay in the triage area to observe so the facts are reported correctly.
rationales: Even without names, staff should not release incident information; numbers may be inaccurate and must come from the official source.
In the hospital incident command system, the public information officer is the single source for media updates; staff refer reporters there.
Directing the media to families is inappropriate and could violate privacy.
Media must be kept out of care areas to protect privacy and allow safe care.
takeaway: In a disaster, the public information officer in the incident command system handles all media questions; staff refer reporters there.

stem: In mass casualty triage, the goal is to do the greatest good for the greatest number. Which victim would receive a lower priority during a mass casualty incident than in everyday emergency department care?
options: A victim in cardiac arrest after major trauma.
A victim with a respiratory rate of 36/min who can follow commands.
A walking victim with a sprained ankle.
A victim with a closed lower-leg fracture, normal breathing and a strong radial pulse.
rationales: In daily practice this victim would receive full resuscitation, but in a mass casualty incident a victim without breathing after airway positioning is tagged expectant/deceased so resources go to those who can be saved.
A respiratory rate over 30/min is an immediate (red) priority in both settings.
This victim has a low priority in both settings (green, minor).
This victim is delayed (yellow) in a disaster and also not top priority in the emergency department.
takeaway: Disaster triage shifts from "most critical first" to "greatest good for the greatest number"; victims unlikely to survive with available resources become expectant.

stem: A nurse at the unit desk answers the phone, and the caller says a bomb has been placed in the hospital. What should the nurse do?
options: Hang up right away and start searching the unit's client rooms for the device
Announce over the overhead page that there is a bomb in the building
Keep the caller talking, write down the exact words, voice details and background noise, and signal a coworker to notify security per the facility plan
Begin evacuating all clients from the unit before telling anyone about the call
rationales: Hanging up ends the chance to gather information, and searching alone for a device is unsafe; searches follow the facility plan.
Plain-language announcements without direction can cause panic; facilities use their emergency code and plan.
Information about the caller helps security and police judge the threat and find the source; the facility's emergency plan guides the response.
Evacuation decisions are made by incident command; moving clients without direction may move them toward danger.
takeaway: For a telephone bomb threat: keep the caller on the line, record details, alert security per the facility plan, and wait for incident command before evacuating.

stem: A nurse educator is teaching staff to use a new ceiling lift for moving clients. Which method best confirms that each nurse can use the lift safely?
options: Having each nurse sign a form saying the policy was read.
Watching each nurse perform a return demonstration with the lift.
Giving a written quiz about the lift's weight limits.
Asking each nurse whether they feel comfortable using the lift.
rationales: Signing a form shows the policy was read, not that the skill can be performed safely.
A return demonstration lets the educator directly observe the psychomotor skill and correct errors, which is the best way to confirm competence.
A quiz checks knowledge but not the hands-on skill.
Self-report of comfort does not confirm actual ability.
takeaway: Return demonstration is the best way to evaluate a psychomotor skill; quizzes and signatures check only knowledge or reading.

stem: A preceptor is orienting a new graduate nurse. The preceptor sees the new nurse about to enter the room of a client on airborne precautions wearing only a surgical mask. What should the preceptor do?
options: Let the new nurse enter and discuss the error at the end of the shift.
Report the new nurse to the nurse manager for unsafe practice.
Correct the new nurse loudly in front of the client's family so others learn too.
Stop the new nurse before entering, explain that a fitted N95 respirator is needed, and review airborne precautions privately afterward.
rationales: Allowing the exposure to occur puts the new nurse at risk; teaching can happen later, but the unsafe act must be stopped now.
The first priority is to prevent the exposure; a report is not needed for a teachable error that is caught in time.
Public correction is embarrassing and unprofessional; feedback should be given privately once safety is ensured.
The preceptor intervenes at once to prevent harm and then uses the event as a private teaching moment.
takeaway: A preceptor stops an unsafe action immediately and then gives private, constructive feedback.

stem: A nurse educator is planning orientation for newly hired nurses who were educated outside the United States. Which strategies are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Assess each nurse's previous experience and learning needs.
Pair each nurse with a trained preceptor.
Provide simulation practice for unit-specific skills and equipment.
Assume the nurses already know U.S. scope-of-practice and documentation rules.
Use lecture only, because it covers the most content in the shortest time.
Use a competency checklist and give regular, specific feedback.
rationales: Correct. Orientation should build on what each nurse already knows and target the gaps.
Correct. Preceptors support skill development and help with the transition to a new setting.
Correct. Simulation lets nurses practice safely before working with clients.
Incorrect. Scope of practice, delegation and documentation rules differ between countries and must be taught directly.
Incorrect. Adults learn best with active, practical methods; lecture alone is less effective for skills.
Correct. Checklists and feedback show progress and confirm competence before independent practice.
takeaway: Effective orientation assesses learning needs, uses preceptors and simulation, teaches local rules explicitly, and confirms competence with checklists and feedback.

stem: A nurse has just received handoff report on five clients on a medical unit. Which action best shows effective time management at the start of the shift?
options: Make a quick round to see each client, then plan the shift around urgent needs and time-critical tasks.
Finish all charting from the previous shift's events before seeing any clients.
Give morning baths first so the clients are ready for the day.
See clients in room-number order regardless of their condition.
rationales: A brief initial round finds problems early and lets the nurse build a realistic plan that puts urgent and timed tasks first.
Documentation matters, but delaying client contact can miss urgent problems.
Hygiene is important but can usually be scheduled flexibly; it should not come before assessing needs.
Room order ignores acuity and time-critical needs.
takeaway: Start the shift by quickly seeing all clients, then plan care around urgent needs and time-critical tasks, adjusting as things change.

stem: At 1300, a nurse learns she will receive a transfer from the intensive care unit at 1330. Her other planned tasks are: discharge teaching for a client whose ride arrives at 1415, hourly neurologic checks for a client with a head injury, and a daily dressing change on a dry, intact surgical dressing. Which task is most appropriate to move to later in the shift?
options: Discharge teaching for the client leaving at 1415.
Hourly neurologic checks on the client with a head injury.
The daily dressing change on the dry, intact surgical dressing.
Receiving the client transferred from the intensive care unit.
rationales: This task has a fixed deadline; delaying it risks rushed teaching or a delayed discharge.
Neurologic checks are time-critical; a missed change in level of consciousness could mean a serious complication.
A daily dressing change on a dry, intact dressing has a flexible time window and can safely wait until later in the shift.
A newly transferred client needs a prompt initial assessment to establish a baseline.
takeaway: When the plan changes, move tasks with flexible timing (such as routine daily care) and keep time-critical assessments and fixed deadlines.

stem: A nurse wants to manage time more effectively across a 12-hour shift. Which strategies are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Cluster care so several tasks are done in one visit to the client's room.
Use a shift worksheet and update it as tasks are completed or added.
Re-prioritize the plan when a client's condition changes.
Save all documentation for the last hour of the shift.
Skip meal breaks to finish tasks faster.
rationales: Correct. Clustering care saves time and lets clients rest between visits.
Correct. A written or electronic plan keeps track of timed tasks and changing priorities.
Correct. Priorities must shift with new information; a rigid plan can cause missed problems.
Incorrect. Delayed charting is less accurate and leaves the record out of date for the team.
Incorrect. Skipping breaks increases fatigue and the risk of errors.
takeaway: Good time management clusters care, uses a living worksheet, re-prioritizes as conditions change, documents promptly, and includes breaks.

stem: Mr. Johansson, 45, is Deaf and uses American Sign Language (ASL). He is scheduled for surgery tomorrow, and the surgeon will explain the procedure today. His hearing wife offers to interpret. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept the wife's offer, because she knows how he communicates best.
Give the client written information and ask him to write down his questions.
Speak slowly and clearly while facing him so he can lip-read.
Arrange a qualified ASL interpreter, in person or by video remote interpreting, for the consent discussion and teaching.
rationales: Family members are not trained medical interpreters, may not be impartial, and may change or leave out information.
Written English may not be fully accessible to an ASL user and is not adequate for complex discussions such as surgical consent.
Lip reading is unreliable; only a small part of spoken English can be understood this way.
Under the Americans with Disabilities Act, hospitals must provide effective communication, which for complex discussions with an ASL user means a qualified interpreter.
takeaway: For Deaf clients who use ASL, provide a qualified ASL interpreter (on-site or video) for consent and teaching; family, notes and lip reading are not adequate.

stem: A nurse who speaks some Arabic but has not been assessed or qualified as a medical interpreter is asked by a coworker to interpret discharge instructions for an Arabic-speaking client. What should the nurse do?
options: Explain that she is not a qualified interpreter and help arrange a qualified interpreter through the facility's service.
Interpret the instructions, because the client will understand her better than a phone interpreter.
Interpret the main points and give the client the full instructions in English.
Use a free online translation app to translate the written instructions and give the printed result to the client.
rationales: Federal civil rights rules require qualified interpreters for clients with limited English proficiency; untested language skill can lead to serious misunderstandings in medical teaching.
Speaking some of a language does not make someone a qualified medical interpreter; errors in key terms are common.
Partial interpretation leaves gaps, and English-only written material is not accessible to this client.

Unreviewed machine translation often mistranslates medical terms; critical health information should be translated or reviewed by a qualified translator, and spoken teaching needs a qualified interpreter.
takeaway: Being bilingual is not the same as being a qualified medical interpreter; use the facility's qualified interpreter service for clinical teaching.

stem: A nurse is troubled because the family of Mr. Ibarra, 79, who now lacks capacity, is asking for aggressive treatment that he had refused when he could still decide. Place the steps of an ethical decision-making process in the correct order.
options: Choose a course of action and carry it out, such as requesting an ethics consultation
Identify the ethical problem and the principles in conflict, such as autonomy and beneficence
Gather the facts: the client's documented wishes, his current condition, and who is the legal decision-maker
Evaluate the outcome and whether the client's wishes were respected
Explore possible actions and their likely consequences for everyone involved
rationales: Fourth: after options are weighed, the nurse acts on the best choice.
Second: once the facts are known, the nurse names the ethical conflict.
First: decisions must rest on accurate facts, including advance directives and the legal surrogate.
Last: evaluation checks whether the action solved the problem and what to do differently in the future.
Third: considering several options and their effects comes before choosing one.
takeaway: Ethical decision-making: gather facts, identify the ethical problem, explore options, act, then evaluate.

stem: During a group session on a psychiatric unit, a client says, "When I get out of here, I'm going to kill my ex-boss, Dana Reyes. I know where she lives." What is the nurse's most appropriate action?
options: Keep the statement confidential, because it was made during therapy.
Report the threat right away to the provider and treatment team and document it, so the duty to warn or protect can be carried out.
Tell the client that such statements are not allowed in group.
Wait to see whether the client repeats the threat before taking action.
rationales: Confidentiality has limits; a serious threat against an identifiable person creates a duty to warn or protect.
A specific threat against a named person triggers duty-to-warn/protect obligations; the nurse reports it promptly so the team can act according to state law and policy.
Setting limits does not address the safety of the threatened person.
Delay could put the named person in danger; a single credible threat must be reported.
takeaway: A serious threat against an identifiable person overrides confidentiality: report it promptly to the provider and team so the duty to warn or protect can be met.

stem: A school nurse suspects that a 7-year-old student is being neglected. The nurse is unsure because there is no proof. Which statements about the nurse's reporting duty are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The nurse must report a reasonable suspicion; proof is not required.
A report made in good faith is protected from legal liability, even if neglect is not confirmed.
The nurse must tell the parents that a report has been made before the child leaves school.
The nurse should document objective findings and the child's own words in quotation marks.
The nurse should wait to report until she has seen signs of neglect on at least two more occasions.
rationales: Correct. Mandated reporters must report when they have reasonable cause to suspect abuse or neglect; investigation is the agency's job.
Correct. All states give good-faith reporters immunity from civil and criminal liability.
Incorrect. Reporters are not required to notify parents, and doing so could put the child at risk; the child protective agency decides how and when to contact the family.
Correct. Factual, objective documentation supports the investigation.
Incorrect. Waiting delays protection; a reasonable suspicion should be reported promptly.
takeaway: Mandated reporters report reasonable suspicion promptly, without needing proof; good-faith reports are legally protected, and documentation should be objective.

stem: A nurse in a federally funded long-term care facility finds a resident with a new, swollen, deformed forearm. The resident says an aide twisted her arm during care. The nurse ensures the resident is safe and receives care. Under federal law, what else must happen?
options: The suspected crime must be reported to the state survey agency and local law enforcement within 2 hours.
The nurse must report only to the administrator, who will decide within 5 days whether outside agencies are told.
The nurse must confirm the abuse with an X-ray and witness statements before making any report.
The resident's family must decide whether to report the event.
rationales: Under the Elder Justice Act, a reasonable suspicion of a crime against a resident that results in serious bodily injury must be reported to the state survey agency and law enforcement within 2 hours (within 24 hours if there is no serious bodily injury).
Reporting to the administrator is also required, but it does not replace reporting to outside agencies within the required time.
Reports are based on reasonable suspicion; proof is not required, and delays are not allowed.
The duty to report belongs to the covered individual; it cannot be handed to the family.
takeaway: In long-term care, suspected crimes with serious bodily injury must be reported to the state survey agency and law enforcement within 2 hours (otherwise within 24 hours).

stem: At discharge, the daughter of Mrs. Kowalski, 80, hands the nurse an envelope with $100 in cash and says, "Thank you for taking such good care of my mother." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: Accept the cash, because refusing could offend the family
Accept the cash and share it with the other nurses on the unit
Tell the daughter that accepting gifts is illegal
Thank her warmly, decline the cash according to facility policy, and mention that a note to the unit or manager is a welcome way to share thanks
rationales: Accepting money blurs professional boundaries and is against most facility policies, even when the gift is offered sincerely.
Sharing the money does not change that a cash gift was accepted from a client's family.
This is inaccurate and needlessly harsh; the issue is professional boundaries and facility policy, not a law that applies to every gift.
Declining kindly keeps professional boundaries while honoring the family's gratitude; many facilities welcome written thanks or recognition programs instead.
takeaway: Decline cash and personal gifts from clients and families in a kind way, follow facility policy, and suggest other ways to express thanks.

stem: Mrs. Osei, 39, has been declared dead by neurologic criteria (brain death) after a stroke, and her family has authorized organ donation. The organ procurement organization is arranging recovery. What is the nurse's priority while awaiting recovery?
options: Stop mechanical ventilation, because the client has been declared dead.
Maintain ventilation, blood pressure and body temperature and monitor urine output closely, following the organ procurement organization's protocol.
Reduce assessments to once per shift, because the client is legally dead.
Move the body to the morgue until the recovery team arrives.
rationales: Stopping ventilation would cause cardiac arrest and loss of organs; support continues until recovery for a donor.
After brain death, hypotension, hypothermia and diabetes insipidus (very high urine output) are common; maintaining oxygenation and perfusion protects the organs for transplant.
Donor management requires close, frequent monitoring to keep the organs viable.
The donor must stay in a critical care setting with full physiologic support until organ recovery.
takeaway: After brain death with authorized donation, the nurse maintains oxygenation, blood pressure, temperature and fluid balance (watching for diabetes insipidus) to preserve organs.

stem: A nurse educator is teaching ICU staff about roles in the organ donation process. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The physician who declares death should not be part of the transplant or organ recovery team.
The organ procurement organization evaluates the donor, supports the family's decision and coordinates matching through the national system.
The bedside nurse chooses which recipient should receive the organs.
The donor's family pays the costs of organ recovery.
Donation after circulatory death may be considered when a family decides to withdraw life support from a client who does not meet brain death criteria.
rationales: Correct. Separating these roles avoids a conflict of interest and protects trust in the declaration of death.
Correct. The OPO manages donor evaluation, family approach and allocation through the national transplant network.
Incorrect. Organs are allocated through the national matching system based on medical criteria, not by hospital staff.
Incorrect. Donor families do not pay for donation-related costs.
Correct. Donation after circulatory death is an option when death will follow planned withdrawal of support; the decision to withdraw is made separately from the donation discussion.
takeaway: In donation, the OPO coordinates evaluation, family support and allocation; the physician declaring death is never on the recovery team; families pay nothing.

stem: A 52-year-old client scheduled for a hysterectomy tomorrow morning says, "My aunt never woke up after her surgery. I keep thinking that will happen to me." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?
options: "You're worried that what happened to your aunt could happen to you. Tell me more about what you're thinking."
"Don't worry. Anesthesia is very safe, and your surgeon has done hundreds of these."
"Why do you think your aunt's surgery has anything to do with yours?"
"Let's focus on your preoperative checklist so you're ready for the morning."
rationales: This reflects the client's feeling and uses an open-ended prompt, inviting the client to explore the fear so the nurse can learn what is driving it and respond to specific concerns.
This is false reassurance; it dismisses the client's feeling and closes the conversation before the nurse understands the fear.
"Why" questions demand an explanation and can make the client feel defensive or judged, which discourages sharing.
Changing the subject to a task ignores the emotional concern the client raised and signals that the nurse is not available to listen.
takeaway: Therapeutic responses reflect feelings and invite the client to say more; avoid false reassurance, "why" questions and changing the subject.

stem: The nurse is reviewing statements made during interactions with a client who has depression. Which statements by the nurse are nontherapeutic? Select all that apply.
options: "Why did you leave the group session early today?"
"You seem quieter than you were yesterday."
"Everything is going to work out fine. You'll see."
"If I were you, I would move back in with your parents."
"You mentioned your sister earlier. Tell me more about her."
"Let's talk about something more cheerful, like your plans for the weekend."
rationales: Correct. A "why" question asks the client to justify behavior and often feels accusatory; a better choice is "I noticed you left group early. What was happening for you?"
Incorrect. Making an observation is therapeutic; it shares what the nurse notices and invites the client to respond without judging.
Correct. This is false reassurance; the nurse cannot promise the outcome, and it dismisses the client's current feelings.
Correct. Giving personal advice takes the decision away from the client and fosters dependence instead of helping the client problem-solve.
Incorrect. Exploring a topic the client raised is therapeutic; it shows the nurse was listening and encourages the client to elaborate.
Correct. Changing the subject to something "cheerful" avoids the client's feelings and tells the client those feelings are unwelcome.
takeaway: Nontherapeutic techniques include "why" questions, false reassurance, giving advice and changing the subject; observations and exploring are therapeutic.

stem: A 47-year-old client with major depressive disorder tells the nurse during a clinic visit, "I finally gave my fishing gear to my nephew, and I wrote letters to each of my kids last night." Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Tell the client that it was generous to share the fishing gear with family.
Ask the client directly, "Are you thinking about killing yourself?"
Document the statement and review it with the provider at the end of the visit.
Suggest that the client call the children tonight to talk about the letters.
rationales: Praising the behavior misses its likely meaning; the client may be putting affairs in order before a suicide attempt.

Giving away possessions and writing letters are warning signs of suicide. Asking directly does not plant the idea; it opens the conversation and lets the nurse assess intent, plan and means right away.
Delaying assessment of possible suicidal intent is unsafe; the risk must be evaluated now, before the client leaves.
This does not assess the client's safety, and the letters may be goodbye notes; the nurse must first find out whether the client is suicidal.
takeaway: Giving away possessions or writing goodbye letters is a suicide warning sign; ask directly and clearly about suicidal thoughts.

stem: A 23-year-old client in the emergency department says, "I've been saving up pills at home, and I planned to take them all on Friday." The client is calm and cooperative while awaiting psychiatric evaluation. Which action by the nurse is the priority?
options: Ask the client to sign an agreement promising not to harm themselves while in the department.
Check on the client every 30 minutes while the psychiatric team is contacted.
Place the client on continuous one-to-one observation, keeping the client within sight at all times.
Call a family member and ask them to remove the stored pills from the home.
rationales: No-suicide contracts are not evidence-based and do not protect the client; they can give staff false reassurance.
Intermittent checks leave long gaps in which a high-risk client could attempt suicide; continuous observation is needed.

A specific plan, available means and a chosen date indicate high risk. Continuous observation in a safe room (with hazards removed) prevents an attempt while the evaluation is completed; calm behavior can follow a decision to die.
Removing access to means is an important part of discharge safety planning, but the immediate priority is the client's safety in the department.
takeaway: A client with a specific plan and access to means needs continuous one-to-one observation; no-suicide contracts are not a safety measure.

stem: The nurse is helping a client who was treated for suicidal thoughts develop a written safety plan before discharge. Which elements should the plan include? Select all that apply.
options: Personal warning signs, such as not sleeping and pulling away from friends
A signed promise that the client will not attempt suicide
The 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and the number of the client's outpatient therapist
Steps to limit access to lethal means, such as storing firearms outside the home
An agreement to keep the plan private from friends and family
Coping activities the client can do alone, such as walking or listening to music
rationales: Correct. Recognizing one's own warning signs is the first step of a safety plan so the client knows when to use it.
Incorrect. No-suicide contracts are not a recommended or effective safety measure and are not part of a safety plan.
Correct. Professional and crisis contacts that are available at any hour are a core element of a safety plan.
Correct. Reducing access to lethal means is one of the most effective suicide-prevention strategies and belongs in every plan.
Incorrect. Safety plans name trusted people the client can contact; keeping the plan secret removes a source of support.
Correct. Internal coping strategies let the client try to manage a crisis on their own before reaching out to others.
takeaway: A safety plan lists warning signs, coping strategies, supportive people, crisis and professional contacts (988) and ways to limit lethal means.

stem: A 36-year-old client comes to a walk-in crisis center the day after losing both a job and housing and says, "I can't think straight." Place the nurse's crisis intervention actions in the correct order.
options: Explore the client's usual coping strategies and available support people.
Arrange a follow-up contact to review progress and make referrals as needed.
Assess for immediate danger, including thoughts of suicide or harming others.
Work with the client to choose specific, short-term actions for the next few days.
Help the client describe the event that triggered the crisis and what it means to them.
rationales: Identifying past coping and current supports shows the strengths the client can draw on.
Follow-up evaluates whether the crisis has resolved and links the client to ongoing resources.
Safety comes first in any crisis; the nurse must know whether the client is at risk before anything else.
Crisis intervention is focused and directive; the plan is concrete and realistic for the immediate period.
Once safety is established, the nurse clarifies the precipitating event and the client's perception of it.
takeaway: Crisis intervention: ensure safety, define the problem, identify coping and supports, plan concrete actions, then follow up.

stem: A client waiting for biopsy results is pacing, trembling and cannot follow the nurse's request to sit down. The client's speech is rapid, and the client keeps focusing on a small stain on the floor. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
options: Teach the client a detailed progressive muscle relaxation routine.
Ask the client to list the possible results and how each would be handled.
Leave the client alone for a while so the client can calm down privately.
Stay with the client in a quiet area and speak in short, simple sentences.
rationales: A client in severe anxiety cannot process new, detailed information; teaching works best when anxiety is mild or moderate.
Problem solving requires the ability to focus and reason, which is lost at this level of anxiety.
Leaving a client in severe anxiety can increase fear and the risk of escalation to panic; the nurse should stay.
These findings indicate severe anxiety, in which the perceptual field is greatly narrowed. The nurse's calm presence, a low-stimulus setting and brief directions help reduce the anxiety level.
takeaway: Severe anxiety narrows perception: stay with the client, reduce stimuli and use short, simple statements; save teaching for lower levels.

stem: A client hospitalized for major depressive disorder stays in bed most of the day, speaks slowly and says, "I can't decide what to do, so I just don't do anything." Which nursing intervention is most appropriate?
options: Plan a simple daily schedule with the client and walk with the client to one short activity.
Ask the client to choose from all the unit activities and plan the full day.
Allow the client to stay in bed until the client feels ready to get up.
Tell the client to try to look on the bright side and think positively.
rationales: Psychomotor slowing and indecision make choices overwhelming. Structure, small achievable goals and the nurse's company help the client become active and experience success.
Many open choices overwhelm a client who has trouble making decisions and may increase feelings of failure.
Waiting for motivation to return tends to deepen withdrawal; gentle structured activity is part of treatment.
Cheerful advice minimizes the client's experience and can increase guilt for not being able to "cheer up."
takeaway: In depression, provide structure and simple, achievable activities, and make minor decisions for the client at first.

stem: The nurse is planning care for a client admitted in an acute manic episode who is hyperactive and easily distracted. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Assign a private room away from the busy dayroom.
Encourage the client to join a competitive volleyball game to use up energy.
Use brief, clear statements and apply unit limits consistently.
Offer to walk with the client or provide a solitary activity such as drawing.
Explain the reasons for each unit rule in a long one-to-one discussion.
Let the client stay in the dayroom watching television late into the night.
rationales: Correct. A low-stimulus environment reduces distraction and overstimulation that worsen manic behavior.
Incorrect. Competitive group games can increase excitement and conflict; solitary, noncompetitive activity is safer.
Correct. A client with flight of ideas and distractibility processes short, direct communication best, and consistent limits reduce manipulation and testing.
Correct. Noncompetitive activities that use large muscles or need little concentration channel energy safely.
Incorrect. Long explanations exceed the client's attention span and invite debate; rules should be stated briefly and simply.
Incorrect. Clients in mania need sleep and a quiet environment; late-night stimulation worsens hyperactivity and fatigue.
takeaway: For mania: reduce stimuli, keep communication brief and limits consistent, and offer solitary, noncompetitive activity.

stem: A client with schizophrenia approaches the nurse and says quietly, "The voices keep telling me to hurt my roommate before he hurts me." Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Tell the client that the voices are not real and cannot make the client do anything.
Ask whether the client intends to act on the voices, and keep the client under close observation away from the roommate.
Encourage the client to join the group activity to take attention away from the voices.
Ask the roommate whether the client has made threats before.
rationales: Stating that the nurse does not hear the voices can be helpful later, but arguing about whether they are real does not address the immediate risk of violence.

Command hallucinations to harm others are a safety emergency. The nurse assesses the risk of acting on the command and immediately protects the client and the roommate, then reports to the treatment team.
Distraction is a useful coping strategy for nonthreatening voices, but it does not address a command to harm a specific person.
This breaches the client's confidentiality and delays the needed safety actions; the risk is assessed with the client and the team.
takeaway: Command hallucinations to harm self or others take priority: assess intent to act, protect everyone at risk and notify the team.

stem: A client with schizophrenia stands by the unit door at lunchtime and tells the nurse, "I'm the governor's chief adviser, and I'm late for a meeting at the capitol." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "You're not the governor's adviser. You are a client in the hospital."
"Tell me more about the work you do as the governor's adviser."
"That sounds important to you. Right now it's lunchtime. Let's walk to the dining room together."
"I'll let the staff know you have a meeting so they can help you leave."
rationales: Directly arguing with a fixed false belief usually makes the client defend it more strongly and can damage trust.
Asking for details of the delusion reinforces it and keeps the conversation focused on unreality.
The nurse acknowledges the feeling behind the delusion without agreeing or arguing, then refocuses the client on a concrete, reality-based activity.
Going along with the delusion supports the false belief and is unsafe for a client who is not able to leave the unit.
takeaway: For delusions, do not argue or agree: acknowledge the feeling and redirect to reality-based topics or activities.

stem: A client with schizophrenia has a flat affect, says very little and has not showered in 4 days. The client sits in the dayroom most of the day. Which nursing approach is most likely to help the client complete hygiene?
options: Tell the client that other clients are complaining about the body odor.
Wait for the client to ask for a shower so the client keeps control over hygiene.
Complete the bath for the client so the task is done quickly.
Set out the supplies and give one simple direction at a time, staying with the client during the shower.
rationales: Shaming the client harms self-esteem and the therapeutic relationship and does not address the lack of motivation.
A client with avolition is unlikely to start the task alone; waiting leads to further self-neglect.
Doing the task for the client fosters dependence; the goal is to support the client in doing as much as possible independently.
Avolition and poor concentration are negative symptoms. Breaking the task into single steps and providing a supportive presence helps the client start and finish self-care.
takeaway: Negative symptoms (avolition, alogia, flat affect) respond to structure, simple one-step directions and supportive presence.

stem: A client with antisocial personality disorder tells the nurse at 2130, "The night nurse always lets me use the courtyard after 2100. You're the only one who makes a big deal about it." The unit rule is that the courtyard closes at 2100. Which response is best?
options: "The courtyard closes at 2100 for everyone. You can use it again tomorrow morning."
"I'll check with the night nurse, and if she agrees, I'll make an exception."
"Why do you keep trying to get around the rules on this unit?"
"Since you've behaved well today, you can have 10 more minutes this time."
rationales: Restating the limit calmly and briefly, and applying it the same way for all clients, is the most effective response to manipulation.
This lets the client play staff against one another and rewards manipulation; limits must be applied consistently.
A "why" question invites argument and debate rather than clearly maintaining the limit.
Bending the rule teaches the client that limits are negotiable and leads to more testing of staff.
takeaway: Respond to manipulation by restating the limit calmly and enforcing it consistently across all staff.

stem: The treatment team is developing a plan to set limits on a client with borderline personality disorder who repeatedly calls staff names during group sessions. Which elements of effective limit setting should the plan include? Select all that apply.
options: State the expected behavior clearly and in neutral terms.
Explain the specific consequence if the behavior continues.
Allow each nurse to decide whether to enforce the limit based on the client's mood.
